articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1710: Azov says its small UAVs have hit more than 100 Russian trains in occupied Donbas
articles.body:
Exclusive
Military
Drones have not killed tank: Ukrainian analyst says Operation Vivaldi shows NATO how to make armor work again. NATO war games convinced some that drones have made the tank obsolete, but Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi shows armor still works.
Azov says it struck more than 100 Russian trains in occupied Donbas in four months, in part thanks to donations. The Ukrainian military struck large diesel locomotives using small UAVs.
“We were told brigade couldn’t be saved”: Ukraine’s 125th grew its manning 430% and won back 1,500 absent soldiers in one year. Two pickups and a minibus: that was a whole Ukrainian brigade’s fleet a year ago.
Fire Point says its drones hit a Russian refinery’s diesel unit hours after WSJ reported Ukraine had paused such strikes under Trump’s pressure. Ukraine's General Staff has not commented, and the US midterms the pause was timed around are days away.
Intelligence and technology
US delays the Patriot missiles Ukraine needs against ballistic strikes but keeps sending older PAC-2s. Zelenskyy says Russia launched 100+ ballistic missiles at Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast in two weeks. Kyiv awaits decisions on Patriot interceptors.
“We need asymmetric effect,” Defense Minister Khmara says, as Ukraine funds its own missiles and radars to stop burning costly interceptors on cheap Russia’s drones. Also, Kyiv continues seeking solutions against Russian KABs.
Dozens of Russian drones fell to gun turrets over Kyiv in a month, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says. The ministry also credits turrets with 60+ targets in a private project—the figure it gave on 14 October for all private teams.
Another Russian “state-of-the-art” Su-57 fighter burned at Akhtubinsk, apparently without anyone shooting at it. A malfunction at engine start is the reported cause, leaving a burn scar visible from orbit and one fewer stealth jet in Russia’s small fleet.
Russia’s Geran-5 has hit 1,000 km/h in maneuvers, and Chinese engineers help develop some technical solutions for Russia’s drones. Ukrainian firms have shown jet interceptors but hit trouble with guidance, target lock, and scaling up, the adviser said.
Destinus says it now makes more cruise missiles a month than Europe did a year before 2022, but engines are what Ukraine’s strike programs are short of. The Dutch-headquartered company also says it expects to be able to meet Europe’s demand, including Ukraine’s, for 1.5-kilonewton-class cruise-missile engines from next year.
Shadows, roofs, job ads give Ukrainian arms plants away to Russian analysts, Ukrainian experts warn. In 2022, a pro-Russian Telegram channel posted the location of a Kyiv tank workshop. Russian missiles hit it two days later.
An armored capsule instead of an open platform: Ukraine develops an evacuation module for the Murakha UGV. The capsule is equipped with a camera featuring day and night channels and two-way audio communication to monitor the person’s condition.
International
The Pentagon wants NATO’s eastern flank to be quiet about Russia while Washington courts Moscow. Ukraine has already felt the same pressure, aimed at its strikes rather than its words.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russia used everything but nuclear weapons against civilians in Ukraine’s Kherson Oblast, its governor says. Drones strike up to 6,500 times weekly. 140,000 residents stay in Kherson.
Poland holds a suspect for stabbing two Ukrainians for their nationality, the latest case in a year of rising hate crimes against them. Both victims went to hospital with multiple wounds, and the 30-year-old man accused of attacking them had hidden in a forest before officers found him.
Ukrainian officials reach Russian-held Oleshky. The question now is where its residents can go. Agreement pages send residents who choose Ukraine through Russia and Belarus, and Ukraine's ombudsman is set to travel the same route.
Russian ballistic missiles kill a man in Kyiv, capping a day that left at least 27 civilians dead across Ukraine. The night also blacked out Dnipro, where people were still mourning the victims of the day before.
It was the only transport serving a village where more than 1,600 people still live: Russian forces strike a social bus with a drone in Bilenke, killing a woman and injuring other passengers. At the time of the attack, the bus was carrying a driver and 23 passengers, most of them elderly, the head of the humanitarian organization said.
Political and legal developments
“We have been killed”: Novaya Gazeta, the last major independent newsroom still working from inside Russia, closes after losing its Moscow office and its reader donations in the same week. The paper will shut down its servers on 9 November, and the Anna Politkovskaya museum in its offices will close with it.
The US is reviewing a request to lift sanctions on Russia’s state investment fund, run by Putin’s envoy. A US official called fund chief Kirill Dmitriev “a helpful envoy.” No decision has been announced.

articles.title: US delays the Patriot missiles Ukraine needs against ballistic strikes but keeps sending older PAC-2s
articles.body:
The US is delaying PAC-3 interceptors for Ukraine’s Patriot air defense systems while older PAC-2s keep arriving, a NATO source told Radio Svoboda on 29 October. PAC-3 is the Patriot missile built mainly to stop ballistic missiles.
The delay comes as Russia leans on ballistic missiles against the capital. In two weeks, Russia launched more than 100 at Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his 27 October evening address. “And above all, we do not have enough missiles for Patriots,” he added. On 29 October, Zelenskyy said Ukraine has intelligence that Russia is preparing new ballistic missile attacks. Kyiv is “awaiting the relevant decisions” on interceptor packages, “primarily for Patriots,” he said.
A question for politicians
The PAC-2s, used mostly against aircraft and cruise missiles, arrive through PURL, the NATO mechanism under which allies pay for US weapons for Ukraine. The PAC-3 delay is under discussion at a high political level, the NATO source said. It is unclear when the situation will change.
What Washington said before
On 20 October, Hegseth said in Wisconsin: “We haven’t changed our posture in any way toward the Ukrainians, but certainly with things like interceptors, we want to make sure our guys have the most possible as well.”

articles.title: U.S. clears sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine
articles.body:
- The U.S. State Department approved a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors to Ukraine on Oct. 30.
- Canada, Germany and Norway are funding part of the sale through JUMPSTART, with the rest financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE interceptors to Ukraine for its Patriot air defense systems, a package worth an estimated $2.1 billion that will be paid for entirely by Ukraine’s allies and partners. The department notified Congress of the decision on Oct. 30.
Canada, Germany and Norway are contributing donations through JUMPSTART, a U.S. Foreign Military Sales mechanism for donor-funded Ukraine purchases, and Ukraine will cover the rest with national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan. No U.S. funds are involved. Besides the missiles, the package includes classified and unclassified PAC-3 MSE spare parts and logistics and program support. Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor.
The notification is not a contract. It opens a congressional review period, after which Ukraine and the U.S. government can sign a letter of offer and acceptance and the U.S. Army can place the order with Lockheed Martin. The State Department gave no delivery schedule, and it did not say how the cost will be split among the three donors and the EU-financed share. Divided evenly, the total comes to about $4.2 million per missile, but that figure also covers spares and support.
The State Department said the missiles will help Ukraine sustain its existing Patriot operations against ongoing aerial threats, and that Ukraine will have no difficulty absorbing them into its armed forces. The sale will not require any additional U.S. government or contractor personnel in Ukraine.
The approval comes days after Ukrainian officials publicly pressed Washington on interceptor supplies. On Oct. 26, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had waited nearly a month for U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to sign off on missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS systems, including transfers from allied stocks that require U.S. approval. A day later, he told journalists that Ukraine had received an average of 12 Patriot interceptors a month from the United States in 2026, while Russia launches about 150 ballistic missiles a month that Ukraine needs to intercept.
PAC-3 MSE is the Patriot system’s main weapon against ballistic missiles. Unlike the older PAC-2 interceptors, which detonate a blast-fragmentation warhead near the target, the PAC-3 family destroys targets by direct impact, a method known as hit-to-kill. The Missile Segment Enhancement version adds a larger two-pulse solid rocket motor, with the second pulse firing late in the flight to extend range and altitude against maneuvering threats. That makes it the interceptor Ukraine relies on against Russian Iskander ballistic missiles and Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched missiles. Ukrainian officials have described PAC-3 as their only effective defense against Russian ballistic missiles.
Ukraine received its first Patriot battery in April 2023, and in May of that year Ukrainian crews shot down a Kinzhal over Kyiv, the first publicly confirmed combat interception of the missile. Ukraine has since received further batteries from the United States, Germany, the Netherlands and Romania, and in July 2025 Germany and Norway agreed to pay for three more systems to be bought from the U.S. manufacturer. Interceptor supply has been a tighter constraint than launchers. In February 2026, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius offered five PAC-3 rounds from German stocks if other allies together supplied 30 more, and in July, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said it was using about $1 billion from the EU loan to buy roughly 100 Patriot missiles.
The financing reflects how Ukraine’s air defense is now paid for. The U.S. Defense Security Cooperation Agency describes JUMPSTART as a channel that lets allies and partners finance Ukraine’s Foreign Military Sales cases with their own donations. Norway reported routing about NOK 10 billion through the mechanism in 2025, much of it for F-16 support. In September 2026, Canada said it would put about C$350 million toward air defense interceptors for Ukraine through JUMPSTART. Separately, NATO allies buy U.S. weapons for Ukraine through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, known as PURL.
EU governments agreed in early 2026 on a €90 billion loan for 2026 and 2027, with €60 billion set aside for defense, and the first disbursements went out in June 2026. The loan gives priority to weapons built in Ukraine, the EU and the European Economic Area, but allows purchases elsewhere when no European alternative exists. Patriot interceptors are one case where none does.
Production is the main limit on how fast the missiles can arrive. Lockheed Martin delivered 620 PAC-3 MSE interceptors in 2025, a company record. In January 2026, the company and the U.S. Department of War signed a seven-year framework agreement to raise annual output from about 600 to roughly 2,000. In April, the U.S. Army awarded Lockheed a $4.76 billion PAC-3 MSE contract, most of it funded through Foreign Military Sales customers. Demand has also climbed since the United States drew on its own Patriot inventory during this year’s conflict with Iran.
At 2025 production rates, the 500 missiles approved for Ukraine equal about 10 months of Lockheed’s output. Where Ukraine’s order falls in the production queue, and when the first missiles from this sale will reach Patriot batteries in Ukraine, has not been disclosed.

articles.title: Iran's Khamenei orders unrestricted response to threats
articles.body:
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned the United States and Israel against resuming attacks, ordering the country's armed forces to prepare for any renewed conflict and bring all US and Israeli assets within striking range.
The warnings come amid continuing tensions between Tehran and Washington, with diplomatic efforts to secure an agreement ongoing.
Other updates:
Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty expresses concern over the prospect of further escalation.
Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency reported that a drone attack south of Qeshm Island wounded two fishermen and left two missing.
Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted drones over Riyadh, Medina, Mecca and the Eastern Province, although Yemen’s Houthis denied targeting the kingdom.
Mideast leaders call for calm as fears mount of renewed war
Regional leaders called for calm Saturday as fears of a new escalation between the US, Israel and Iran grow.
On Saturday, Saudi Arabia's vice minister of foreign affairs said the message from the region is that it wants a return to peace. Speaking at a security forum in Bahrain, Waleed ElKhereiji told the audience that efforts were being made to prevent a military escalation and reach an agreement that ends the crisis with Iran.
“If you look at … the efforts that everybody is trying to do, the message is very clear. People in this part of the world want to bring peace back to the region," he said. But he said no one can predict the outcome of the efforts.
Concerns are rising about a return to an all-out Iran war.
Speaking at the same event, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said an escalation in the region would be extremely destructive.
“We are very confident that … the second round will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere,” he said.
Syria's Foreign Minister said Saturday that border security is a shared responsibility between his country and Jordan and that a high-level meeting is expected next month to discuss arrangements.
Speaking Saturday at the security forum in Bahrain, Assad al-Shibani said there are no “skirmishes” between the countries.
The announcement came after Jordanian strikes in Syria raised tensions between the neighbors.
Iran sets conditions for reopening Hormuz, resume talks
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said Tehran is prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz on its own terms, arguing that an agreement over the strategic waterway could pave the way for renewed negotiations with Washington.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Araghchi said Iran was demanding international recognition of a new shipping route agreed with Oman, alongside the closure of other routes through the strait.
He said Tehran's conditions also included lifting sanctions imposed after the Islamabad memorandum of understanding and reducing US military forces in the region.
Araghchi described Iran's proposal as the only plan currently on the table to restore shipping through the waterway, which has been heavily disrupted since the US-Israeli war on Iran began.
He added that mediators had presented proposals on the nuclear issue, which Tehran was reviewing.
While describing Washington's efforts to establish broader dialogue with Iran as a positive step, Araghchi said there were currently no plans to meet US officials.
He added that Tehran would decide whether future negotiations would be direct or indirect once Washington accepted its conditions.
Yemen's Foreign Minister Afrah Al-Zuba has condemned the Houthis' siege of Taiz as a war crime, accusing the group of exploiting residents' need for food, medicine and fuel to exert political pressure and blackmail, state news agency Saba reported.
Al-Zuba called for the immediate lifting of the siege and the permanent and safe reopening of roads leading into and out of the city.
Speaking during the third plenary session of the Manama Dialogue 2026 in Bahrain, the minister said ending the Houthis' attempted “coup” and restoring Yemen's state institutions was a collective responsibility shared by members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).
She stressed that lasting regional security could not be achieved without a safe and stable Yemen.
“The repercussions of the coup against the state have extended beyond Yemen’s borders, affecting the security of neighbouring countries, navigation, and international interests,” Al-Zuba said in her speech.
“This necessitates translating solidarity into practical steps to address the source of threats and to establish sustainable stability.”
Al-Zuba made history in July 2026 when she became Yemen's first female foreign minister.
Iran: Fishermen found after accusing US of attack in Hormuz
Iran said two fishermen it had reported missing on Saturday have now been found, following what it called a US attack on a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.
"Two fishermen from Qeshm, who had gone missing following an attack by the American enemy on their fishing boat this morning, have been found," state television said.
Earlier, state TV had cited a provincial official as saying that two fishermen had gone missing and two others were wounded in what he called an attack by the United States on their vessel in the crucial Hormuz waterway.
Jordan stops fighters attempting to enter from Syria
Jordanian border guards stopped a group of 14 armed individuals attempting to cross into northern Jordan from Syria, the armed forces said in a statement on Saturday.
The group tried to infiltrate on Friday under heavy fire and direct engagement, causing numerous casualties among the armed group, while the remaining members fled back into Syria, the armed forces said.
Oman said Friday it had rescued 25 sailors from a merchant ship set ablaze in an attack.
Muscat's navy "carried out an evacuation operation for 25 crew members of the merchant ship RITI, flying the Panamanian flag, after it was targeted, which led to a fire breaking out on board," Oman's Maritime Security Centre said in a statement.
The crew members were provided with medical care, the Omani statement said, without giving details.
Iran's supreme leader warns US against renewed attacks
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned the United States against resuming military attacks, saying Tehran will determine the timing and terms of any future conflict if its enemies launch further strikes.
In a statement, Khamenei also ordered Iran's armed forces to update their target list to bring “all US and Israeli assets, tangible and intangible” within striking range.
He said Iran would decide how and when any new conflict would end if its enemies resumed military or terrorist attacks.
He also called on the military to strengthen its intelligence capabilities and develop domestic defence capabilities, while ordering an increase in the production of ammunition and weapons for reconnaissance, support and combat operations.
Khamenei said Iran would decide how and when any new conflict would end if its enemies resumed military or terrorist attacks.
MOJTABA KHAMENEI [Getty]
Iran's army warns any new US attack would spread war wider
Iran's army warned Saturday that any new US attack would only spread their war wider, following threats by America and Israel of further military action as they hold crucial elections.
The Iranian warning comes with fresh diplomatic efforts underway to avert a resumption of fighting, with Qatari mediators in Tehran and US Vice President JD Vance reportedly sending a letter to Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei.
"If the US president once again embarks on more regional adventurism under pressure from, and in an attempt to appease, the Zionists, the flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area," Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said in a post on X, without elaborating.
Two fishermen missing after attack in Hormuz: Iran official
Two fishermen were missing and two others injured in an attack on two boats in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, an official said, blaming the United States for the incident.
"An attack by the American enemy occurred around 11:30 (0800 GMT) today on two fishing boats, each carrying two people, near Qeshm Island," said Ahmad Nafisi, deputy provincial governor of Hormozgan province, according to state TV.
"Two of those were transported to Qeshm and the other two remain missing while search and rescue operations are currently underway to locate them," he added.
Turkey nominates former FM in race for next UN chief
Turkey has officially nominated a former foreign minister and yearslong ambassador to the United Nations for the next UN secretary-general, state-run media reported Saturday.
The next UN chief will succeed António Guterres, who has led the world body for almost 10 years. The organization is under pressure to reform as it finds itself sidelined in wars in Iran, Ukraine and Gaza while also facing a financial crisis that has forced major cuts to humanitarian and development programs.
Feridun Sinirlioglu, a 70-year-old former Turkish foreign minister and UN diplomat, had floated his candidacy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly’s high-level meeting in New York last month.
Sinirlioglu was Turkey's top diplomat for a few months in 2015, an interim period between elections, and its UN ambassador between 2016 and 2023. He currently serves as the secretary-general of the Vienna-based Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
His current three-year mandate is scheduled to end in December 2027, but the top UN job would have a Jan. 1 start date.
Ahmet Yildiz, Turkey’s current representative to the UN, told the Anadolu news agency that Sinirlioglu's name was officially submitted with backing from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Erdogan has been vocal in calling for reform of the UN Security Council, especially criticizing the dominance of its five permanent members. Sinirlioglu is likely to reflect the president’s agenda.
The next U.N. secretary-general will be decided by the 15-nation UN Security Council, especially its five veto-wielding members — the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France. The 193-member General Assembly must give final approval.
OSCE Secretary General Feridun Sinirlioglu [Getty]
Syria weighing whether to enter Mecca pact: foreign minister
Syria's top diplomat on Saturday said Damascus was considering whether to join the Mecca alliance that binds Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in a Nato-style defence pact.
"Discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria's entry into the Mecca alliance," Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said during the IISS Manama Dialogue event in Bahrain.
Asaad Al-Shaibani [Getty]
US attacked fishing boats off Qeshm Island: official
Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, citing a Hormozgan province official, said on Saturday that the US attacked two fishing boats near Qeshm Island, leaving two fishermen missing and one wounded.
There was no immediate US confirmation of the attack.
Iran has warned of major retaliation if attacked again, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi threatening an “earth-shattering blow” as tensions across the region continue to escalate.
The latest warnings come amid renewed diplomatic efforts to secure a deal between Tehran and Washington, with Qatari mediators returning to Iran and Egypt voicing concern over another escalation.
Meanwhile, drone attacks have been reported off Iran’s Qeshm Island, while Saudi Arabia says it intercepted drones over Riyadh and several other regions.
Follow The New Arab for the latest developments as the Iran war continues to threaten regional stability.

The latest warnings come amid renewed diplomatic efforts to secure a deal between Tehran and Washington, with Qatari mediators returning to Iran and Egypt voicing concern over another escalation.
Meanwhile, drone attacks have been reported off Iran’s Qeshm Island, while Saudi Arabia says it intercepted drones over Riyadh and several other regions.

articles.title: “We need asymmetric effect,” Defense Minister Khmara says, as Ukraine funds its own missiles and radars to stop burning costly interceptors on cheap Russia’s drones
articles.body:
Ukraine is opening grant money for home-built air-to-air missiles and radars, aiming to shoot down Russia’s fastest drones without paying a huge price. The Defense Ministry, the Ministry of Digital Transformation, and the Brave1 defense-tech cluster are launching the competitions, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara announced in an address to manufacturers, adding that a grant contest for turbojet engines will follow.
Ukraine is being forced to use expensive air defense missiles against relatively inexpensive Russian drones and cruise missiles. Developing cheaper interceptors, domestically produced radars and engines could change the economics of warfare.
The move comes as Russia leans harder on faster, jet-powered drones that strain the cheapest layer of Ukraine’s defenses. It also follows an earlier round of Brave1 grants that had already flagged anti-bomb systems and Ukrainian radars as priorities.
What Kyiv wants built, from navigation to radars that see the faint targets
Khmara laid out the threats the money is meant to answer: ballistic missiles, cheap cruise missiles, high-speed drones and guided bombs.
From Ukrainian producers, the ministry wants domestic navigation systems, stronger electronic warfare, radars able to pick out low-signature targets, and affordable designs that can be developed in quantity.
“Our requirements are clear: effectiveness, affordable cost, interoperability between systems, and sufficient volume of supply,” Khmara says.
The grants are one tool among others, meant to carry developments that can later scale for the Security and Defense Forces. Earlier, the ministry and Brave1 ran a large-scale test of drones with AI-assisted targeting.
The next contest targets the guided bombs Ukraine still cannot reliably stop
The minister singled out a separate job for manufacturers: new ways to counter Russia’s guided aerial bombs, known in Ukraine as KABs, and to blunt their use.
These are the glide bombs Russian aircraft release from a distance, and Ukraine has struggled to answer them without reaching the launch aircraft themselves.
“It is important to create innovative solutions that let us act ahead and prevail. We need asymmetric effect. We need technologies that change the rules of the game in our favor,” he argues.
Grants for turbojet engines, the ministry says, are the next step after the missiles and radars.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia strikes Dnipro railway station again, day after attack killed 15
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russia strikes Dnipro railway station again, day after attack killed 15
Key developments on Oct. 30:
- Russia strikes Dnipro railway station again, day after attack killed 15
- Evacuation convoys from Russian-occupied Oleshky split toward Ukraine and Russia, officials say
- Ukraine destroys Iskander-M missile launcher in Russia's Kursk Oblast, General Staff says
- Russia has damaged more than 800 Ukrainian energy assets since September
- Russian deputy PM confirms strikes on 3 refineries, gas-chemical complex
Russian forces launched new strikes on the railway station in Dnipro on Oct. 30, Ukrainian Railways (Ukrzaliznytsia) reported.
Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said that a fire had broken out at the station and that a woman had been injured.
The station came under attack for the second day in a row, after a Russian drone strike on Oct. 29 killed 15 people and injured 14 others.
Ukrzaliznytsia said an evacuation had been announced ahead of the strikes. The company added that areas for extended stays had been set up in the station's underground facilities to accommodate passengers sheltering from the attacks.
Ukrzaliznytsia warned that trains arriving in and departing from Dnipro could face significant delays due to repeated Russian attacks on the station and locomotives.
read also
Evacuation convoys from Russian-occupied Oleshky split toward Ukraine and Russia, officials say
Evacuation convoys carrying residents of Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast have separated, with some heading toward Ukrainian-controlled territory and others toward Russia, Ukrainian and Russian officials said on Oct. 30.
Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said he was continuing to personally coordinate the humanitarian mission and was heading back to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Earlier, Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova said that buses carrying evacuees had reached Armiansk in Russian-occupied Crimea, where they were to split into two convoys.
The Ukrainian delegation had traveled to Oleshky via Anapa in Russia's Krasnodar Krai, from where they reportedly flew to Belarus before continuing by bus to Ukrainian-controlled territory, David Arakhamia, head of President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary faction, said earlier on Oct. 30.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion. Located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, the city has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, which have prevented humanitarian aid from reaching residents.
Residents have faced severe shortages of food, water, and electricity. Mined roads and constant drone attacks have made safe evacuation virtually impossible, and civilians trying to flee on the only roads in and out of the city have frequently been targeted by drones.
Despite efforts by the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and even Pope Leo XIV, a ceasefire agreement has only come about since the intervention of Melania Trump.
Twenty-five buses with a combined capacity of 750 passengers, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility, had been prepared to evacuate residents from Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, Lubinets said.
Lubinets's statement came amid reports that Russia had begun evacuating residents ahead of the agreed date.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to leave safely. At the same time, those who have decided to stay can stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian support," Lubinets said.
Lubinets and Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova held a joint press briefing in Armiansk, Russian-occupied Crimea, ahead of the evacuation from Oleshky.
Lubinets said the Ukrainian and Russian delegations were accompanied by media representatives from three countries. However, photos published by Ukraine's Ombudsman's Office show predominantly Russian media outlets.
Around 11:30 a.m. Kyiv time, the Ukrainian delegation had safely reached Oleshky, and the ceasefire had been in effect for 80 hours and was still holding, Lubinets said.
Lubinets added that he was speaking with local residents to hear about their needs and understand what kind of assistance they required most.
Arakhamia said around noon that humanitarian aid had been delivered to Oleshky and that "technical support" was being provided to those wishing to evacuate.
Lantratova also confirmed on social media that the evacuation from Oleshky had begun, with people gradually boarding buses. She added that some residents wanted to travel to Russia, while others wished to go to Ukrainian-controlled territory, without specifying how many people were in each group.
Following the separation of the convoys, Lubinets proposed making humanitarian missions coordinated by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump a regular initiative, saying the operation in Oleshky demonstrated that such agreements could help civilians.
read also
Ukraine destroys Iskander-M missile launcher in Russia's Kursk Oblast, General Staff says
Ukrainian forces struck an Iskander-M missile launcher in Russia's Kursk Oblast, along with several ammunition depots and repair facilities in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories between Oct. 29 and Oct. 30, the General Staff said.
Ukraine struck the missile launcher near the town of Fatezh, at a site used to reload ballistic missiles, the General Staff said.
The Iskander-M is a short-range ballistic missile system that Russia uses to attack Ukrainian cities. During its overnight attack on Oct. 30, Russia launched ballistic missiles from Voronezh, Kursk, and Bryansk oblasts as part of a combined assault that mainly targeted Kyiv, Poltava, and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts, Ukraine's Air Force said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 5 that Ukrainian forces would prioritize strikes on Russian missile launchers as Moscow steps up its use of ballistic missiles. Zelensky also said international deliveries of air-defense interceptors to Ukraine had fallen threefold from 2025 levels.
Ukraine's military also reported strikes on Russian ammunition depots in the occupied parts of Donetsk, Kharkiv, and Luhansk oblasts.
Ukrainian forces hit several other Russian military targets in occupied Luhansk Oblast, including a logistics depot near Bilovodsk, a repair unit near Rubizhne, and a repair and recovery base near Pysarivka, the General Staff said on Oct. 30.
The General Staff did not specify which weapons were used in the strikes.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the extent of the damage.
Zelensky said on Oct. 29 that Ukraine had carried out two missile strikes, destroying an Iskander-M missile launcher and two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets.
On Oct. 29, Ukraine's Navy also struck two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets at the Marinovka military airfield in Russia's Volgograd Oblast using domestically produced Neptune missiles, the Navy reported.

Russia has damaged more than 800 Ukrainian energy assets since September
Russia has carried out more than 350 attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure since September, damaging more than 800 pieces of equipment, Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said on Friday.
The strikes are increasing pressure on the country’s power system as the heating season approaches. Ukraine is stepping up efforts to protect energy facilities while expanding generation capacity to reduce the impact of further attacks on an already crippled system after years of Russian missile and drone attacks.
Speaking during a question-and-answer session with the government in parliament, Shmyhal said the damaged equipment included facilities at substations and power generation sites.
He said a second level of physical protection had been built for 235 transformers. According to the minister, only one piece of protected equipment had been hit by a ballistic missile over the past six months.
"Without this protection, restoring energy facilities under the current intensity of Russian attacks would take months," Shmyhal said.
Alongside protecting existing infrastructure, Ukraine is working to expand its electricity generation capacity through smaller, decentralized power plants.
On Oct. 29, the government approved the mechanism and terms for providing almost Hr 939 million ($20 million) in loan financing from the Finnish-Ukrainian Investment Fund to state-owned energy company Ukrnafta.
The funding will support four projects to install gas-engine power plants in the western Ivano-Frankivsk and Lviv oblasts, adding around 60 megawatts of capacity to Ukraine’s power system, Shmyhal reported.
The money will cover the purchase of the power plants and related equipment, as well as installation, testing and commissioning. The loans were raised for Ukraine’s state budget under a framework agreement between the Ukrainian and Finnish governments signed in November 2024.
The projects are part of broader efforts to develop distributed generation, spreading electricity production across multiple locations rather than relying solely on large power plants.

Russian deputy PM confirms strikes on 3 refineries, gas-chemical complex
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Ukraine had attacked three Russian oil refineries and a gas-chemical complex on Oct. 30, Russian state news agency TASS reported.
"Today, there was another attack on Russian refineries, four processing plants. More precisely, three refineries and one gas-chemical complex. There was minor damage at one plant, but overall, our defense system, the air defense system, worked," Novak said, without specifying the locations of the facilities.
"We had a brief pause, but today, attacks on refineries have resumed, and our facilities are working to protect themselves," he added.
Kyiv had not commented on the reported strike at the time of publication.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the footage or establish the extent of the damage.
Earlier, a fire broke out at the Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery in Russia's Samara Oblast overnight on Oct. 30.
The Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ published photos and videos submitted by local residents that appear to show fires burning in the area around the refinery, alongside reports of drones flying overhead.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point said Ukrainian forces used its FP-1 drones to strike the Novokuybyshevsk refinery, with multiple hits reported across the facility, including its diesel hydrotreating unit.
Schemes, an investigative journalism project by Radio Free Europe's Ukrainian service, shared a satellite image of the Novokuybyshevsk refinery taken on Oct. 30. The image shows a large fire still burning at the facility, with thick black smoke covering much of the surrounding area.
"We are repelling an attack by the Ukrainian Armed Forces on our territory. Air defense and mobile fire teams are operating. Remain calm and remain in a safe place," Samara Oblast Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said.
The governor did not specify which facilities in the city were targeted.
Fedorishchev later said that two people died in Samara Oblast while clearing up the aftermath of the drone attack.
Monitoring channels have described the reported attack as a "resumption of strikes," as it appears to be the first such attack following an unofficial pause in Ukraine's campaign against Russian oil refineries that began in mid-October.

articles.title: Avenger Air Defense Missiles Deployed Near Trump’s Mar-a-Lago Resort
articles.body:
Avenger surface-to-air missile systems have been deployed on a floating barge near US President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida amid warnings from the US Secret Service of an “elevated threat” environment, The Telegraph reported.
Photographs published by the Palm Beach Daily News showed two Avenger air defense platforms positioned on a barge moored in the waters adjacent to the presidential estate in Palm Beach. The deployment reflects an extraordinary escalation in domestic protective security protocols surrounding the US head of state.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The US Secret Service operates in an elevated threat environment, and we continuously adapt our security posture by integrating the most advanced capabilities, technologies, and methodologies to ensure the safety of our protectees,” a Secret Service spokesperson told The Telegraph.
Mounted on armored High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicles (Humvees), the AN/TWQ-1 Avenger system utilizes short-range FIM-92 Stinger surface-to-air missiles alongside an M3P .50-caliber machine gun, engineered specifically to intercept low-altitude aerial threats, including cruise missiles, fixed-wing aircraft, and loitering unmanned aerial vehicles.
Avenger units were previously spotted providing perimeter air defense in August while Trump was golfing at his club in Bedminster, New Jersey.
Federal court filings
The air defense positioning coincides with efforts by federal authorities to establish permanent flight restrictions over the Palm Beach estate.
Trump Criticizes Russia Sanctions Calls, Citing Hubbard Release
While temporary flight restrictions (TFRs) are standardly enacted by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) during presidential visits, federal court filings submitted by the Secret Service indicate the agency is seeking permanent airspace prohibitions around Mar-a-Lago.
The filings cite adverse intelligence regarding threat matrices, specifically referencing prospective terrorist threats and aerial intrusion vectors.
The Secret Service, tasked with protecting high-level US officials including the president and vice president, reported earlier this year that documented threats against its protectees surged by 40 percent compared to the prior year.
In court documents supporting the permanent airspace ban, Secret Service Deputy Director Matthew Quinn characterized the operational threat profile as “heightened, real, and dynamic.”
“The airborne threat vector at Mar-a-Lago is persistent and substantial. As the location of a primary residence of the president, from which he frequently conducts the business of the government’s highest office, that threat vector must be mitigated to the extent possible whether he is in residence or not,” Quinn stated in the legal filing.
Armed conflict with Iran and heightened threat environment
Security analysts assess that the active armed conflict between the US and the Islamic Republic of Iran represents a primary catalyst for the heightened protective perimeter, alongside past domestic assassination attempts targeting Trump.
The escalation in physical security comes amid open indications from the White House regarding further military action in the Middle East. Speaking at a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Oct. 23, Trump suggested that Washington could execute follow-on strikes against Tehran, referencing prior combat missions.
“We may do another little Epic Fury,” Trump told supporters, invoking the operational code name associated with US kinetic operations against Iranian military assets.
The regional conflict with Iran has also fueled diplomatic friction between Washington and Kyiv over energy security. Trump administration officials have linked domestic US retail diesel price inflation to Ukrainian long-range drone interdictions against Russian oil refineries, using the price pressures to justify bilateral diesel arrangements with Moscow.
President Volodymyr Zelensky rejected that rationale in an interview on The Diary of a CEO podcast, emphasizing that international fuel benchmark volatility stems directly from maritime bottlenecks in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz caused by hostilities with Iran.
Zelensky has also highlighted deepening defense-industrial collaboration between Moscow and Tehran, stating during an Oct. 20 press conference in Oslo that Ukrainian intelligence identified evidence of Russian drone deliveries and space-based satellite reconnaissance provided to Iranian forces.

articles.title: US approves $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine amid delayed missile deliveries
articles.body:
The US State Department said on Friday it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, in what would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since the start of the second Trump administration.
Ukraine will pay for the interceptor missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US JUMPSTART, along with national funds financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan, the State Department said in a statement.
The program uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defense following Russia's invasion, according to a Pentagon website.
Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia's military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.
On Thursday, a Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while five died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed one person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.
Delayed missile deliveries strain US-Ukraine relationship
Delayed missile deliveries have added to Ukraine's tensions with the US after US President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticized Zelensky for Ukraine's unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies, as Russia stepped up attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure.
Ukraine will not receive the missile interceptors quickly.
Weapons sales typically take years to fulfill, but given Ukraine's urgent need for defensive weapons, these Patriot missiles may move to Kyiv on a faster timeline.
The JUMPSTART program was used in August to buy 3,350 air-launched cruise missiles worth $825 million made by Zone 5 Technologies and CoAspire.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defense and precision-guided weapons.
Lockheed Martin to increase production of Patriot interceptors
In July, the US Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to $58.6 billion to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.
Lockheed has said that deal would allow it to follow through on a promise to triple PAC-3 MSE production capacity by the end of 2030 and increase jobs at its Camden, Arkansas, plant by 50%, to about 1,850 from 1,200. Lockheed previously announced Patriot PAC-3 missile interceptor production would go to 2,000 units annually.
Pentagon negotiators are pressing contractors to move much faster, with tentative production agreements struck earlier this year at the center of efforts to increase missile output.

articles.title: Newly Approved $2.1B Patriot Missile Sale Faces Post-2030 Delivery
articles.body:
A newly approved $2.1 billion US sale of 500 Patriot surface-to-air interceptors to Ukraine will not see deliveries begin until after 2030, according to diplomatic sources, prompting urgent appeals from Kyiv to secure immediate transfers from existing allied stockpiles ahead of winter.
Radio Liberty correspondent Alex Raufoglu reported, citing informed sources, that the newly contracted Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (PAC-3 MSE) munitions represent newly manufactured weapons rather than drawdowns from current American inventories.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“As sources inform me, these are new missiles, with deliveries not expected until after 2030,” Raufoglu stated. “This does virtually nothing to resolve the acute deficit of interceptors in Ukraine ahead of winter.”
Raufoglu added that bilateral negotiations have yet to secure an agreement for joint coproduction within Ukraine, noting that the Pentagon remains engaged in an extended review regarding whether to grant Kyiv manufacturing licenses for the advanced interceptors.
UPDATE!!   The U.S. Patriot PAC-3 announcement comes with a major caveat: these are new missiles, with deliveries not expected until after 2030, sources tell me.
It does little to address Ukraine’s urgent interceptor shortage ahead of winter
1/3 https://t.co/Awmu2unUMS
— Alex Raufoglu (@ralexdc) October 30, 2026
Zelensky urges stockpile swaps to bridge acute pre-winter gap
The extended delivery schedule addresses a bottleneck in Ukraine’s integrated air defense architecture. While the Trump administration authorized the Foreign Military Sale on Friday, Oct. 30, the multi-year production horizon leaves Ukrainian air defense brigades without immediate reinforcements as Russian forces intensify ballistic strikes against municipal power grids.
Pentagon Says Ukraine’s Patriot Missile Production Request Requires ‘Further Review’
President Volodymyr Zelensky responded to the State Department announcement late Friday, welcoming the strategic approval while emphasizing the stark mismatch between long-term procurement horizons and immediate survival requirements.
“It has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelensky wrote on X.
“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors.”
To prevent catastrophic power grid failures, Zelensky proposed an operational swap framework under which Washington and European allies would immediately transfer PAC-3 MSE missiles from active national inventories, later replenishing their own arsenals with the factory-fresh munitions rolling off assembly lines under the $2.1 billion contract.
Kyiv has requested an emergency winter allocation providing 100 PAC-3 interceptors per month to establish a reliable defensive shield against Russian ballistic barrages. Ukrainian government data shows that during the final two weeks of October alone, Russian tactical and strategic forces executed more than 30 coordinated strikes against critical electricity generation and transmission infrastructure.
Zelensky stressed that 500 interceptors delivered in the near term would transform Ukraine’s airspace defense, arguing that Western partners possess sufficient reserves to execute immediate drawdowns without compromising their baseline defensive postures.
Defense-industrial bottlenecks
The State Department’s formal notification to Congress authorizes the possible sale of up to 500 PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles alongside telemetry kits, spare parts, ground support equipment, and associated logistical services. The transaction remains subject to standard statutory congressional review before formal procurement contracts can be signed.
The production backlog reflects an industry-wide challenge facing Western defense manufacturers, where surging international demand has outstripped available manufacturing capacity.
The PAC-3 MSE, manufactured by primary defense contractor Lockheed Martin, constitutes one of the few Western weapon systems capable of defeating Russian 9M723 ballistic missiles fired by the Iskander-M system, alongside air-launched Kinzhal aero-ballistic weapons.
Lockheed Martin has initiated major capital investments to ease supply chain friction and expand production outside the US. Dan Tenney, the company’s senior vice president for global business development and strategy, previously disclosed to Kyiv Post that the defense contractor is investing up to $9 billion through 2030 to fortify tier-one supply chains, eliminate sub-tier production bottlenecks, and establish overseas assembly lines with allied nations.
However, because expanded manufacturing nodes will require years to achieve full-rate output, Ukrainian defense planners caution that long-term procurement authorizations cannot substitute for immediate munition transfers, leaving frontline cities vulnerable to pre-winter infrastructure interdiction unless partner nations release existing ammunition stocks.

articles.title: Iran lawmakers call for withdrawal from NPT: Will we have war or peace?
articles.body:
Iran lawmakers call for withdrawal from NPT: Will we have war or peace?
Withdrawal from the nuclear treaty doses not mean that Iran would build a nuclear weapon, observers say.
Several Iranian lawmakers have called for the country’s withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), as United States President Donald Trump says the war on Iran will be “wrapped up” soon.
The lawmakers’ demands come as Qatari mediators returned to Tehran this week to mediate peace talks with the US.
Before the US and Israel’s war on Iran began on February 28, Washington and Tehran had already been engaging in indirect nuclear negotiations mediated by Oman. Iran had also stated on numerous occasions that it had no plans to develop nuclear weapons.
Trump has also repeatedly stated that Iran “cannot have a nuclear weapon”, making it a non-negotiable condition for ending the ongoing conflict and securing a permanent deal.
Iran, however, has demanded certain conditions be met before it will talk again about its nuclear programme – including an end to the US naval blockade of its ports in and around the Strait of Hormuz, the lifting of sanctions and a guarantee there will be no more attacks.
The war, which is entering its ninth month, has upended global energy and financial markets with the closure of Hormuz.
On Friday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi hit back at Friedrich Merz after the German chancellor said the war on Iran has added more than 100 billion euros ($112bn) to Europe’s energy costs.
In a post on X, Araghchi noted that Merz had “hailed” the US and Israel’s attacks on Iran in June of last year, when he said: “This is the dirty work Israel is doing for all of us.”
The Iranian foreign minister then warned that any renewed attacks could come at a far higher cost for Europe.
“100bn Euro is nothing compared to the Earth-shattering blow Iran’s Powerful Armed Forces will deal against those who dare harm our people,” Araghchi wrote. “Red lines are a thing of the past,” he added.
Could Iran withdraw from the NPT, and what would that mean for diplomatic efforts to end the war?
Here’s what we know:
Which Iranian lawmakers are calling for withdrawal from the NPT, and why?
On Saturday, Iranian legislator Mahmoud Nabavian called for Iran to withdraw from the NPT and change its nuclear doctrine, adding to similar demands from other lawmakers and public figures.
“Now that we have paid the heavy costs of war and sanctions, it is time for the Iranian nation to withdraw from the NPT treaty and change the nuclear doctrine,” he wrote on X.
In parliament, Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said 10 proposals to withdraw from the treaty had been registered, and withdrawal was under consideration, according to the Fars news agency.
Mohammad Javad Haj Ali Akbari, an Iranian politician and scholar, also called for a review of Iran’s nuclear doctrine, describing it as a “national demand” during his sermon on Friday, state broadcaster IRIB reported.
He said the demand was not a hasty or emotional reaction, but reflected Iranians’ awareness of what he described as US failures to honour commitments.
Separately, in a report earlier this week, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported calls for Iran to withdraw from the NPT and accused the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) of becoming politically aligned with the US and Israel.
Last month, an IAEA resolution expressed “grave concerns” about Iran’s “continued noncompliance” with its obligations under the NPT, to which it is a signatory.
But the IAEA has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since the US and Israel launched a 12-day war against the country in June 2025, which included attacks on key Iranian nuclear sites, such as the Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan facilities.
Iran has condemned the IAEA resolution, calling it baseless and politically motivated.
What is the NPT?
The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons is a landmark international treaty aimed at preventing the spread of nuclear weapons and promoting peaceful uses of nuclear energy.
It was opened for signature on July 1, 1968, and entered into force on March 5, 1970. The treaty was negotiated by the US, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom.
Under the NPT, nuclear-weapon states agree not to transfer nuclear weapons or assist non-nuclear-weapon states in developing them.
Non-nuclear-weapon states also agree not to seek or acquire nuclear weapons.
The treaty views nuclear-weapon states as those which manufactured and tested a nuclear weapon or other nuclear device before January 1, 1967. Those countries are the US, UK, France, China and Russia. The treaty also paves a path for these original nuclear weapons powers to phase out their arsenals.
A total of 191 countries are now part of the treaty. Non-signatories include India, Pakistan, Israel and South Sudan.
The treaty supports the right of all signatories to access nuclear technology for peaceful purposes under safeguards overseen by the United Nations nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
Among the 11 articles of the treaty, one allows a country to withdraw with three months’ notice “if it decides that extraordinary events … have jeopardised the supreme interests of its country”.
Iran signed the NPT in July 1968 and ratified it in February 1970 as a nonnuclear-weapon state.
It has since stated consistently that its nuclear programme is for peaceful purposes and research only. The IAEA has conducted inspections under the treaty’s safeguards system.
Has there been any response from Iran’s leaders?
Iranian leaders have not yet responded to demands from lawmakers to withdraw from the NPT.
But on October 24, according to Iranian media reports, the Paydari Front, a hardline faction aligned with conservative groups, also called on parliament to withdraw from the NPT.
Withdrawal from the NPT would not automatically mean that Iran would build a nuclear weapon. Officially, the Iranian government’s position on not seeking nuclear arms remains unchanged.
In June, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs noted that lawmakers are preparing a bill to withdraw Tehran from the NPT.
“In light of recent developments, we will take an appropriate decision,” ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei had said at a news conference. “[The] government has to enforce parliament bills, but such a proposal is just being prepared, and we will coordinate in the later stages with parliament.”
But Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian has said Tehran’s policies align with Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei’s longstanding religious edict against weapons of mass destruction. “The Zionist regime is the only possessor of weapons of mass destruction in the region,” Baghaei had said, referring to the Israeli government.
What has Trump said about ‘wrapping up’ the war?
The US President has repeatedly stated that Iran “cannot have a nuclear weapon” and made this a non-negotiable condition for ending the ongoing conflict and securing a permanent deal.
In a speech at Daytona Beach, Florida late on Friday, he brought up Iran several times and repeated claims about destroying its navy and air force. “We are never going to give them a nuclear weapon,” he said.
Trump also denied that the US had started the war, saying, “This was a war they started many years ago,” and “Iran has been waging war on America since 1979.″
Separately, in an interview with Kansas City radio station KCMO on Friday, he said the war is “going to get wrapped up soon” but said Washington needs “a guarantee there’ll never be a nuclear weapon”.
Mohamed Elmenshawy, a Washington-based analyst, told Al Jazeera that Trump wants to end the standoff with Iran “whether through peace or war as quickly as possible”, and may launch new attacks after the November 3 midterm elections.
“What breaks this state of stalemate, this condition of ‘no peace, no war’, is either achieving some progress in the negotiating track, or the attacks beginning anew,” Elmenshawy told Al Jazeera.
He said Trump believes “time is on his side”, pointing to “strict economic pressure” on Iran, including the US naval blockade that has curtailed Tehran’s ability to export oil as well as sanctions on Iranian aviation and land border closures by several other countries.
Elmenshawy said Tehran “must realise” Trump will not let the conflict “remain suspended like this” and that this pressure should push “the Qatari and Pakistani mediators to drive the efforts more forcefully in order to avoid the path of war”.
Trump faces “pressure from the Israeli side to launch the attacks, and opposite pressure from the Arab Gulf side to push the negotiating track”, he added, saying Trump, “whose next moves cannot be predicted”, could yield to either.
On Saturday, the spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Mohammad Akraminia, sent a warning to US President Donald Trump, writing on X that its armed forces are “closely monitoring America’s movements in the region”.
Akraminia said that if the US president “resorts to another adventure in the region” along with Israel, then Iran will retaliate significantly.
“There is no doubt that the flames of war will engulf a much wider area, and the end of the conflict will not be in his [Trump’s] hands,” Akraminia wrote.
“Given the US President’s track record of betraying diplomacy,” and citing Trump’s “distrustful” nature, Akraminia said the IRGC’s armed forces are “relentlessly enhancing their combat readiness”.
What was the position before the war began?
Before the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28 this year, Tehran and Washington were in active nuclear negotiations.
At talks in Geneva, mediator Oman said both countries had made “significant progress”.
Just one day before the US-Israeli attacks started, Oman’s foreign minister said Iran had agreed to reduce its nuclear stockpiles to “the lowest level possible”. Then the war began.
Almost eight months later, the war has brought this position no further forward.
In fact, more problems, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz upending global energy markets and most recently, the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia locking horns, have threatened the Middle East’s regional stability.
Furthermore, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera in September that Iran no longer trusts negotiations with Washington because attacks had come during previous rounds of talks.
Christopher Featherstone, associate lecturer at the Department of Politics and International Relations at the University of York in the UK, told Al Jazeera that the war has set the potential for negotiations all the way back to square one, and it will take significant diplomatic effort to initiate any meaningful negotiations, let alone achieve success in those negotiations.
“Intermediaries will be cautious about being seen to be too close to the US if the conflict reignites, and Iran has shown a strong willingness to reject a ‘deal’ that would favour the Trump administration too heavily,” he said.
What diplomatic efforts are happening to de-escalate the war?
On Friday morning, Qatari mediators, in coordination with US officials, returned to Tehran in an apparent bid to revive the June ceasefire that quickly fell apart over control of the Strait of Hormuz.
Days earlier, they delivered a letter from US Vice President JD Vance to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, proposing renewed peace talks, according to US media.
Iranian sources have confirmed to Al Jazeera that Tehran received a letter from the US on ending the war and suggested the Qatari delegation had come to collect Iran’s response.
The sources said a meeting to discuss a new diplomatic path could be held within a week, either in Doha or Istanbul.
Meanwhile, Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, spokesman for Pakistan’s military, told the Reuters news agency his country is “cautiously optimistic” about mediation efforts between Iran and the US as regional countries seek to revive a ceasefire in the eight-month-old war.
He suggested on Friday that there were positive signs in attempts to de-escalate the conflict. His comments to Reuters were the first since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.
Ali al-Sari, a former member of Iran’s parliament, said there are positive indications from both Tehran and Washington on the diplomatic track, despite a military buildup on both sides.
“The response has not been clear so far, but there are indications on the Iranian side, and also in my view on the American side, that the signs are somewhat positive rather than negative,” al-Sari told Al Jazeera.
He said the US is reinforcing its military buildup, while Iran is strengthening its forces “in the Strait of Hormuz and along the borders”. He added that “the coincidence of this message with the Qatari mediation is significant.
“For this reason, Tehran is studying its response carefully and has not rushed, but it wants something in return, even amid a tense situation between the two parties,” he said.
He pointed to the repeated visits of the Qatari delegation, which “came, then returned, then came again”. In his view, this suggests that the Qatari mediation and other mediation efforts, including Russia’s mediation, mean coordination with the US is continuing and is a “positive sign”. Al-Sari also highlighted the US ambassador to Turkiye Tom Barrack’s recent comments that the US and Iran are “very close” to a deal to de-escalate tensions.
Is peace or renewal of war more likely after the US midterm elections?
Currently, Washington and Tehran have sent mixed signals about whether the eight-month war is heading back to full-scale attacks or towards a peace deal.
On Thursday, the head of US Central Command (CENTCOM), Admiral Brad Cooper, briefed US President Donald Trump on options for renewed attacks on Iran, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported.
The Wall Street Journal also reported that Trump was briefed on options for renewed attacks on Thursday. On the same day, US Senator Chris Murphy said he had been briefed on the war plan and described it as “insane”.
Separately, US media reported that Washington has warned Gulf allies to prepare for potential military action after the November 3 midterm elections.
“There has been little signal from either side of a move to a formal peace, but there is the potential for another cautious temporary ceasefire,” Featherstone said.
“After the midterm elections, if Trump loses both Houses, he will be severely limited in his ability to pursue his domestic agenda. This could push him to be more active on the international stage, and the Iran conflict would likely be a focus for his attention,” he added.
“However, he has set out almost no sign of how he would measure victory or success in this war, so a path out of the conflict is incredibly unclear,” he said.
Abas Aslani, a researcher at the Center for Middle East Strategic Studies in Tehran, said a deep lack of trust lies behind Iran’s failure to respond to the US proposals it has received.
“Washington wants Iran to make concessions on the nuclear issue in advance, but Iran insists on the seven conditions,” Aslani told Al Jazeera, referring to Tehran’s seven-point plan to end the war.
“In Iran, they fear that if they commit and fulfil their obligations, the United States will not honour its obligations and will backtrack. Instead, the United States would launch another attack.”
He noted that Trump is “trying to use this potential agreement to promote it to the public and to use it for electoral purposes in the United States”, while “Iran wants an agreement that will be vital and bring peace to the region.”
Aslani said “the conditions and the sequencing” also remain in dispute.
Iran is using mediators to send a message “that its position has not changed”, he said, but Washington “also insists on its position”.
“We don’t see any tangible progress – but despite this, efforts are still ongoing,” he added.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy praises US over $2.1bn Patriot missile deal but warns it could take years
articles.body:
The US has approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1bn, but Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned deliveries could take years and stockpiles were needed now to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.
“The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capabilities,” the US state department said in a statement on Friday.
The statement did not provide an estimate for when the weapons could be delivered to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision by the US state department” but said in a post on X early on Saturday: “However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS. We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors.
“Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day.”
Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.
On Thursday, a Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while five died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed 1 person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.
Zelenskyy said US and European allies had sufficient stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to provide to Ukraine now, which could be replenished in the coming years through contracts already paid for by Ukraine and its partners.
He said this would “be the right approach” and was “entirely feasible”.
Delayed missile deliveries have added to Kyiv’s tensions with Washington after US president Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Zelenskyy for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will probably not receive the missile interceptors quickly. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles – which are yet to be manufactured – are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense was encouraging the Pentagon to bring forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US Jumpstart, along with national funds financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan, the state department said in a statement.
The programme uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defence following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defense and precision-guided weapons.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Germany is accelerating military preparations amid the threat of a possible Russian attack on the Baltic states - media
articles.body:
Germany is accelerating military preparations amid the threat of a possible Russian attack on the Baltic states - media
Kyiv • UNN
More than 70 generals assessed the defense of the Baltic states and urged NATO to prepare more quickly for a confrontation with Russia. Germany plans to reinforce its troops and stockpiles.
More than 70 generals and senior officers from Germany and the Netherlands visited Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania to assess potential combat areas on the border with Russia. The military leadership believes that NATO needs to accelerate preparations for a possible military confrontation. Die Welt reports this, UNN writes.
Details
According to the publication, since Tuesday, military leaders from both countries have been visiting border areas with Russia. The trip, which was largely organized in secret, is being called unprecedented. It is intended to demonstrate the seriousness of the European NATO members' intentions to fulfill their mutual assistance obligations.
Germany's Inspector of the Army, Christian Freuding, together with his Dutch counterpart, Jan Swillens, is studying possible areas for operations in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
We have all reached the shared conclusion that we need to prepare even faster for an immediate response, improve our capabilities every day, and only in this way will we be able to fulfill our great responsibility
Germany has already deployed the 45th Armored Brigade in Lithuania, whose formation is still under way. In addition, since July, the German-Dutch Corps has been responsible for the possible conduct of NATO ground operations in Estonia and Latvia.
Thus, the Baltic countries have become the main area of responsibility for the German Army. If necessary, German troops are to be rapidly redeployed there in large numbers.
Freuding said that he currently sees no indications that Russia is preparing for a possible limited attack on NATO territory. At the same time, he does not consider such a scenario entirely implausible.
According to him, Vladimir Putin could potentially use captured Alliance territory as an instrument of political pressure on the allies, demanding that they end support for Ukraine in exchange for ending the offensive.
The Russian armed forces will probably have a numerical advantage over us in this region
Among the preparation priorities, he named protection against threats in low-altitude airspace, countering electronic interference, and the development of unmanned systems and digital communications supported by artificial intelligence.
Germany also plans to pre-position weapons and material stocks in the Baltic countries to ensure that its troops are ready for prolonged defense.
Particular attention is being paid to long-range strike capabilities. The German Army is considering purchasing cheaper cruise missiles with a range of up to 1,500 km. They are planned for use in strikes against troop concentration areas and the enemy's supply routes. According to the publication, the purchases could be made both in Ukraine and in Germany.
Meanwhile, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are building the "Baltic Defense Line" along NATO's eastern flank. It involves constructing military obstacles and communications infrastructure, as well as deploying unmanned systems for attacks, defense and reconnaissance.
Directly near the Russian border, the Baltic countries are also digging trenches and building bunkers. One potential flashpoint is said to be the Estonian border city of Narva, where about 87% of the 52,000 residents are of Russian origin.
During the visit, the German and Dutch generals were presented with a detailed report on the defense preparations. At the same time, details of the military planning remain classified.
According to Die Welt, Estonian troops play loud music by the German band Rammstein from loudspeakers. The noise is intended to prevent Russian border guards from eavesdropping on conversations. Their post is reportedly located just over 100 meters from the site of the work.

articles.title: Yemeni army claims 336 Houthis neutralized in ‘Dawn of Yemen’ operation

Yemen’s armed forces said they had neutralized around 336 Houthi fighters and commanders during ongoing military operations under the “Dawn of Yemen” offensive, Anadolu reports.
On US social media company X, military spokesman Col. Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said government forces had carried out 1,087 strikes in recent hours using warplanes, drones, field artillery, and rocket launchers.
He said the strikes targeted Houthi command and control centers, troop concentrations, reinforcements, firing positions, fortifications, and supply routes.
In the southwestern province of Taiz, government forces and allied Popular Resistance fighters continued raids and counterattacks on strategically important Houthi positions, he added.
Al-Nuzaili said warplanes also carried out concentrated strikes on Houthi troop concentrations, reinforcements, and military positions in the province.
In the provinces of Al-Jawf, Marib and Al-Bayda, as well as southern and southwestern fronts, reconnaissance operations were followed by targeted strikes aimed at preventing infiltration attempts and disrupting Houthi reinforcements, he said.
The operations resulted in the neutralization of approximately 336 Houthi commanders and fighters, while 112 military vehicles, pieces of equipment, supply assets and heavy weapons were destroyed or damaged, according to the spokesman.
