articles.title: Drones have not killed tank: Ukrainian analyst says Operation Vivaldi shows NATO how to make armor work again
articles.body:
The lesson for NATO is not to abandon armored warfare, but to rethink how it is conducted. That is the argument Ukrainian military observer Oleksandr Kovalenko draws from Operation Vivaldi, the Third Army Corps’ counteroffensive near Lyman, which he says proves tanks still have a place on a battlefield many had already written them off.
Vivaldi is Ukraine's counteroffensive aimed at disrupting Russian forces' plans to encircle the fortress-belt cities in Donetsk Oblast from the north and south that protect the region from the entire occupation. Among them are Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka. These cities have helped hold back Russian forces since 2014.
Kovalenko's claim runs against a view that hardened as drones came to dominate the front: that massed armor is finished, kept alive only by habit.
It matters because NATO’s own recent exercises have fed that view, with small Ukrainian drone teams beating Alliance armor again and again. Kovalenko says the Alliance now risks taking the wrong lesson from its own defeats.
What NATO’s war games got wrong about the tank
Kovalenko points to two drills. At Estonia’s Hedgehog exercises in May 2025, Ukrainian FPV-drone units ran rings around NATO troops, who he says lost vehicles by the dozen and failed one task after another.
In one episode, Ukrainian pilots notionally knocked out a large combat group built around a British brigade.
A year later, during the Aurora 26 exercises on the Swedish island of Gotland, the pattern repeated, and the NATO units, in his telling, in a sense lost control of the island.
The skeptics’ case leaned on exactly these results, Kovalenko says, with many concluding that the Alliance faltered in part because it still fielded large amounts of armor, a tool they believe has lost its relevance in modern warfare.
How the Third Army Corps made armor move again
Vivaldi is the counterexample, Kovalenko argues. During it, the Third Army Corps carried out two mechanized assaults that pushed into the Russian rear, not armor used the old way.
A similar idea appeared in the 2024 Kursk operation, he notes, paired there with intense electronic warfare; Vivaldi widened the package, with deeper reconnaissance and dedicated work against the enemy’s own strike systems.
The vehicles carried extra passive and active protection, and crews trained for the task, and Ukrainian forces moved to suppress Russian surveillance and communications.
None of these ingredients is new on its own, he says. What mattered was adapting the working formulas to attack a heavily outnumbered enemy.
“Ukrainian forces are showing that even what seems at first glance to be a battlefield anachronism can be adapted and given a new function,” Kovalenko says.
The corps’ commander made the same point about armor specifically.
“These operations prove that maneuver by armor remains possible on a battlefield increasingly dominated by reconnaissance drones, loitering munitions and precision weapons,” Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, who leads the Third Army Corps, said in a comment Kovalenko cites.
His own conclusion is a warning: NATO armies are stuck near Cold War templates for attack and defense, and unless they study and absorb what Vivaldi did, the Alliance could one day find itself routed not in an exercise but on a real battlefield.

Zelensky: Russia fired 17 ballistic missiles overnight, took no steps toward de-escalation in energy sector
According to Ukrinform, the head of state stated this in his nightly video address.

Unfortunately, additional emergency power outages have been introduced. We have the personnel and equipment needed for restoration. In Kyiv and the region, in the Chernihiv region, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv and Sumy regions – restoration work must proceed promptly everywhere. Today, Russian ballistic missiles also struck the Poltava region. Kremenchuk. Our oil refining infrastructure was targeted. The Russians have not taken a single step toward energy de-escalation. They continue to carry out terrorist strikes against our cities," Zelensky said.
At the same time, he stressed that Ukraine would continue working with all its partners to strengthen air defense and secure ammunition for F-16 fighter jets.
"We are preparing new decisions in the near future," the head of state said.
As reported, Russian attacks caused extensive damage to energy infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and the Dnipropetrovsk region. It will take time to fully restore electricity supplies, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry said.

articles.title: Swiss components also found in new Russian weapons
articles.body:
Swiss components also found in new Russian weapons
Ukraine has now named 11 Swiss companies whose components have been found in Russian drones and missiles.
What new discoveries have the Ukrainian authorities made?
The Ukrainian military intelligence service, HUR, regularly publishes details of electronic components found in the wreckage of Russian weapon systems in a publicly accessible database. Findings from spring, September and October of this year show that Swiss components continue to be used in new or upgraded Russian drones, missiles and cruise missiles. Ukraine has identified components from 11 Swiss companies. Swiss components have also been found in North Korean ballistic missiles fired at Ukraine.
How important are these parts for Russian weapon systems?
Very important, says Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the Ukrainian president’s adviser on international sanctions, speaking to Swiss public broadcaster SRF. According to Vlasiuk, 95% of Russian drones and missiles contain parts from Swiss companies. The electronic components supplied by Swiss firms are mass-produced industrial goods. They are used as microcontrollers in the control systems of missiles and drones, in the processing of satellite navigation data, as voltage converters, as sensors or as memory chips.
These components are not military equipment, nor are they dual-use items
And yet these electronic components are of military use. Countries are still struggling to define these goods in a uniform manner, as they have hitherto regarded them as civilian products. With changes in the nature of warfare – for example, the widespread use of low-cost drones – these mass-produced goods are becoming strategically significant. Together with the G7 countries, the EU has placed these goods on a joint sanctions list. Switzerland has adopted this sanctions list. As a result, Swiss companies are also no longer permitted to sell them to Russia.
What is Switzerland being accused of?
Switzerland is not doing enough to prevent shipments to Russia. This is the criticism levelled by Vladyslav Vlasiuk, an adviser to the Ukrainian president. He is calling on the Swiss government to involve the law enforcement authorities and to strengthen the export control bodies. He is dissatisfied with Switzerland’s responses to date. Sanctions regimes have evolved, as has Russia’s ability to circumvent them, he says, adding that Switzerland cannot simply stick to the logic that there are no production facilities in Switzerland and that it does not export to Russia. That is not enough.
More
Swiss Army combines horses and high-tech drones
What does the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) say?
SECO is aware of the issue regarding the components, the State Secretariat stated in response to an enquiry. It explains that, in most cases, the goods are not produced in Switzerland. Consequently, no exports take place. The export of these goods from Switzerland – including indirectly – to Russia is prohibited. Swiss companies are obliged to comply with certain due diligence requirements. This includes, in the case of exports or sales to third countries, contractually prohibiting the re-export of these goods to Russia. The effective and comprehensive enforcement of sanctions against Russia is a priority for the government, SECO writes.
What is required of companies?
They should take a closer look. Particularly when selecting their distribution partners and intermediaries, says Vladyslav Vlasiuk. He cites the example of the Dutch company NXP. A few years ago, this company attracted even more negative attention than the Swiss firms. By 2026, NXP electronic components were almost entirely absent from Russian weapons.
The Ukrainian government lists 11 manufacturers based in Switzerland, two of which belong to the same group. We have asked the four companies with the most entries in the Ukrainian database for their comments:
STMicroelectronics: The company is headquartered in Plan-les-Ouates (canton Geneva). It emphasises that the use of its products for purposes other than those for which they are intended is neither authorised nor tolerated. The company has a comprehensive global compliance programme that includes training, procedures and guidelines for all sales channels. Since the end of February 2022, STMicroelectronics has taken measures to implement all sanctions packages and export control measures imposed by the EU, the US and other partner countries against Russia and Belarus. The company says it no longer conducts any business in Russia.
u-blox: In its statement, the Thalwil (canton Zurich)-based company condemns Russia’s attack on Ukraine in the strongest possible terms. Upon the outbreak of war, the company suspended all cooperation and deliveries to Russia and Belarus; sales to countries in the Eurasian Economic Union were subsequently halted as well. Since 2021, u-blox has also been working with the organisation Conflict Armament Research (CAR) to investigate how its own components ended up in drones used in the war in Ukraine. On the basis of this collaboration, it says several companies involved have been identified and blacklisted.
Traco Power: The company, based in Baar (canton Zug), points out that its products are electronic components for civilian industrial applications which are not listed in any dual-use regulation and are not intended for military purposes. Until the sanctions came into force, the company had supplied the Russian market exclusively via closely monitored authorised distribution partners. With immediate effect from February 28, 2022, Traco Power says it ceased all deliveries and business relations with Russia – including those via third countries. Any of the company’s components that may be found could therefore under no circumstances have originated from deliveries made after the sanctions came into force. The company says it conscientiously and strictly complies with all applicable regulations, embargoes and sanctions.
TE Connectivity (Schaffner / Axicom): TE Connectivity states that it complies with all export controls and sanctions applicable worldwide and has therefore fully complied with all sanctions imposed following the Russian invasion. Since these came into force in March 2022, the company has not supplied any products to Russia from any of its sites. TE Connectivity says it is committed to a business policy that excludes both direct and indirect deliveries to Russia or other sanctioned countries. These guidelines are communicated to its distribution partners, who are also expected to comply strictly with them.
So why are Swiss components still finding their way into Russia?
There are many indications pointing to China. Research and investigations by thinktanks, NGOs and the media show that intermediaries and distribution partners from China are supplying the goods to Russia. Some Swiss companies have their products manufactured in China.

articles.title: Satellite photos confirm Ukraine destroyed two Russian Su-34s
articles.body:
- Satellite imagery shows two Su-34 fighter-bombers destroyed at Russia’s Marinovka air base after a Ukrainian Neptune missile strike on Oct. 29.
- Ukraine’s Navy says the jets belonged to the 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment; Russia has not confirmed any losses at the Volgograd region base.
Satellite imagery shows the wreckage of two Su-34 fighter-bombers destroyed at Russia’s Marinovka air base in the Volgograd region, confirming Ukraine’s claim that its Neptune cruise missiles knocked out the jets on Oct. 29, open-source analysts said.
The open-source monitoring group CyberBoroshno said the post-strike image shows the effects of hits in two parking spaces where Su-34s were stationed, with the remains of the aircraft visible. It compared the image with a Sentinel satellite picture taken on Oct. 28, which shows a Su-34 standing at the same spot, a sign the location was the aircraft’s regular parking position.
“This confirms that the strike hit the places where the aircraft were based, not random points on the airfield,” CyberBoroshno said.
The Russian aviation-focused account Avivector also published satellite frames showing the destroyed aircraft, writing that the Ukrainian Navy’s Oct. 29 strike on Marinovka “destroyed two Su-34 fighter-bombers.” Russia has not publicly confirmed any losses at the base.
The Ukrainian Navy said on Oct. 29 that its units hit the base near the settlement of Oktyabrsky with a coastal Neptune missile system, in what it called a “Long Neptune” strike, the extended-range land-attack version of the Ukrainian-made cruise missile. The Navy said the two Su-34s belonged to the 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment of Russia’s 4th Air and Air Defense Forces Army, Ukrainska Pravda reported. President Volodymyr Zelensky later confirmed the result. NASA’s FIRMS satellite fire-detection system picked up a fire at the airfield on the night of the attack, and the base lies more than 400 km (250 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
The Su-34 is the main aircraft Russia uses to drop glide bombs, known in Ukraine as KABs, on Ukrainian cities, frontline positions and the troops holding them. Each jet can carry up to 8 metric tons of weapons. Russia had about 140 Su-34s in service as of Oct. 22, Ukrinform reported, and Ukraine’s military intelligence agency HUR has estimated that Russian industry can build only 14 to 18 of the aircraft a year.
Marinovka has been hit before. In June 2025, Ukrainian drones struck the base, and Ukraine’s General Staff said four Su-34s and a maintenance area were hit, with a Russian air force-linked Telegram channel later acknowledging losses. Earlier this month, on Oct. 15, Ukraine said Neptune missiles struck Su-34s at Borisoglebsk airfield in the Voronezh region, and satellite imagery of that base also showed destruction.
Ukraine has not said how many Neptune missiles it fired at Marinovka or whether other aircraft at the base were damaged in the strike.

“The strike was complex – attack drones and missile troops were engaged: ‘Neptune’ coastal missile systems of the Naval Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine,” the General Staff stated.
“The ignition of a finished products warehouse has been confirmed. In addition, four production workshops were damaged.”
The Kamensky plant functions as an essential supplier for the Russian defense industry, specializing in the chemical synthesis of solid rocket propellant and propulsive charges for multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), including the 220mm Uragan, 300mm Smerch, and modernized Tornado-S systems, alongside specialized propellants for tactical guided missiles and aircraft-delivered munitions.
Lavrov Protests Poland’s G20 Role as US Backs Full Membership
Destruction of rear military supply depots across occupied territories
In parallel with the cross-border operation in Rostov region, Ukrainian precision forces executed synchronized strikes against four material-technical logistics supply depots operated by the Russian armed forces across occupied Ukrainian territory.
The General Staff confirmed successful kinetic impacts against Russian military warehouses near Khartsyzk and Dokuchaievsk in Donetsk region, Novovasylivka in Zaporizhzhia region, and Novoaidar in Luhansk region.
Defense analysts observe that targeting ammunition storage sites, fuel depots, and transport distribution centers across occupied sectors degrades frontline tactical replenishment and complicates logistics for Russian assault groupings operating along the eastern and southern fronts.
The combined interdiction operations in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky and the occupied zones form part of an escalating campaign to degrade Russian strike capacity and weapon assembly chains at the source.
Synchronized interdiction of downstream oil and chemical infrastructure
The strike on the Kamensky propellant plant follows concurrent long-range strikes against Russian downstream energy and refining infrastructure. Overnight into Saturday, Ukrainian strike drones struck the Bashneft-Novoil refinery and the adjacent Bashneft-UNPZ facility in Ufa, approximately 1,400 kilometers east of Ukraine’s borders.
Open-source intelligence analysis by independent outlet Astra confirmed that the Ufa attack ignited a major blaze engulfing the critical L-35 catalytic reforming unit, an irreplaceable technological installation responsible for manufacturing high-octane gasoline reformates and hydrogen needed for fuel desulfurization.
Monitoring group Crimean Wind reported strikes hitting multiple enterprises across the 23.5-million-ton Ufa refining complex, prompting emergency airspace closures across Ufa, Kazan, and Samara.
The Bashkortostan operation arrived 24 hours after Ukrainian drones hit the 8.8-million-ton Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery in Samara region, which produces aviation kerosene for the Russian Aerospace Forces, alongside a military food ration factory.

articles.title: Houthis continue to engage in ‘fierce battles’ in mountains near Aden, Taiz - report
articles.body:
The Houthis continue to attack Saudi Arabia and are also continuing to engage in “fierce battles” in Yemen. This is an important issue because any talks with Iran, which appear to be happening, will take the Houthis into account. Arab News in Saudi Arabia said on October 30 that the “Saudi-led coalition said on Friday it intercepted and destroyed in the Makkah region a drone fired by Yemen’s Houthis.”
According to the Saudis, “a drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Makkah region.” The report noted that “the Iran-backed militia has for weeks targeted airports, energy infrastructure and cities across the Kingdom with drones and missiles.”
Now, Al-Ain media in the UAE also says that “dozens of government forces and Houthis were killed and wounded on Friday in fierce battles in Al-Maqatra district of Lahj, following a large-scale attack by the militias.”
Sources in Yemen told Al-Ain News that the Houthi militias launched a large-scale ground attack on government forces’ positions in Al-Maqatirah district, the northern gateway to Lahj, in an attempt to make progress on the ground and control key mountain ranges in the area.
This is an area in southern Yemen where the Houthis are fighting a tough and complex war against the Yemeni government and also other factions aligned with the government. Some of these factions were linked to the Southern Transitional Council, which had been backed by the UAE.
The UAE has excellent sources in this area.
“The sources confirmed that the Houthi militias aim, through the attack, to control the ‘Al-Muqatara Tunnel’ area and the strategically important Al-Muqatara mountain fortress, as well as to reach the Al-Rubu’ market located in the Heijah Al-Abd valley, where the main road linking Taiz and Aden is located.” The sources explained that the battles extended to the Haifan front, where the militias are trying to reach Mount An’an, which overlooks large areas between Haifan and Al-Maqatirah.
Events in Yemen could affect Iran, UAE, Qatar, US
This area appears to be only around 40 to 50 miles from Aden. This means the battles in these mountains, amid palm trees and scrub brush and steep terrain, could determine the next moves in Yemen. What happens here, could also matter in Tehran, Doha, Riyadh and Washington.
Let’s recall why the Houthis matters. The Iran-backed Houthis have emerged as one of the most important armed terrorist armies in the Middle East, using Yemen as a base to threaten Saudi Arabia, Israel and international shipping. The movement, also known as Ansar Allah, emerged from northern Yemen's Zaydi Shi'ite community and seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014.
In early 2015, Houthi forces advanced south toward Aden, forcing Yemen's internationally recognized government to flee. Saudi Arabia intervened in March 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition seeking to restore the government and prevent the Houthis from consolidating control over Yemen.
The war devastated the country but failed to defeat the Houthis. Iran's support helped the movement develop an increasingly sophisticated arsenal of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones. These weapons enabled the Houthis to strike Saudi Arabia and eventually target Israel.
Following the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, the Houthis began launching missiles and drones toward Israel and attacking commercial shipping in the Red Sea. Israel, the United States and Britain subsequently carried out strikes against Houthi targets. The Houthis resumed attacks on Israel during the 2026 conflict involving Iran.
Yemen's war escalated again in July 2026, when the Houthis renewed attacks on Saudi targets and shipping. In September, Houthi forces advanced along the Red Sea coast, capturing Mocha and reaching the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait. The strait connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is a vital route for international trade and energy shipments.
Fighting has also intensified around Taiz, where the Houthis have sought to threaten the road linking the city to Aden, the internationally recognized government's main base.
The renewed conflict illustrates how Yemen's civil war has become intertwined with the wider regional confrontation involving Iran, Saudi Arabia and Israel. Control of territory around Bab al-Mandab gives the Houthis additional leverage over regional security and international commerce.
Al-Ain says that as the battles in the mountains have continued, “warplanes launched a series of raids on Houthi positions and gatherings to repel the militia's attack on Al-Maqatirah district in Lahj governorate.” Al-Ain concludes that “by attacking Al-Maqatirah, the Houthi militias are trying to reach Tur Al-Bahah district in Lahj, a coastal province that is the main gateway to the capital, Aden.”
Yemen has been witnessing fierce battles since the beginning of last September, following a large-scale, multi-pronged attack launched by the Houthis on areas of the western coast, Bab al-Mandab and Taiz, which resulted in thousands of deaths and injuries.
Houthis lay seige to Taiz
The Houthis are also laying siege to the city of Taiz in the mountains. Arab News says that the Houthis are also facing growing international criticism over their detention of United Nations personnel and the worsening humanitarian crisis in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.
According to Arab News, the Houthis are holding 71 UN staff members, severely restricting the organization's ability to operate in areas under their control. “These actions render the delivery of humanitarian aid in areas under the control of the Houthis untenable at this time,” Shirin Yaseen, associate spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, told Arab News.
The reports indicate that the humanitarian situation has deteriorated further around Taiz, where more than 800,000 people have been cut off from essential supplies. The Houthis intensified their siege in early October after seizing the road connecting Taiz with Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government. According to the World Food Programme, approximately three-quarters of the affected population depend on humanitarian assistance. Taiz has faced varying degrees of Houthi siege since 2015.

articles.title: “We were told brigade couldn’t be saved”: Ukraine’s 125th grew its manning 430% and won back 1,500 absent soldiers in one year
articles.body:
A year ago, Ukraine’s 125th heavy mechanized brigade was written off as beyond saving, manned at 17% with not a single tank, gun, or drone crew to its name. A year on, the brigade says it now ranks first among the army’s heavy brigades and that 1,500 soldiers who had gone absent without leave have returned to serve.
The 125th, part of Ukraine’s Third Army Corps, drew the comparison as it summed up its first year under new command. It comes as Ukraine struggles with a force-wide shortage of soldiers and leans on the Third Army Corps, the formation the 125th now fights under, for its counterattacks around Lyman.
The figures behind a brigade rebuilt from 17% strength
In the unit’s telling, the collapse was never the whole story.
“We were told the brigade couldn’t be saved. But they didn’t account for the main thing, people,” the brigade recalls.
By its own count, manning has risen 430% over the year, and its main units now stand at 95-100%. The crews that grew fastest were the ones flying drones: the number of aerial-reconnaissance teams is up 1200%, FPV crews 950%, heavy-bomber crews 1400%, and fixed-wing drone crews 600%.
The brigade also built units of uncrewed ground vehicles from scratch and stood up its own training, air defense, electronic warfare, reconnaissance, and medical structures.
Now, it is among the most effective brigades for destroying Russians, mining, artillery, air defense, ground robots, and reconnaissance, and for three months running it has placed first among the army’s heavy mechanized brigades on those combined measures.
From two pickups and a minibus to Bradleys and Leopards
The starting point was close to empty. At the beginning of the reform, the brigade had almost no combat equipment, its commander, Volodymyr Fokin, told ArmyInform in June.
“For the whole brigade we had two pickups and one minibus,” he said.
In the first six months, he added, the brigade replaced about 90% of its commanders in key posts and stood up a tank battalion, a drone battalion and a ground-robotics company.
Today it fields American Bradley infantry fighting vehicles, German Leopard tanks and artillery of various calibers.
A captain with the callsign “Skamer” told ArmyFM in July that the new equipment came with new ways of running the brigade, with more authority given to commanders who had real combat experience.

articles.title: Vance offers to meet with former IRGC commander Rezaei as Pentagon preps new attack - report
articles.body:
The White House believes Mohsen Rezaei, one of the Iranian regime’s staunchest hardliners, could be the key to an agreement that would prevent renewed war between the US and Iran, Washington Post columnist David Ignatius reported Thursday evening.
Ignatius, a veteran Washington journalist who covers foreign affairs and national security, cited conversations with a US official familiar with the negotiations, providing new details about the Trump administration’s latest effort to reach an agreement with Tehran.
Previous reports revealed that Vice President JD Vance sent a personal letter last week to Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council and a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. In the letter, Vance expressed willingness to meet with him personally to discuss ending the war through negotiations.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the letter’s existence. Ignatius disclosed additional details about its contents and why the White House chose to approach a senior member of Tehran’s hardline camp.
According to the US official who spoke with Ignatius, the letter emphasized putting both countries’ national interests at the center of negotiations. Vance made clear that Washington’s primary interest was ensuring Iran did not acquire nuclear weapons.
He also pointed to Iran’s interest in rebuilding its economy, which has been severely damaged by the war and sanctions, and preserving its national sovereignty. Vance stressed that Iran must send representatives with the authority to negotiate the nuclear issue and reach binding agreements.
Rezaei the only person capable of building support for deal, US official says
A central finding in Ignatius’s report concerns US intelligence assessments of Rezaei’s influence within the Iranian regime. According to the US official, the Trump administration has concluded that Rezaei is its most important negotiating contact in Tehran and effectively the only person capable of building broad support for an agreement limiting Iran’s nuclear program.
US intelligence officials assess that Rezaei maintains regular contact with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. The two are believed to have spoken in recent days, after the American letter arrived.
Rezaei, who commanded the Revolutionary Guards for years, is believed by US officials to retain the trust of commanders who previously served under him. Over the past year, he has also strengthened his position by reorganizing the Supreme National Security Council and appointing allies to influential posts.
He maintains close ties with senior officials responsible for Iran’s economy, which has been severely damaged by the naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz and economic sanctions.
The Trump administration believes Rezaei understands the severity of Iran’s situation. His standing among hardliners could enable him to persuade opponents of compromise to accept an agreement.
If the two sides agree to meet, Istanbul or the Qatari capital, Doha, would be the most likely locations.
Ignatius noted that Vance has already played a central role in US efforts to reach an agreement with Iran. In April, he traveled to Islamabad, Pakistan’s capital, and met with Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.
During those talks, the administration offered to lift economic sanctions on Iran and pursue broad economic cooperation, an approach Trump officials called the “golden bridge,” in exchange for a binding nuclear agreement.
Ghalibaf, however, failed to secure support from the regime’s leadership in Tehran. The two countries signed a limited, vaguely worded memorandum of understanding, but it collapsed after exchanges of fire resumed in the Strait of Hormuz.
Since then, according to Ignatius, US intelligence has concluded that the Iranian regime’s real power rests with Rezaei, rather than necessarily with those who have led the formal negotiations.
Qatar continues to play a central role as a mediator, with its representatives maintaining regular contact with Rezaei and other senior Iranian officials.
Iran sees Vance's letter as respectful gesture
According to the report, Iran’s leadership viewed Vance’s personal outreach as a respectful gesture. However, there is still no indication that Iranian officials have softened their positions on the nuclear issue, which remains the main obstacle to an agreement.
The report comes as military tensions surrounding Iran rise and the Pentagon prepares for the possibility of renewed, large-scale combat operations.
Earlier Thursday, US Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper reportedly visited the White House and presented Trump with options for further military action against Iran. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine also attended the meeting.
Ignatius wrote that White House officials fear time is running out to reach an agreement without resuming the war.
He also highlighted a significant difference between Washington’s and Jerusalem’s approaches. According to Ignatius, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing for regime change in Iran, believing it is the only way to eliminate the threat once and for all.
Trump, meanwhile, continues to say he wants to “finish the job” in Iran as additional US forces deploy to the region. In Ignatius’s assessment, however, Trump and Vance clearly prefer a diplomatic agreement to another round of fighting.
Even as the US military prepares for a possible attack, a significant diplomatic effort is underway to reach an agreement with one of the figures most closely associated with the Iranian regime’s anti-American stance.
Ignatius, who has covered US foreign policy and the intelligence community for decades, expressed skepticism about the initiative’s prospects. He noted that Rezaei has effectively built his entire career on staunch opposition to the US and Israel.
Although Rezaei has the political influence needed to secure an agreement with Washington, doing so would represent a dramatic change of direction for him.
The initiative also illustrates Vance’s growing role in leading diplomatic efforts with Iran and his reservations about continuing a war that lacks broad support among the American public.
According to Ignatius, the political timing also matters. The initiative comes just days before the November 3 congressional midterm elections, as the Trump administration faces public criticism over the war and its economic consequences.
Beyond those political considerations, however, Ignatius concluded that pursuing a diplomatic solution is a worthwhile alternative to another round of fighting.
It remains to be seen whether Rezaei, whom Washington identifies as Tehran’s true center of power, will take the step US officials hope for: moving from decades of opposition to any agreement with the US to becoming the person capable of bringing the war to an end.

articles.title: Patriot sale to Ukraine approved, but first missiles may be years away
articles.body:
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said deliveries of 500 U.S.-approved PAC-3 MSE interceptors may begin only in several years, too late for this winter.
- He asked the United States for 100 Patriot interceptors a month from existing stocks, replenished later by the newly approved production.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the 500 Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptors the United States cleared for sale to Ukraine on Oct. 30 will not help this winter, because deliveries may not begin for several years. He asked Washington to send interceptors from existing U.S. and allied stocks now and replace them later from the new production run.
The U.S. State Department notified Congress of the possible $2.1 billion sale on Oct. 30. It is funded by donations from Canada, Germany and Norway through the JUMPSTART mechanism and by Ukrainian national funds drawn from the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan, with no U.S. money involved. The notification gave no delivery schedule.
“Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defense package. However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
Alex Raufoglu, a correspondent for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, reported that the 500 are new-build missiles and that, according to his sources, deliveries are not expected until after 2030. Neither the State Department nor Lockheed Martin has published a delivery date.
Lockheed Martin built 620 PAC-3 MSE interceptors in 2025, and in January it signed a seven-year framework agreement with the U.S. Department of War to raise annual output from about 600 to roughly 2,000. New Foreign Military Sales orders join a queue that already includes U.S. Army replenishment and earlier buys by Poland, Germany, Japan, Gulf states and other operators. A new case also has to clear congressional review, be turned into a signed letter of offer and acceptance, and be placed on contract before the missiles enter that queue.
Zelenskyy asked instead for a winter package of 100 interceptors a month from existing stocks, which would deliver the equivalent of the 500 approved missiles in about five months, with partners’ arsenals replenished later by the production Ukraine and its allies have already paid for.
“The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses. Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach,” Zelenskyy wrote.
On Oct. 27, Zelenskyy told journalists that Ukraine had received an average of 12 Patriot interceptors a month from the United States in 2026, a fraction of the 100 a month he is now requesting, while Russia fires roughly 150 ballistic missiles a month that need intercepting. In his post, he said Russia had made more than 30 strikes on critical parts of Ukraine’s power grid in the past two weeks of October alone, targeting electricity, heating and water supplies before winter began.
PAC-3 MSE is the Patriot interceptor Ukraine relies on against ballistic missiles: it destroys its target by direct impact, and its two-pulse motor extends range and altitude against maneuvering threats such as Russia’s Iskander and Kinzhal. Ukraine also uses older PAC-2 interceptors, but Ukrainian officials have repeatedly described PAC-3 as their only effective defense against Russian ballistic missiles. Shortages have pushed Ukrainian crews to engage some ballistic targets with a single interceptor instead of the usual two or more.
In April, Zelenskyy said U.S. deliveries under NATO’s PURL program had not stopped but that Ukraine’s interceptor shortage remained critical. In August, CNN was given access to a Ukrainian Patriot battery that had not fired in six weeks because its launchers had no interceptors to load. On Oct. 19, Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had not approved the transfer of a significant batch of Patriot interceptors that Ukraine’s allies had already paid for, and suggested the delay was meant to pressure Kyiv. A U.S. government official called those claims “not true.” The Washington Post reported the same day that the Trump administration had not approved transfers of interceptors from partner countries.
Asked about the delayed transfers, Hegseth said on Oct. 20 that Washington’s posture toward Ukraine had not changed, but that the U.S. military wanted to keep as many interceptors as possible for its own forces. U.S. inventories have been drawn down by the war with Iran that began in February; the Center for Strategic and International Studies has estimated that U.S. stocks of Patriot and other interceptors fell by about half during that conflict. The Hill reported this week that President Donald Trump is weighing new military strikes on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. U.S. officials have not publicly linked that decision to the interceptor transfers.
Citing NATO sources, Euronews reported that allies were pessimistic about Ukraine receiving more interceptors before the midterms, and that NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte had asked Greece and Spain to hand over some of their own interceptors without success.
In September, the European Commission approved €6.1 billion in defense procurement for Ukraine, including PAC-3 interceptors bought under a special exception to the EU loan’s preference for European-made weapons, though it did not disclose how much went to Patriot missiles.
“We are asking for decisions that can guarantee the protection of lives not the day after tomorrow or sometime later, but at the very moment the threat is there – when Russia is killing and destroying,” Zelenskyy wrote.
Zelenskyy thanked President Donald Trump, the State Department and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, with whom he said he had recently discussed PAC-3 interceptors. Washington has not responded publicly to his request for interim deliveries, and the delivery schedule for the 500 missiles approved on Oct. 30 remains undisclosed.

articles.title: Pentagon Says Ukraine’s Patriot Missile Production Request Requires ‘Further Review’
articles.body:
Ukraine’s efforts to manufacture American-made Patriot interceptor missiles domestically have encountered another obstacle, with the Pentagon opting for “further review” rather than granting the licensing authorization Kyiv has been seeking.
The response leaves Ukraine without a confirmed agreement or timetable for producing the critical air defense interceptors on its own territory, even as Russia continues its missile attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The development follows Washington’s approval Friday, Oct. 30, of a proposed $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (PAC-3 MSE) interceptors to Ukraine.
But President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that the newly approved missiles might not begin arriving for several years, highlighting the widening gap between Ukraine’s immediate defensive requirements and Western weapons production schedules.
“It has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelensky wrote on X.
He urged Washington and European allies to release interceptors from their existing inventories, with newly manufactured missiles replacing them later.
The Pentagon’s decision to keep the licensing request under review raises a separate question: whether Ukraine will eventually be allowed to manufacture the weapons itself rather than remain dependent on overseas production and deliveries.
Russia Strikes Kharkiv With Jet-Powered Shahed Drone, Injuring 3, Damaging 10 Homes
No authorization or timeline for production in Ukraine
Ukraine has repeatedly sought to expand domestic weapons production as part of its broader effort to reduce dependence on foreign military assistance.
Manufacturing Patriot interceptors domestically would be a significant step toward that objective, potentially allowing Kyiv to build a more sustainable supply of missiles needed to counter Russian ballistic attacks.
However, the Pentagon’s response of “further review” does not constitute approval, nor does it establish when a decision might be made.
Production would require more than political authorization. It would involve licensing agreements, technology-transfer arrangements, industrial investment and the participation of the American companies responsible for manufacturing the interceptors and their components.
The PAC-3 MSE is produced by Lockheed Martin, while Boeing manufactures its advanced seeker components.
Even if Washington approved Ukrainian production, building the necessary manufacturing capabilities would take time and would not immediately resolve the country’s current shortage.
Lockheed Martin confirms ‘deep’ talks on overseas production
Lockheed Martin has acknowledged that it is exploring international manufacturing partnerships as demand for Patriot interceptors rises sharply.
In an exclusive interview with Kyiv Post, Dan Tenney, Lockheed Martin’s senior vice president for global business development and strategy, revealed that the company was engaged in advanced discussions with several countries about expanding production overseas.
“We are in pretty deep discussions on this,” Tenney said when asked about the prospect of international production partnerships.
He declined to identify the countries involved or confirm whether Ukraine was among them.
The company has outlined plans to expand annual PAC-3 MSE production capacity to approximately 2,000 interceptors by the end of 2030, compared with roughly 600 annually at the beginning of the expansion effort.

articles.title: Russia used everything but nuclear weapons against civilians in Ukraine’s Kherson Oblast, its governor says. Drones strike up to 6,500 times weekly
articles.body:
Russia has fired more than 925,000 shells at Ukraine’s Kherson Oblast since late 2022 and now sends up to 6,500 drone attacks against it every week. Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson regional military administration, set out the toll at the Council of Europe’s Congress of Local and Regional Authorities in Strasbourg.
Approximately 70% of Kherson Oblast remains under Russian military occupation, primarily across the left (east) bank of the Dnipro River, while Ukrainian forces control and have liberated the right bank, including the regional center of Kherson city.
“Everything except nuclear weapons”: the toll Kherson carried to Strasbourg
Prokudin told European partners that his region has spent nearly five years at the epicenter of the war, a few kilometers from Russian positions.
“It used everything except nuclear weapons. A separate danger is the ‘drone safari,’ today up to 6,500 drone attacks a week. This is deliberate, targeted terror against civilians, children, medics and rescuers. But we stayed, adapted and learned to counter this terror,” Prokudin said.
What nine European countries are now coming to learn
The region has answers that are already keeping 140,000 residents alive, he said: coordination among local authorities, the military, emergency services and volunteers; underground schools and hospitals; the pace of demining in deoccupied areas; and anti-drone defenses that let Ukraine’s forces bring down most of the incoming UAVs.
“We paid an extremely high price for this knowledge. That is why our unique experience of civil-military administration is already being studied by nine European countries, from the Baltics and Scandinavia to Germany and Poland,” he stressed.
His central message, he added, was that a large-scale crisis leaves no time to prepare, and that Europe must ready its communities, energy, medicine and local government, not only its armies, while it still holds the one thing Ukrainians lacked in February 2022, which is time.
“Our pain must gain meaning, and our lessons must save thousands of lives,” Prokudin added.
He thanked the Council of Europe and international partners for their solidarity with the region.

articles.title: Russia loses about 13 warplanes in a month
articles.body:
- Russia lost about 13 military aircraft from late September through October, including seven Su-34s destroyed by Ukrainian strikes and a Tu-95MS bomber in a crash.
- Two Su-30SMs crashed on Oct. 21, and a Su-57 reportedly burned at Akhtubinsk on Oct. 29, though Russia has not confirmed the Su-57 loss.
Russia’s military aviation has lost about a dozen aircraft in roughly five weeks, including at least seven Su-34 fighter-bombers destroyed on the ground by Ukrainian missiles and drones, a Tu-95MS strategic bomber and two Su-30SM fighters in crashes, and a Su-57 stealth fighter that reportedly burned out during an engine start.
The Ukrainian open-source project Oko Gora counted 11 Russian fighter aircraft and one helicopter lost in October alone, with two more Su-34s partially damaged. Adding the Tu-95MS that crashed on Sept. 29 brings the tally to about 13 airframes since late September. Russia has confirmed only the two crashes during training flights and has not acknowledged losses from Ukrainian strikes.
The heaviest losses fell on the Su-34, the jet Russia uses most to drop glide bombs on Ukrainian cities and front-line positions. On Oct. 4, drones from Ukraine’s SBU security service hit a Su-34 and a Su-35 fighter at Khanskaya air base in Russia’s Republic of Adygea, about 500 km (310 miles) from Ukrainian-held territory, along with an ammunition depot. On the night of Oct. 14-15, Ukrainian Navy Neptune missiles struck Borisoglebsk air base in the Voronezh region, and satellite imagery showed four Su-34s destroyed and two more badly damaged. On Oct. 29, another Neptune strike destroyed two more Su-34s at Marinovka air base in the Volgograd region, with satellite images showing the wreckage at their parking spots.
That puts confirmed Su-34 losses for the month at seven destroyed, or nine counting the two damaged at Borisoglebsk. Ukraine’s military intelligence agency HUR said Russia had about 140 Su-34s of all versions in service as of Oct. 22, and that Russian industry delivered 22 new ones between October 2025 and October 2026, Ukrinform reported. October’s losses alone equal about a third of that annual output.
On Sept. 29, a Tu-95MS bomber crashed on takeoff near Ukrainka air base in the Amur region of Russia’s Far East, killing six of the seven crew members. The Russian Defense Ministry said the aircraft was on a training flight without weapons. Russia no longer builds the Tu-95, which it uses to launch Kh-101 cruise missiles at Ukraine, and it was the first Tu-95MS lost in a crash since 2015.
On Oct. 21, a Su-30SM crashed during a training flight in the Kaliningrad region, and the Defense Ministry said both crew ejected. Russian and Ukrainian outlets reported that a second Su-30SM was lost the same day. Days later, the Russian Knights, the Russian Air Force’s aerobatic display team, announced the deaths of two of its pilots, Col. Oleg Yerofeyev and Lt. Col. Vladimir Kochetov, without saying how they died, and Ukrainian analysts have linked their deaths to the second crash. Russian authorities have not confirmed the connection.
The most unusual loss came on Oct. 29 at Akhtubinsk, the Russian Air Force’s main flight-test center in the Astrakhan region. A Su-57 fifth-generation fighter caught fire during an engine start and burned completely, the Ukrainian open-source channel Absolutely Reliable Source said, publishing satellite images of a burn scar on the airfield. Russia has not confirmed the loss. If verified, it would be the fourth Su-57 lost or damaged this year, after a Ukrainian drone strike in April and a crash near Moscow in July that Russia blamed on a technical malfunction.
The tallies also include helicopters. On Oct. 30, Ukraine’s Third Assault Brigade said it destroyed a Mi-8 transport helicopter in the Luhansk region with two Hornet attack drones after the helicopter landed.
The losses span thousands of kilometers, from Kaliningrad on the Baltic Sea to the Far East. The open-source project Oryx had visually confirmed 205 Russian aircraft destroyed or damaged since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, with the Su-34 the most-lost type at 48.

articles.title: Russia-Africa Summit: Four days of dealmaking the West wanted Africa to skip
articles.body:
Russia-Africa Summit by the numbers: What was achieved despite Western pressure
Delegations from 48 African countries, including 21 leaders, gathered in Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit under the motto “For Peace, Security and Development.” The gathering concluded on Thursday with a final declaration and a new cooperation plan. Organizers reported 146 documents signed across the Summit and its accompanying economic, humanitarian and media forums, comprising 92 agreements and 54 memorandums.
More than 3,500 participants from 74 countries attended, including over 1,200 business representatives from around 630 companies.The forum hosted more than 40 sessions.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has already held at least nine bilateral meetings with African leaders, including the presidents of Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Mozambique, Namibia, the Republic of the Congo, Burundi, and Kenya, as well as Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Libya’s Presidential Council Chairman Mohamed Al-Menfi.
Bilateral talks continued on Friday, with the day’s lineup including the leaders of Sudan, Madagascar, Ghana, Mali, South Sudan, the Central African Republic, DR Congo, and Eritrea, as well as Togo’s prime minister.
The October 28-29 summit capped four days of events, beginning with Monday’s media forum and including Tuesday’s separate gas exporters’ summit. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told RT that Western governments had tried to discourage African leaders from attending.
An overnight Ukrainian drone attack also prompted temporary restrictions at three Moscow airports before Thursday’s proceedings. Mayor Sergey Sobyanin reported 231 drones destroyed on the approaches to the capital. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov questioned the timing during an international gathering and praised air defenses.
Here are the main outcomes and key moments.
A framework through 2029
Putin and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the African Union chair, co-chaired Wednesday's and Thursday’s proceedings. Leaders addressed a plenary session in Kremlin before continuing over a working breakfast.
They adopted the Moscow Declaration, a Russia-Africa Partnership Forum action plan for 2027-2029 and a declaration on civilian applications of artificial intelligence.
The political declaration backed greater African representation in international institutions, opposed unlawful unilateral sanctions, and supported efforts to address colonial-era damage. It also called for South Africa’s full G20 participation to be restored, following its exclusion from meetings under the US presidency. Pretoria remains a member.
At their closing press conference, Putin emphasized the potential for further cooperation, while Ndayishimiye pressed for measurable benefits. Another summit will follow, with its date and location to be agreed.
Partnership: ‘Africa has not come to ask for aid’
Russia and Africa are “natural allies in building a multipolar, genuinely democratic world order,” Putin told the plenary. He backed stronger African representation in global decision-making and described Russian businesses as partners investing in host countries rather than pursuing colonial exploitation.
African leaders also stressed that cooperation should strengthen their ability to make independent decisions and develop their economies.
“Contrary to what malevolent forces might think, Africa has not come to ask for aid,” Ndayishimiye told the Kremlin plenary. He called for commitments to become concrete investment programs and for international cooperation to follow African priorities.
Democratic Republic of Congo President Felix Tshisekedi made a similar distinction. “Diversifying our partnerships is not about choosing sides: it is about strengthening our freedom of decision-making in the service of our populations,” he said.
Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa highlighted the need to turn agreements into action while processing more minerals domestically. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi presented his country’s cooperation with Russia, including the El Dabaa nuclear plant and planned Suez Canal industrial zone, as a model for wider partnerships.
Russia also signed several documents to deepen cooperation with African regional organizations. These included memorandums with the East African Community, the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa, and the African Continental Free Trade Area Secretariat, alongside an action plan with the African Union Commission.
Sergey Lavrov met counterparts from 41 African states.
Ghanaian Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa said Lavrov pledged support for Accra’s application for BRICS partner status and would seek consensus among founding members.
Peskov said Putin presented country-specific cooperation roadmaps during bilateral meetings. Putin also highlighted expanding diplomatic representation: eight Russian embassies have opened in Africa since 2023, bringing the total to 48. Six trade missions cover 16 countries, while Botswana, Seychelles, and Togo plan embassies in Moscow.
Financing and nuclear cooperation
Signings included a Wednesday memorandum between Russia’s development institution VEB.RF and BCID-AES, the joint investment bank serving Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, to identify and assess development and integration projects.
Rosatom also signed a peaceful nuclear cooperation memorandum with Togo, establishing working groups to examine potential projects and training. Floating nuclear power units are among the possibilities.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed sought priority for nuclear cooperation, including financing, engineering training and medical isotopes. A roadmap for Ethiopia’s first nuclear plant was signed in March, Rosatom chief Aleksey Likhachev said in an interview published Friday. Site-selection preparations are underway. Burundi expressed interest in small modular reactors. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi highlighted El Dabaa and the planned Russian industrial zone near the Suez Canal as examples of bilateral cooperation.
Trade and technology at Gostiny Dvor
Wednesday’s Economic and Humanitarian Forum at Gostiny Dvor in the Russian capital set much of the practical agenda. Putin proposed at least doubling Russia-Africa trade to more than $50 billion. On Thursday, he reported that the ruble accounted for up to 85% of commercial transactions between the two sides.
Putin and African leaders toured the “Platform for Sovereign Development” exhibition, showcasing energy, healthcare, agricultural, and digital technologies.
Elsewhere, Kenyan President William Ruto visited Sberbank’s smart city development and highlighted potential AI cooperation in healthcare and education.
Gas diplomacy alongside the summit
Tuesday’s eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit adopted its own Moscow Declaration, separate from the Russia-Africa documents. It reaffirmed sovereign rights over gas resources and supported supply security, investment, and a balanced transition toward lower-carbon energy.
At Monday’s ministerial meeting, Russian Energy Minister Sergey Tsivilev promoted a proposed gas bank for long-term infrastructure financing, including in Africa. The initiative remained under discussion.
Media cooperation and liberation legacies
The Russia-Africa Media Forum ran from Monday to Thursday, organized by RT alongside Sputnik and TASS. Organizers welcomed more than 200 participants from 46 African countries for discussions on reporting, professional cooperation, and media sovereignty.
The forum also produced several media partnerships. These included Ethiopia’s Fana renewing its agreement with RT and Libya’s national news agency signing with RT Arabic. Rossiya Segodnya concluded partnerships with outlets in Algeria, Chad, Morocco, Ghana, and Zimbabwe, as well as Ethiopia’s Debre Markos University and Niger’s Higher School of Journalism and Communication.
RT’s Thursday session, “Forging Independence: Lessons from the Founders of African Nations,” featured descendants of African liberation leaders. Samia Nkrumah, daughter of Ghana’s first president Kwame Nkrumah, credited Russian support during Africa’s independence struggles, saying, “We are all here in Russia for a reason.” Ndileka Mandela, granddaughter of South Africa’s Nelson Mandela, recalled first meeting him through a prison window on Robben Island in 1981, aged 16: “I touched the window on one side and he touched on the other.”
Education and healthcare commitments
Putin extended Russia’s epidemic-control assistance program for Africa through 2029.
Eight countries have received 15 mobile laboratories, and around 450 African specialists have been trained under the program, he said.
Among the healthcare agreements was a five-year memorandum with DR Congo covering training, research, maternal and child health, nuclear medicine, and digital healthcare.
Nearly 40,000 Africans study at Russian universities, up 50% since 2020, according to Putin. Government-funded scholarship places have nearly tripled over that period, reaching 5,500 for 2026-2027. Announced initiatives include ten centers helping African applicants enter Russian universities and vocational training programs.
Andrey Maslov, director of HSE University’s Center for African Studies, told RT that extended visits by African leaders and their separate business programs showed political ties with Moscow are gaining practical substance.

articles.title: General Staff reports strike on rocket fuel plant in Russia's Rostov region
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defense Forces, in a combined strike utilizing drones and Neptune missile systems, hit a military plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Rostov region of Russia, which specializes in the production of rocket fuel, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"Strike on rocket fuel production. On the night of October 31, units of Ukraine's Defense Forces hit the Russian military-industrial complex enterprise Kamensky Combine in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Rostov region of Russia," the General Staff reported on Telegram on Saturday.
The strike was carried out using a combination of attack drones and rocket troops, specifically coastal missile systems of the Ukrainian Navy's Neptune. A fire at the finished goods warehouse has been confirmed, and four production workshops were also damaged.
Kamensky Combine produces solid rocket fuel for ammunition of the Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple launch rocket systems (MLRS), as well as for a number of missile systems and air-launched strike weapons."
The General Staff explained the significance of the event: strikes on solid rocket fuel production reduce the Russian army's capability to shell Ukrainian settlements using MLRS.
It is also reported that four logistics supply depots of the Russian army were hit in the areas of Khartsyzk and Dokuchaievsk in Donetsk region, Novovasylivka in Zaporizhia region, and Novoaidar in Luhansk region.

articles.title: Ukraine Requests Emergency UN Security Council Meeting Over Russian Strikes
articles.body:
Ukraine requested an emergency meeting of the United Nations (UN) Security Council on Friday, Oct. 30, over Russia’s latest wave of missile and drone attacks that left at least 25 people dead and 110 wounded nationwide.
“From Dnipro and Chernihiv to Kremenchuk and Kyiv, the scale and geography of the strikes show that no part of Ukraine is beyond the reach of Russian terror,” Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry stated, noting that the strikes targeted children, private homes, civilian infrastructure and railway facilities.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Moscow accused of blocking the UN
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, who described the strikes as another gross violation of international law and the UN charter, accused Russia of undermining international peace.
He reiterated that Russia is exploiting its status as a permanent member of the Security Council to prevent the body from carrying out its mandate. As one of the council’s five permanent members, Russia holds veto power over its final resolutions, allowing Moscow to block action on its own war against Ukraine.
As early as December 2022, Kyiv called for Russia’s removal from the Security Council.
In its latest statement, Kyiv has once again called on partners to provide Ukraine with more air-defense capabilities, to increase pressure and impose tougher sanctions on Moscow.
“Russia must understand that its campaign of terror leads only to consequences, not concessions,” Sybiha said, adding that Russia must be held accountable for the “crimes it has committed.”
European Diplomats Refuse to Pose for Photo With Russia’s Lavrov at G20
His remarks came as the Trump administration continues to ease economic pressure on Moscow.
On Oct. 9, US President Donald Trump struck an abrupt diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, after which Washington formally authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The move came just three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which was intended to target Russia’s energy and defense sectors.
The Russian Direct Investment Fund, which helped arrange the diesel shipments, is now also seeking the removal of US sanctions against it, The New York Times reported.
On Oct. 21, senior US envoy Steve Witkoff publicly confirmed that Washington and Moscow are discussing future economic and trade cooperation, alongside negotiations to end the war.
He also revealed that the US Treasury Department is working directly with Kremlin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, the fund’s chief executive, who has emerged as an increasingly prominent intermediary in Washington’s efforts to end Russia’s war through economic engagement.
A day of terror
Russia’s deadly attack on Thursday, Oct. 29 hit a railway platform in Dnipro, where a Russian jet-powered drone killed 14 people waiting near a Dnipro-Zaporizhzhia passenger train.
Russian forces struck the city’s railway station again on Friday, injuring a woman, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
In Chernihiv, a Russian Banderol strike on the city center killed two 15-year-old girls and injured 27 people, among them a 10-month-old girl.
In Kremenchuk, attacks on two locations, including an area where a boarding school was damaged, killed three people and injured 32, six of them children.
Russian guided aerial bombs (KABs) also hit an apartment building in Izium, Kharkiv region, while late in the evening, ballistic missiles struck Kyiv, setting warehouses on fire and damaging residential buildings.
In the evening of that same day, Russian forces attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles.
During the 81st UN General Assembly (UNGA) in New York late September, 51 UN member states signed a joint statement backing Ukraine and urging Russia to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations.
On that same day, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the UN Security Council that Russia will not halt its aggression against Ukraine even during negotiations, rejecting growing international calls for a ceasefire.
