articles.title: Gulf states scramble to avert another U.S.-Israeli war on Iran they cannot stop
articles.body:
The first of two elections that many believe are the final bell before all out war is resumed against Iran is now complete. Although it seems likely that the efforts to cobble together a governing coalition in Israel, if that is even possible, will take weeks, the American midterms are expected to be the last milestone before the United States and Israel launch a massive attack on Iran.
There is no doubt that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is almost bursting with anticipation of the bloodshed to come. Donald Trump, as always, seems unsure of how to proceed, but seems very uncomfortable with the situation as it stands, while also being unwilling to make the concessions necessary to end this futile, destructive war he started for no good reason.
Iran can do little to deter an American attack, if that is what Trump decides to do. But it can retaliate with devastating consequences, which will be felt by its Gulf Arab neighbors, Israel, and the global economy.
That is why the countries of the newly created Mecca Pact—Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye—took the dramatic step of meeting Iranian officials in Tehran.
Iran trumpeted the meeting as demonstrating the seriousness with which the Sunni Muslim states take the Islamic Republic, meeting in the Iranian capital rather than in a third country.
Saudi Arabia said the meeting was aimed at mediating between the United States and Iran, but there is no evidence the United States had any part in the planning of this meeting. Indeed, the indications are the opposite; one purpose of the confab was to establish regional dialogue specifically on security matters.
Participants included Pakistan’s Chief of Army Staff Field Marshall Asim Munir, Saudi Minister of Defense Prince Khalid bin Salman, and Turkish Director of National Intelligence Ibrahim Kalin. They met with Iran’s Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei.
The fact that the meeting included leaders of the countries’ respective militaries indicates that the description of the meeting—that it was to deal with regional security—is likely accurate.
And, while little has been made public about the substance of the meeting, it also seems fair to say that there was little progress that could have been made on the major issues—the war with U.S. and the ongoing battles between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni Ansar Allah.
Little room for negotiations
Regarding Ansar Allah, Saudi Arabia was feeling Iran out to see if they would intervene with the Yemeni fighters whom the Saudis have been unable to defeat.
But Iran doesn’t have much reason to do so. While they could benefit from pulling the Saudis away from the American war effort, the compromises Tehran would have to make are far too great.
Reports out of Israel state that the Saudis offered Ansar Allah $1 billion for a ceasefire. But the Yemeni group will not budge on its understandable demand that Saudi Arabia drop its air blockade of Yemen.
This is not an issue Iran can try to mediate. If they try to get Ansar Allah to compromise on the air blockade, it undermines their argument that the United States must end its sea blockade of Iran.
Iran supports Ansar Allah’s cause, but if they thought they could get concessions from the Saudis on the kingdom’s support for American military efforts, Ansar Allah might find it reasonable to agree to a temporary ceasefire to help their ally.
But they cannot compromise on the air blockade, nor would Iran want them to. As long as Saudi Arabia maintains its efforts to block air traffic in Yemen, they can’t buy their way out of Ansar Allah attacks.
On the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, the Saudis are very worried, as are all the countries of the Gulf and their neighbors. They should be, given that Trump has warned the Gulf states to get ready for a “short, intense military campaign.” Considering that the war started on February 27 was supposed to end in just a few days, or weeks at most, no one is counting on the “short” part. But it is likely to be intense, and that intensity will be felt in Iran and the Gulf Arab states.
The problem for Iran is that its interlocutors can do little to turn Trump’s mind. Even Saudi Arabia, which is in a terrible position right now if the war restarts, has few options outside of registering its reservations with Trump, which it surely has already done.
Türkiye and Pakistan have even less leverage over Trump’s decisions. If he is reckless enough to risk the consequences of restarting the war with Iran, what can they do to stop him?
And those consequences are potentially very dire.
The costs of war
Iran has made it clear that it intends to target data centers, AI hubs, and underwater fiber networks that are the backbone of the internet in addition to oil infrastructure. No one doubts they have the capability of doing so.
The amount of damage that can be inflicted on the world dwarfs anything we’ve seen until now.
That has produced fear among the Gulf states, but it has also produced tension between them and Iran. Gulf states are angry at Iran for targeting them in response to American attacks, but Iran is aggravated because the Gulf states have cooperated with Washington.
This double-edged sword was visible this week when Qatar submitted a proposal for a ceasefire and a path back to negotiations, including reciprocal but revocable steps each side could take, presumably offering each side the assurances they needed to proceed.
But at the same time, Qatar publicly supported the call for Iran to allow international traffic through the Strait of Hormuz unconditionally. That did nothing to help the case for Qatar’s proposal, which Iran eventually dismissed as a collection of random ideas rather than a serious proposal and which Trump ignored.
Vice President JD Vance, who has quietly been opposing the resumption of large-scale fighting, tried reaching out via a letter to Rezaei, but the letter reportedly offered no immediate relief from any of the pressures the U.S. is putting on Iran while demanding that any talks include the nuclear issue, which Iran insists be left to be discussed after its minimal terms are met. In other words, it was just Vance delivering Trump’s unacceptable terms in nicer language.
If that wasn’t enough to make the Vance letter a non-starter, the fact that Vance’s earlier efforts were routinely contradicted by Trump soon after empties the vice president of any credibility, even if Tehran believes he is personally sincere in his desire to avoid another round of full-scale fighting.
This leaves only one hope: that Trump, in his eternally mercurial and indecisive way, will back away from what will be a devastating conflict.
One unknown is how much Trump understands about the danger that an Iranian response presents and how certain it is that a devastating response will be coming.
Trump’s threat of a “short intense” attack would seem to imply that he is being led to believe that the United States can overwhelm Iran with devastating force. Of course, that is exactly what he tried in February, and it failed dismally. Outside of insanity, does he have any reason to think that the same action would produce a different result this time?
It could be that what the U.S. and Israel are planning is a multi-phase attack.
American planners may think the weakness of their initial strike was that they targeted Iranian leadership while devastating large areas of civilian and military infrastructure, believing that this would lead to the collapse of the Iranian government. When that failed, there was no plan B.
It may be that the idea this time is to simply start with doing as much damage to Iranian infrastructure as they can, then pinpoint where the response is coming from and take out those missile and drone launchers.
That is consistent with what Senator Chris Murphy is warning about when he says that what the Trump administration is planning is “insane.”
“It will lead to devastating escalation, and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law. There’s been open reporting as to what we may be planning and the civilian infrastructure that we may be targeting,” Murphy said. “They’ve been asked by the president to develop a plan. Whether they believe it will work or not, I do not know. But the plan that they have developed will lead, in my view, to a prolongment and an escalation of this war that will be devastating for our security interests.”
The result, then, would be one of two things. If the U.S.-Israeli attack is successful, the Gulf states will suffer significant damage, but they can recover and, theoretically, come out with a weakened Iran. But that would mean that what failed in February magically works in November, and there is no evidence to support that expectation.
The other, far more likely scenario is that Iran continues to weather American and Israeli attacks and responds by devastating the Gulf states, further demolishing American positions, and inflicting a far greater degree of damage on Israel than they have in the past.
In that scenario, Gulf oil and civilian infrastructure could be damaged beyond repair. Moreover, given the region’s inherent instability—governed as it is mostly by iron-fisted dictators ruling over states of mixed and often clashing ethnicities drawn up by colonial map-makers—such a scenario could well mean the end of one or more of the Gulf states.
It is that scenario that the Mecca Pact countries are trying to avert.
They are not fools; they knew there was little that Iran could do to change the strategic playing field. Instead, they hoped that sending their top security leaders to Tehran would signal to Washington how concerned they were. They understood that the meeting, by its very existence, would give Iran a diplomatic win and, more importantly, would show that the Mecca Pact is intended to forge a new regional security system that will want to work with Iran, potentially even including it in the group someday.
The Mecca Pact countries, as well as Iran, hope that this message of the region’s strong desire to avert the oncoming catastrophe will convince Trump to back off.
Meanwhile, in Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu is even more incentivized to see the war roar back to life. With the election process in deadlock, he needs to move swiftly, before the opposition can make the case to the public that they are better suited to defeat Iran than Netanyahu.
He needs the war to make it more difficult to replace him, and he will push hard for it. He has already tried to provoke Iran into an act that would have restarted the major fighting before Trump was ready. He will surely try again before too long.

articles.title: ‘I Won’t Hold Back’: Estonian PM Refuses to Soften Criticism of Putin
articles.body:
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said on Friday, Oct. 30, that he would not soften his criticism of Russian President Vladimir Putin after a report that Pentagon officials had urged Baltic allies to tone down their rhetoric about Russia.
Speaking to Delfi, Michal said Estonia would maintain its position and continue speaking openly about the Russian threat.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I won’t hold back. Putin is a dictator who kills women and children,” he said.
Michal added that Putin would continue doing so until he was forced to change course.
Appeasing dictators brings humiliation without preserving freedom, Michal argued. Estonia and its Baltic neighbors would continue warning about the threat posed by Russia, he said.
Michal said he had not personally received a US request to moderate his language. The issue did not arise when he last met President Donald Trump in Ankara during the summer, he added.
He noted that domestic critics accused his government of being insufficiently assertive, even as reports suggested the US wanted greater restraint.
Pentagon reportedly urges restraint
Reuters reported that Pentagon officials had privately asked several NATO allies, including Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, to tone down their rhetoric about Russia.
Four people familiar with the discussions told Reuters the requests were made during bilateral meetings in recent weeks. Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby was among the officials involved.
Zelensky Ready to Discuss Territory With Putin, Sybiha Says
One source said Colby advised a Baltic official against “poking” Russia and cited descriptions of Moscow as cornered and increasingly desperate.
Michal had called Putin a rat in a corner in September, linking Russia’s difficulties in Ukraine to suspected sabotage in Europe. Reuters could not establish whether Colby was referring specifically to those remarks.
The sources described the conversations as cordial. The Pentagon declined to discuss private exchanges between allies, and NATO also declined to comment.
The reported appeals to Baltic governments come as Washington reviews its military presence in Europe and presses European allies to take greater responsibility for their defense.
Estonia backs continued pressure on Russia
At an October summit in Brussels, Michal backed Ukrainian refinery strikes despite US pressure on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil production.
“The faster all the Russian refineries and ability to sell energy will be blown to smithereens the better,” Michal said at the time.
His comments came as European leaders discussed additional financial support for Ukraine and relations between Kyiv and Washington deteriorated following Trump’s diesel agreement with Russia.
On July 7, President Volodymyr Zelensky and Michal signed a Drone Deal agreement on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara. Zelensky thanked Estonia for its military and humanitarian assistance, as well as its diplomatic support for Ukraine’s EU and NATO ambitions.
Allies debate how to describe the threat
Some believe emphasizing it risks amplifying the fear Moscow seeks to spread; others argue that frank warnings help explain the need for greater defense spending and continued support for Ukraine.
Western intelligence officials have warned of an expanding Russian sabotage campaign in Europe. Moscow denies conducting such a campaign.
Michal said a clear assessment of the threat was essential to preparedness and warned that Ukraine faced a difficult winter.

articles.title: Fire Point will not produce new cruise missiles because the “Flamingo” is sufficient: Stielerman explained Terekh’s statement on the marathon broadcast
articles.body:
Fire Point will not produce new cruise missiles because the “Flamingo” is sufficient: Stielerman explained Terekh’s statement on the marathon broadcast
Kyiv • UNN
Fire Point has focused on producing the FP-5 “Flamingo” and developing the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles. Production of the “Flamingo” is not being discontinued.
Fire Point does not plan to create new cruise missile models, as the FP-5 "Flamingo" is sufficient for the company. Its production is being ramped up, while the developers’ main efforts are focused on ballistic missiles. Fire Point co-founder and chief designer Denys Shtilerman said this on the air of the National Marathon "United News," UNN reports.
Details
Shtilerman explained that during the interview, the journalist drew attention to the missing indices in Fire Point’s lineup between FP-5 and FP-7 and between FP-7 and FP-9, and asked the company’s CEO, Iryna Terekh, whether new cruise missiles would appear in those places.
Iryna said that there would be no new cruise missiles and no new models. We are currently focused on producing ballistic missiles and developing ballistic missiles. And we are continuing to ramp up production of the FP-5, that is, Flamingo
He stressed that there was no talk of discontinuing production of the "Flamingo." The company simply does not intend to expand its lineup of cruise missiles.
We do not plan to make new cruise missile models because we believe that Flamingo is sufficient for our company
The company’s main focus for its developers now is ballistic technology. Fire Point is working on the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles, and on October 1, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported the first combat use of the FP-7.
Context
Several days ago, an edited fragment of an interview with Iryna Terekh circulated on social media, presented as if Fire Point had discontinued production of the FP-5 "Flamingo" cruise missile. Terekh denied this information on the social network X and noted that the company would continue improving the missile.
We do not plan to develop additional cruise missile models; instead, we are focusing on developing the existing model, while also directing our greatest efforts toward two ballistic models
Recall
The day before, Shtilerman called the wave of manipulation surrounding Terekh’s interview another attack on the company and said that production of the "Flamingo" and the FP-1 and FP-2 strike drones was being scaled up. According to him, those who spread the distorted claim without checking the original source are helping promote Russian narratives.
Fire Point produces the FP-1 and FP-2 strike drones and the FP-5 "Flamingo" cruise missile, with a range of approximately 3,000 km. The company is also developing the FP-7.x anti-ballistic interceptor, on the basis of which the European Freyja system is being built.

articles.title: Rubio urges G20 cooperation amid rifts over wars in Ukraine, Middle East
articles.body:
By Andrea Shalal
ATLANTA, Oct 30 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged fellow G20 foreign ministers on Friday to work together for greater geopolitical stability and economic prosperity, warning that a series of crises posed serious threats to the global economic order.
But Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov’s participation in the two-day gathering in Atlanta - at Rubio’s invitation - has roiled many G20 ministers, aggravating deep rifts over the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East during a meeting that is expected to end without a joint declaration. Such statements require consensus that has been elusive if not impossible since Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband addressed Lavrov directly during the meeting, telling him: “Only yesterday your drones attacked and killed 15 people. And there are countless examples like this of you killing innocent civilians throughout this war. We all know you are the aggressor.”
Lavrov later told reporters that Moscow’s position on the Ukraine conflict was unchanged, and Russia could not accept Ukraine as a “military threat to the lawful security interests of the Russian Federation,” according to Russian news agencies.
US officials said they skipped a traditional G20 family photo after European officials refused to be photographed with Lavrov. One US official said Washington wanted to avoid a “spectacle” that could overshadow the meeting. A third of members objected, including Australia and Canada, a Western diplomat said.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters a photograph with Lavrov was unacceptable because “there is no normalcy with Russia.” Lavrov himself acknowledged that there had been “concerns” about the family photo, drawing head nods from many in the room, one participant said.
Rubio, saying the world faced interconnected crises that threatened global energy and food supply, trade and the freedom of navigation, urged his counterparts to find areas of agreement during the final ministerial meeting before a leaders summit in Miami, Florida, from December 14 to 16.
“We are tasked, on behalf of the nations that we serve, to work together … to coordinate responses to emerging crises and to protect our shared interests,” he said. “We can help set the context for expanded geopolitical stability and the broader economic prosperity agenda that our leaders will tackle.”
Two Western officials said G20 members were in broad agreement about the severity of the economic challenges facing nearly every country as a result of the war in the Middle East. Many participants worried that renewed US strikes on Iran would send oil prices sharply higher, deepening the pain, they said.
“The possibility for a new military operation in Iran is on everybody’s mind,” said one of the officials, who spoken on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. “Everybody is under deep pressure.”
The foreign ministers’ meeting was expected to end with a chair’s statement, with the bigger effort focused on hammering out a joint declaration that could be signed by G20 leaders at their summit in December, Western officials said. It remains unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend the December gathering.
With G20 members Russia, China and middle powers such as Brazil and India trying to navigate US-China strategic competition, you have “much more of a split than we’ve ever had,” said Heidi Crebo-Rediker, who was chief economist at the State Department during the Obama administration.
Over the past decade or so, G7 countries would at least “have agreed a coordinated platform before they came to the G20, but now we don’t even really have that,” she added.
Ministers are expected to discuss supply chain issues and challenges in procuring the critical minerals needed to produce advanced technologies during their discussion on Saturday.
Rubio has championed the Pax Silica initiative, aimed at uniting G20 countries concerned about China’s dominance in rare earths and other critical minerals.
But any movement on that front will probably come afterwards, experts said, pointing to a US-led statement on excess industrial capacity that some G20 trade ministers signed after the group failed to reach consensus.
Elaine Dezenski of the Washington-based Foundation for Defense of Democracies said such statements by ad hoc groups could offer a way forward in the current difficult environment.
“The right test is whether the US can build cooperation with partners when all-member consensus appears to be out of reach,” she said. She noted the Quad — a security grouping of the US, India, Japan and Australia — would also meet in Atlanta on Saturday, on the sidelines of the G20 gathering.
US President Donald Trump’s recent decisions on Russia, including a deal to buy diesel and waiving some sanctions, formed a challenging backdrop for the talks, along with Ukraine’s problems with its Starshield satellite services, participants said. Ukraine was not invited to attend.
Washington announced a multibillion-dollar sale of Patriot interceptors late on Friday, offering some good news to Kyiv.
Before the meeting, European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she would call for increased support for Ukraine, while pushing for progress on accountability measures through the Special Tribunal and Claims Commission.
“Russia must be accountable,” she wrote on X.

The Federal State Unitary Enterprise Kamensky Combine is located in the city of Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, the Rostov region, at coordinates 48.322833, 40.243132.

The plant’s products are used in cartridges ranging from 5.45 to 14.5 mm in caliber, as well as in artillery and mortar ammunition, grenades, and rounds for 23–30 mm cannons.
The company also collaborates with the Russian JSC Scientific-Research Institute of Polymer Materials on the development of new high-energy compositions for propellants and artillery gunpowder.

The governor of the Rostov region confirmed a nighttime airstrike on Kamensk-Shakhtinsky and four districts in the region.

Pentagon officials have asked several NATO allies, including Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, to tone down public rhetoric about the threat posed by Russia, Reuters reported on October 30.

A Pentagon official declined Reuters’ request to comment on the substance of the discussions.

Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby was among the officials delivering the message, according to the report. Colby is also involved in an ongoing review of US troop levels in Europe.

The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia did not respond to Reuters requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment.

articles.title: Trade, sovereignty and reform: key Russia-Africa Summit 2026 takeaways
articles.body:
Trade, sovereignty and reform: key Russia-Africa Summit 2026 takeaways
Russia and African countries have agreed to deepen economic cooperation, strengthen political coordination, and push for reforms of global institutions, Russian President Vladimir Putin and African Union chair Evariste Ndayishimiye said in a joint press statement on Thursday.
Speaking at the conclusion of the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, the two leaders outlined the results of the October 28–29 gathering, which brought together senior delegations from 48 African countries, including 21 led by heads of state.
The gathering resulted in the adoption of three documents: the Declaration of the 3rd Russia-Africa Summit, the Declaration of Cooperation in the Civilian Application of Artificial Intelligence Technologies, and the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum Action Plan for 2027–2029.
Turning political solidarity into economic cooperation
Ndayishimiye said African countries are seeking to diversify their international partnerships and strengthen their sovereignty, with Russia playing a role in accelerating economic development and regional integration.
Speaking about the summit’s three-year action plan, he said that the leaders “outlined priorities, financing mechanisms, implementation schedules and areas of responsibility, and set dates by which expect to see results.”
The African Union chair called for greater Russian investment to help African countries create added value locally. He also stressed that African youth expected tangible results, including more scholarships, reliable energy supplies, and digital solutions.
Expanding trade and financial independence
Putin said Russia-Africa trade currently stood at $27 billion but remained well below its potential, and called to double it.
The Russian president noted national currencies, including the ruble, now accounted for 85% of settlements in commercial transactions between Russia and African countries.
Reducing technological dependence
Ndayishimiye called for reducing Africa’s technological dependence. He stressed the summit had adopted a separate declaration on artificial intelligence, advocating equitable international cooperation with a central role for the United Nations.
Putin said Russia and African countries had signed agreements aimed at introducing Russian digital solutions, including AI-based technologies, in African economies and public administration.
Africa must choose its own partners
Asked whether Africa risked becoming an arena for competition between major powers, Putin rejected the suggestion that Moscow viewed African countries as objects of geopolitical rivalry.
“We have not pursued any colonial policies. It is the opposite: we helped them to liberate themselves from the neo-colonial yoke,” he stated.
Ndayishimiye similarly stressed that African nations were no longer in a position where outside powers could determine their partnerships.
Reforming global institutions
Putin backed permanent African representation on the UN Security Council. “I am absolutely convinced that Africa must be represented there on a permanent basis, including in the Security Council,” he said.
Ndayishimiye reaffirmed Africa’s position on UN reform, while calling for greater representation in global financial institutions and closer cooperation with BRICS.
Strengthening security and humanitarian cooperation
Putin said Russia would continue consultations with parties involved in African conflicts and expressed hope that Moscow’s diplomatic efforts could help prevent further escalation.
He also pledged to expand cooperation in healthcare and education, including medicine supplies, mobile laboratories, and training for African students.
Russia’s epidemic-control assistance program for African countries has been extended through 2029, Putin said, adding that African partners supported expanding Russian university branches and educational centers on the continent.
Moscow Declaration sets out common political positions
The 101-point declaration, adopted in Moscow on October 29, is divided into five sections covering political and legal cooperation, security, economic ties, humanitarian cooperation, and environmental protection and climate issues. Here are its key points.
- Maritime security: Oppose the unjustified detention, seizure or arrest of civilian vessels, including African-flagged ships, in violation of international law. The document warns that such actions against commercial vessels turn maritime trade into “a tool of economic and political pressure.”
- Sanctions: Oppose unilateral coercive measures that violate international law, including measures imposed outside the UN Security Council, and strengthen coordination to reduce their impact on trade, energy, healthcare and food security.
- Sovereign assets: Oppose the freezing and attempted confiscation of sovereign assets, as well as political and economic coercion against sovereign states.
- Colonial reparations: Pursue legal mechanisms to assess and compensate for damage inflicted on African countries during the colonial era, alongside efforts to complete the continent’s decolonization.
- International justice: Counter the politicization and misuse of international criminal justice mechanisms, including their use to exert neocolonial pressure on African states, and strengthen cooperation to ensure the independence and impartiality of international courts.
- UN reform: Work toward reforming the Security Council to increase African representation, taking into account the continent’s common position under the Ezulwini Consensus and the 2005 Sirte Declaration.
- Counterterrorism: Strengthen cooperation against terrorist groups’ use of drones, encrypted platforms, and digital finance, while also addressing terrorist financing, organized crime, and maritime piracy.
- Arms control: Oppose the politicization of international arms control, disarmament, and nuclear nonproliferation mechanisms, and support compliance with existing treaties governing nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons.
- IMF and World Bank: Push for reforms to give African countries greater representation in the leadership of both institutions and more influence over decision-making.
- G20: Call for South Africa’s full and active participation in the group to be restored as soon as possible, while strengthening the voice of African countries and the wider Global South.
- Cultural heritage: Support the return of cultural objects and historical artifacts removed from African countries during colonial rule, alongside efforts to protect cultural heritage from illicit trafficking.
- Space cooperation: Expand cooperation in peaceful space exploration, satellite communications, Earth observation, and joint research, including spacecraft technologies and equipment.
- Trade and infrastructure: Expand cooperation in precious metals, strengthen industrial value chains, and develop maritime, river, road, rail, and aviation infrastructure. Remove trade barriers, increase African exports of value-added products and establish reliable financial settlement mechanisms to support trade and investment.
- Energy cooperation: Expand cooperation across oil and gas, nuclear, hydropower, hydrogen, and renewable energy to strengthen energy security and improve access to electricity.
- Education and healthcare: Expand academic exchanges, Russian-language education and joint research, while strengthening healthcare systems through medical training, laboratory development, and epidemic preparedness.
- Media cooperation: Strengthen ties between Russian and African media through the opening of representative offices, journalist training, information exchanges, and joint media projects.
- Climate policy: Oppose discriminatory protectionist measures introduced under the pretext of combating climate change, while expanding cooperation on climate adaptation and environmental projects that take national priorities into account.
- Sovereignty: Counter neocolonial practices that undermine states’ independence, restrict their decision-making, or facilitate the exploitation of natural resources, while upholding countries’ right to determine their own development paths.
- Conflict resolution: Support African-led efforts to resolve and prevent conflicts on the continent, guided by the principle of “African solutions to African problems.”

articles.title: Zelenskyy Warns Of Long Delay As US Approves Patriot Interceptors Sale
articles.body:
The US State Department has announced the approval of a critically needed sale of Patriot air defense interceptors to Ukraine worth $2.1 billion to strengthen Kyiv's defenses against increasing Russian aerial attacks that have been targeting civilian populated areas and infrastructure over the past few months.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, however, warned that the 500 missile interceptors could take “several years” to arrive.
Welcoming the US State Department’s move as a “strong decision,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post that “500 PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number” and could form an effective defense package this winter, but noted that “deliveries may begin only in a few years.”
“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” the Ukrainian president said while noting that that his country’s energy infrastructure is under Russian attacks.
The State Department said that the proposed sale of the missile interceptors, being purchased with funds from Canada, Germany, and Norway, will support the foreign policy and national-security objectives of the United States “by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe.”
The announcement of the proposed sale came after Zelenskyy repeated his calls on October 30, asking the United States to speed up the release of the interceptors, which are seen as the most effective weapon against the ballistic missile attacks from Russia.
In September, the European Commission approved 6.1 billion euros ($6.82 billion) in defense procurement for Ukraine.
This amount also included the purchase of US PAC-3 Patriot missile interceptors under special exception to EU rules. The European Commission did not specify how much money was allocated for these interceptors, citing operational security considerations.
At a closed-door meeting of the European Council in October, Zelenskyy told the participants how many Patriot interceptor missiles Ukraine would need to get through the winter.
Evacuation From Oleshky Completed
Meanwhile, evacuation of residents from the Russian-occupied southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky had been completed as Moscow and Kyiv continued to stick to the temporary cease-fire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.
Buses filled with civilians left the area for the first time in more than four years without any incident. The cease-fire is set to remain in effect until November 1.
Russian human rights ombudswoman Yana Lantratova said in a social media post on October 30 that after arriving in Ukraine's Russia-occupied Crimea, one convoy of buses then headed toward Russia, while a second convoy was bound for Ukraine.
"We are concluding our humanitarian mission in Oleshky. We are currently in the territory of Armyansk (in northern Crimea)," she said in a video posted on Telegram, adding that both sides had praised the high standard of its organization.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets confirmed the evacuation saying those residents of Oleshky who wished to travel to Ukraine were on their way.
"At this point, those who wished to leave Oleshky for Ukraine have been able to do so and are now on their way. Humanitarian aid has been delivered. The convoys have split up, and I am heading to Ukraine," he wrote.
Hundreds of Oleshky residents were expected to return to Ukrainian-controlled territory via a roundabout route: once in Anapa, in southern Russia, the civilians will head by plane to the Belarusian city of Homel, and from there by bus into Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region.
The circuitous route was needed to avoid roads along front lines that have been heavily mined and destroyed by the conflict, sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title: Zelenskyy thanks US over deal for 500 Patriot missiles but warns delivery could take years
articles.body:
Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian missile and drone attacks. The rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has praised the US for its "strong decision" to approve the sale of 500 much-coveted Patriot missiles to Ukraine - but he has warned that delivery could take years.
The US State Department announced on Friday that Washington had green-lit a package of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors worth $2.1 billion as Kyiv continues to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks.
"Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on social media in response.
"However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS," he continued. "We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors."
Earlier this week, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on a batch of missiles for both the Patriot and NASAMS systems.
Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian attacks, and the rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need. Russia has repeatedly sought to target Ukraine's power grid over wartime winter periods as Moscow has looked to break the country's resolve.
Dwindling stocks of interceptors have already encouraged Russia to ramp up missile attacks in recent months, and there are fears this trend could lead to an especially brutal winter for Ukrainians.
"The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses," Zelenskyy said overnight. "Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach."
The Patriot missile platform is one of the world's most advanced air defence systems and can be used to defend against a variety of threats, including incoming aircraft and ballistic missiles.
Ukraine receives the majority of its Patriots through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which facilitates the purchase of military equipment and munitions from the US by allies and partners.
As of June 2026, allies had committed to funding more than $6 billion of defence equipment for Ukraine through the scheme, per NATO.

articles.title: North Korea says sanctions don’t work to deny its status as nuclear weapons state

SEOUL, Oct 31 (Reuters) - North Korea denounced a joint statement by a group of countries monitoring sanctions enforcement against Pyongyang as a “wanton violation of its sovereignty” born out of hostility by the US and the West, KCNA state news agency reported on Saturday.
A statement issued this week by the group that includes the US, Australia, the UK and South Korea called on UN member states to fully implement UN sanctions resolutions that ban the use of North Korean workers and military cooperation with Pyongyang.
“Sanctions and pressure may work on the weak but never on us,” KCNA reported the country’s unnamed foreign ministry spokesman as saying.
“The stereotyped sanctions racket of the US and the West can neither influence the position of the DPRK as a nuclear weapons state,” the spokesperson said.
UN Security Council resolutions adopted starting in 2006 are aimed at ending the North’s nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles programmes.

The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks.
However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned it could take "several years" for the deliveries to arrive.
The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.
On Friday night Zelensky repeated his calls for the US to speed up the release of its Patriots – the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.

In an update on Saturday morning, Zelensky said around 200,000 households in the Dnipro region were left without electricity as well as at least 80,000 households in the Kyiv region following Russian strikes on Friday night.
He accused Russia of "deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure every day".
The US approved sale of Patriot missiles comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel.
The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east.
Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.
In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".
It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".
The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".
Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.
The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.
Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies that the country was running critically low on.
In a post on X late on Friday, he welcomed the US announcement but said Ukraine needed the Patriot missiles "right now".
He said Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter with "more than 30 Russian strikes" on "critical parts" of Ukraine's power grid over the past two weeks.
Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.
It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.
Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.
In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles - three weeks after offering the country such a right.

US approves Patriot missiles sale to Ukraine
The US State Department has green-lit a $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine.
The announcement follows a report by CNN earlier this month that Kiev had completely exhausted its stockpile of US-made interceptors used to defend against Russian missile and drone strikes at military-related targets.
The State Department said in a statement on Friday that the Ukrainian government had requested that Washington sell it 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles and spare parts for launchers.
Kiev will pay for the interceptors with funds donated by Canada, Germany, and Norway, the State Department said. “No US funds are involved in this sale,” it added.
The principal contractor for the deal will be Lockheed Martin, according to the statement.
“There will be no adverse impact on US defense readiness as a result of this proposed sale,” the department stressed.
The US depleted much of its Patriot missile stockpile during the war with Iran, which was widely reported by American media and confirmed in a Pentagon inspector general’s report last month. A separate Congressional Budget Office assessment said that the Pentagon had consumed between one-half and two-thirds of its inventory of certain missile-defense interceptors since June 2025.
However, US President Donald Trump has downplayed the shortages, claiming that American stockpiles are virtually unlimited.
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky reacted to the State Department announcement in a post on X, saying that he was grateful to Trump and that 500 Patriot missiles was “a substantial number.”
However, he complained that “it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin only in a few years,” while Kiev needs the interceptors “right now.”
Zelensky claimed US and European countries currently have “sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses,” urging Washington to find a solution that would see them supplied to Ukraine immediately.
“The Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day. In just these past two weeks of October, there have already been more than 30 Russian strikes on critical parts of our power grid,” he said.

Among other things, a heating and power plant in Kiev and workshops used for production of UAVs and weapons’ parts in Kharkov were hit, according to the ministry.

articles.title: EU to fast-track €45 billion for Ukraine amid acute financial crunch
articles.body:
In 2027, the EU will provide Ukraine with €32 billion in military aid and €13 billion in budget support. But more funds will be needed as Russia escalates.
The European Union intends to accelerate the disbursement of its €90 billion support loan to Ukraine as the country faces a financial crunch amid Russia's all-out escalation and blockade in the Black Sea.
The loan is split evenly: €45 billion for 2026, with payments underway, and €45 billion for 2027. Initially, the credit was meant to last until the end of next year, but the brutality of the war has upended the calculation.
As a result, Brussels will concentrate funds in the first half of 2027 to avoid a cut-off of assistance that could have catastrophic consequences on the ground.
The second €45 billion envelope will allocate €31.7 billion for the military and €13.3 billion for the budget, according to a strategy published on Friday by the European Commission.
The €31.7 billion will be paid out gradually as Kyiv submits new contracts for weapons. The submissions can begin this year to ensure timely deliveries in 2027.
The €13.3 billion will be conditional on reforms, some of which relate to Ukraine's accession process. EU leaders have urged the country to keep the legislative pace on track.
A €3.7 billion payment has already been delayed.
"We are providing Ukraine with much-needed predictability and helping maintain essential public services," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
"Together with our allies, we must also do everything in our power to mount pressure on Russia to stop its barbaric war of aggression."
Ahead of the announcement, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked Brussels to speed up disbursements.
"The sooner we start receiving the corresponding tranches for our drone production, air defence procurement, budget support and other vital expenditures, the better our position in 2027 will be," he said.
In the meantime, the Commission is searching for ways to fill the €70 billion shortfall that Ukraine faces next year, which will require fresh funding on top of the existing loan.
Commission officials insist the bloc will cover no more than two-thirds of the gap, roughly €46 billion, with the remainder to be handled by other allies. Joint debt has quickly emerged as the frontrunnerto plug the hole.
An internal document seen by Euronews identifies three main reasons for the deficit.
First, the prolongation of the war, now well into its fifth year. When Brussels designed the €90 billion loan, it did so under the assumption the conflict would end sometime in 2026. The premise, which raised eyebrows last year, has now come apart.
Second, the intensification of Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure and the blockade of the Black Sea, which are "weakening economic activity and Ukraine's capacity to raise domestic revenues", further compounding its reliance on global donors.
Third, the decrease in assistance from non-EU allies. The document says that if all NATO allies deliver on their pledges made at the summit in July, the gap in military aid will be reduced by up to €13 billion next year.
Ukraine's financial needs, the document adds, will be "largely determined" by the ability to resist Russia's airstrikes, which need costly US-made Patriot interceptors.
Kyiv has accused Washington of delaying Patriots that have been paid for with European money. The impasse has been linked with US President Donald Trump's insistence that Ukraine cease attacks on Russia's oil refineries, claiming they raise global fuel prices.
On Friday, a Ukranian drone attack was reported at the Novokuibyshevsk refinery in Russia's Samara region.

articles.title: Satellite Images Confirm Destruction of Two Su-34s by Neptune Missiles
articles.body:
Satellite images have confirmed the destruction of two Su-34 bombers as a result of a strike by Neptune cruise missiles on the Russian military airfield Marinovka in the Volgograd region.
The satellite images were published by the monitoring channel AviVector.
The strike on the deployment site of the 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment took place on the night of October 29. After the strike, satellites detected a fire at the aircraft parking area.
Judging by the published images, the Su-34 was completely destroyed. In addition, one of the aircraft hangars near the impact site was damaged as a result of the missile’s warhead exploding and the subsequent fire.
As noted by the OSINT community CyberBoroshno, low-resolution satellite imagery from October 28 shows that the Su-34 was already at the site of the subsequent strike, meaning this was its usual parking spot.
According to a statement by the Navy, the strike was carried out using Long Neptune ground-launched long-range cruise missiles.
According to estimates, this is the farthest publicly known use of this variant of the Neptune missiles. The likely distance the missile had to travel is over 600 km.
Compared to the original R-360 missile, the Long Neptune features a longer fuselage with a larger diameter, a modified nose section, enlarged control surfaces, and the new designation R-360L.
The stated flight range of the missile for the Long Neptune system is up to 1,000 km; the missile is 6 m long, has a fuselage diameter of 500 mm, and a warhead weight of 260 kg.
It is also claimed to be capable of flying over complex terrain, following a route without satellite navigation, and targeting ground targets.
The Long Neptune has been equipped with a new launch system mounted on a Tatra chassis, featuring two large square-section transport-launch containers — likely due to incompatibility with the old launch system resulting from the increased dimensions.
It was a strike by these missiles on Borisoglebsk airfield on October 15 that enabled the Defense Forces to destroy at least four Su-34 bombers and damage two more.

articles.title: UK Defence Secretary warns Putin may yet turn on NATO
articles.body:
Britain has to invest and has to be ready because President Putin is waging a war in Europe while saying he has no interest in one, the Defence Secretary has said, describing investment in capability, in the defence industrial base and in alliances as the things that make war less likely, according to remarks made to reporters in Glasgow.
Wes Streeting was speaking at BAE Systems Scotstoun, where a new offsets policy was announced. Asked by this publication what his warning that Britain has around a thousand days to be ready to fight and win a war means for the armed forces and for the public, and what sacrifices the public are being asked to make to get there, he said: “Well, we’re investing in our capability, we’re investing in our defence industrial base, and we’re investing in our alliances. Those things make us stronger, and the stronger we are, the stronger our deterrence, and the less likely we are to find ourselves at war.
“We don’t seek confrontation with Russia. We have no quarrel with the Russian people. But what we can’t avoid is the hard reality that at the same time that President Putin says he’s not interested in war in Europe, he’s currently waging one, and he gave the Ukrainians those assurances that he had no plans to invade only weeks before the Russian invasion took place.
“So in that climate, we have to invest. We have to be ready. And in terms of what we’re asking of the country, as the Chancellor’s Budget showed this week, we are asking people to make that contribution right across government, and so defence is our number one duty, our number one priority, and that’s why it’s my responsibility to make sure that every penny that goes in is well spent, and that every bit of value we can extract for jobs and growth here in Scotland and right across the United Kingdom is realised. That’s my commitment.”
The contribution he describes falls across government and therefore on departmental budgets, and his answer turned on deterrence, which holds that a force strong enough to make an attack unprofitable is a force that never has to fight.
He was speaking after the announcement of a new offsets policy, under which overseas companies winning British defence contracts worth more than £50 million can be required to put benefits back into the country worth up to the full value of the contract, through jobs, apprenticeships, factories, investment in British suppliers or transfers of technology. A central Offset Authority will agree, value and monitor each arrangement, and the policy applies to a select number of procurements from April 2027. Ministers consulted industry on the approach earlier this year.
Asked what role Scotland will play in the Defence Investment Plan, John Healey, who moved from defence to the Treasury and delivered Wednesday’s Budget as Chancellor, said: “Defence is our number one priority. We also announced today the defence secretary and policy, where people have seen this is a government that will direct our defence investment first and foremost in British jobs and British businesses. But there will be things that we need to buy from abroad and from allies.
“So Norwegians, for instance, are part procuring some of this portion behind us, and they will require us because they have a policy that we’re now introducing for the first time ever in Britain, which we call an offset policy. We will buy some of the things the Norwegians produce that we can’t here.
“Now, in future, when Britain places contracts abroad, we’ll make sure that those we place those contracts with invest in Britain as well, jobs, business support, innovation, so that we can make sure that every pound of British taxpayers’ money works twice.”
Norway ordered five Type 26 frigates from Britain in a £10 billion deal supporting 2,000 jobs on the Clyde, and Oslo has run an industrial cooperation requirement of its own for decades, obliging foreign suppliers of significant equipment to place work with Norwegian firms. More than £35.2 billion has been spent with overseas industry since 2016, eleven per cent of direct departmental expenditure with industry and commerce, while 85 per cent already goes to British firms.
Streeting also attacked the Scottish National Party’s position on nuclear weapons, responding to the First Minister’s claim that the government is leaving Scotland short of defence. He said: “We’ve got HMS Prince of Wales currently out on a major exercise now, so I think it’s very visible proof that what the First Minister said is both irresponsible and unfounded. I don’t think the SNP should be playing party politics with national defence and security.
“In terms of the risk of leaving the UK with insufficient defence, one of the biggest risks facing that security is the SNP’s position on unilateral nuclear disarmament. It is by far and away the most important deterrent that we have, and it’s not just the UK’s deterrent, it’s NATO’s deterrent. So any time the SNP says that a separate Scotland can be a NATO member, they have to first explain how their white flag policy on unilateral nuclear disarmament would work under a nuclear alliance.”
The party voted narrowly in 2012 to drop its opposition to NATO membership while keeping its opposition to nuclear weapons, a position that would require an independent Scotland to join an alliance whose strategic concept describes nuclear weapons as the supreme guarantee of allied security, while removing the British deterrent from Faslane and Coulport. New members are admitted by unanimous agreement of the existing ones.
Asked whether Scotland is a target for Russia, Streeting said: “The people of Scotland and people right across the United Kingdom can draw comfort and security in the knowledge that we have some extraordinary capability at our disposal. Across our armed forces, as well as our special forces, and the protection of the NATO alliance, and that principle that an attack on one is an attack on all.
“I don’t think that Putin would be foolish enough to seek a direct war with NATO today. What I can’t be certain of is that at some point in the future he might not try, and that’s NATO’s threat assessment, and that’s why we are building our capability, building our defence industry, including here in Scotland, and building our alliances so that we are strong and therefore able to deter any potential Russian threat.”
He added that governments across the United Kingdom and local councils should play their part in national resilience, work led by the Cabinet Office through the Home Defence Programme, whose public awareness campaign launched on 22 October.
Healey rejected the Scottish government’s claim that its budget is being cut by £650 million in real terms, telling reporters: “No, they’re wrong. The Scottish budget is bigger than it’s been before.”
The Budget set a target date of 2030 for defence spending to reach three per cent of gross domestic product, with the route to the NATO commitment of three and a half per cent by 2035 left to next year’s Spending Review, and the Defence Investment Plan is backed by £298 billion over four years. The Scottish defence economy is worth £2.5 billion and directly supports 12,200 jobs, including 300 roles in Edinburgh on a £453 million Typhoon radar contract.

articles.title: Iran's Khamenei warns US against attacks, orders military buildup
articles.body:
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned that any renewed U.S. or Israeli attack would trigger an immediate and geographically wider Iranian response, ordering the armed forces to expand their target lists, strengthen intelligence capabilities and accelerate weapons production.
In a written message following a meeting with senior military commanders Saturday, Khamenei said Iran would determine the timing and conditions for ending any future conflict if its adversaries resumed military or terrorist attacks.
He ordered the armed forces to prepare an "immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response" to any threat, stressing that maintaining a high level of combat readiness was essential to deterring further aggression.
"Intelligent combat readiness for a powerful confrontation with enemies is a fundamental prerequisite for achieving maximum deterrence," he said.
Khamenei also instructed military commanders to update their target database to bring "all U.S. and Israeli assets, tangible and intangible," within striking range, signaling an effort to broaden Iran's potential targeting capabilities in the event of another confrontation.
The directives included strengthening military intelligence, developing domestic defense capabilities and adapting military doctrine and tactics to emerging threats. He also ordered increased production of ammunition and weapons for reconnaissance, logistical support and combat operations.
The meeting brought together senior military officials, including Maj. Gen. Abdollahi, chief of the Joint Staff of the Armed Forces; Maj. Gen. Hatami, commander of the Iranian army; and Maj. Gen. Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The commanders briefed Khamenei on military readiness along the Persian Gulf coast, in the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, as well as along the country's northwestern and southeastern borders.
They also reported a significant increase in the production of key ammunition and various weapons systems for reconnaissance, support and combat missions. Khamenei expressed satisfaction with the preparations and asked the commanders to convey his appreciation to military personnel, police officers, Basij forces, Defense Ministry employees and their families.
Beyond military preparations, the supreme leader stressed the importance of strengthening the armed forces' ideological and spiritual foundations while addressing the welfare needs of personnel.
He also described public support as a central element of Iran's deterrence strategy, portraying continued public gatherings across the country as an extension of the national solidarity displayed during the 1980-1988 Iran-Iraq War, which Tehran calls the Sacred Defense.
Khamenei praised the resilience of the so-called Resistance Front, referring to Iran-aligned groups across the region, and highlighted closer coordination among operational fronts as a factor in shaping a new political and security order in West Asia. He expressed hope that such cooperation would encourage greater unity among Muslim nations.
His latest instructions come amid continuing tensions following the U.S. and Israeli military campaign against Iran, which began Feb. 28 and killed then-Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and several senior military commanders.
Iran retaliated with attacks against Israel and U.S. military assets across the Middle East, widening the confrontation and raising concerns about the security of regional shipping and energy supplies.
Although Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum in June following diplomatic efforts, disagreements over regional security arrangements and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz have kept tensions high.
The strategic waterway, through which a significant share of the world's oil shipments passes, has remained a major point of contention, with Iran maintaining pressure on maritime traffic as the U.S. sustains its military presence in the region and reported blockade measures affecting Iranian ports.
Regional diplomatic efforts, including mediation involving Qatar, have yet to produce a lasting resolution.
Iranian army spokesman Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia reinforced Tehran's warnings Saturday, saying a renewed confrontation would spread beyond its previous geographical boundaries if U.S. President Donald Trump launched another military operation against Iran alongside Israel.
"If the U.S. president once again embarks on another military adventure in the region under pressure from and inducement by the Zionists, the flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area," Akraminia wrote on X.
"And the end of the conflict will not be in his (Trump's) hands," he added.
Accusing Washington of repeatedly undermining diplomatic efforts, Akraminia said the Iranian army was continuously strengthening its combat readiness and closely monitoring U.S. military movements across the region.
His remarks came as Tehran and Washington remained at odds over the terms of any lasting settlement, particularly security arrangements and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his father earlier this year, has maintained a relatively low public profile since taking office amid the conflict. His previous warnings have focused on U.S. military bases in the region, the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's conditions for ending hostilities, including demands concerning sanctions, blockades and regional security.

articles.title: "A strong decision": Zelenskyy called on the United States to speed up the transfer of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
articles.body:
"A strong decision": Zelenskyy called on the United States to speed up the transfer of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy is asking the United States to provide 500 PAC-3 interceptors as early as the winter of 2026–2027. Providing them to Ukraine right now is the right course of action.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on the United States to speed up the delivery of 500 PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems to Ukraine. This was reported by UNN.
Details
The head of state called the US State Department’s decision to allow Ukraine to purchase interceptors for "Patriots" against Russian ballistic missiles "strong."
Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is significant, and soon—in the winter—it could be a very effective defense package. However, it has been determined that deliveries can begin only in several years. We ask our American partners to find a solution precisely when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3
He emphasized that the Russians are currently striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure every day.
In just the last two weeks of October, there have already been more than 30 Russian strikes on critical parts of our energy network. Right now, still on the eve of winter, Putin has begun carrying out his strike operation against the life-support systems of our cities and communities. The targets are electricity, heating, water supply, bridges, and life in the cities in general
He clarified that Kyiv had indeed asked the United States to provide Ukraine with a winter support package based on 100 interceptors for "Patriots" per month.
Five hundred missiles would be enough to protect our skies in the coming months—precisely when it is so important for Ukraine to be in a strong position in negotiations and for Russia to be unable to break life in Ukrainian cities and communities
He emphasized that the United States, European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses.
Providing them to Ukraine precisely now, in the winter of 2026–2027, and then replenishing the partners’ arsenals in subsequent years through this production, which has been contracted and paid for by Ukraine and its partners, would be the right path, and it is entirely realistic
The head of state thanked US President Donald Trump, the State Department, and the "US Administration as a whole for the authorization."
"But we ask that decisions be made that can guarantee the protection of lives not the day after tomorrow or sometime later, but precisely when there is a threat—when Russia is killing and destroying," Zelenskyy concluded.

The US State Department made a decision to approve the possible sale to Ukraine of 500 missiles for Patriot air-defense systems worth $2.1 billion.

articles.title: Pakistan military 'cautiously optimistic' on Iran-US mediation
articles.body:
Pakistan’s military is “cautiously optimistic” about its mediation between Iran and the United States, its spokesman said on Friday in his first interview since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.
Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir – Pakistan's chief mediator in its efforts to de-escalate the now eight-month-old Iran war – has been to Tehran twice this month, most recently on Monday alongside Saudi and Turkish officials.
“Why would the Field Marshal be going twice if it is not for some positivity? So yes, of course,” spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said when asked whether the trips were a positive sign.
Pact does not bar new members
“The word that we would use is always cautiously optimistic,” added Chaudhry, director general of Inter-Services Public Relations.
There were still "powerful spoilers and detractors," who believed conflict serves them, he added without naming them.
Speaking in the garrison city of Rawalpindi, where Pakistan's armed forces are headquartered, Chaudhry declined to say what was discussed or whether the United States had backed the trip.
Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin joined Munir in Tehran on Monday.
Their two countries signed a joint defense pact with Pakistan on August 7, saying an attack on any signatory will be treated as an attack on all.
The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement has taken on added significance as the Iran war has redrawn regional alliances and raised fears of a broader Middle East conflict.
While the three signatories say the agreement is aimed at collective deterrence and regional security, analysts see its evolution as closely tied to efforts by regional powers to manage the fallout from the Iran-US confrontation.
After Monday’s talks, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said regional security should be ensured by regional countries without foreign intervention.
The wording of the pact does not bar new members, Chaudhry said on Friday when asked whether Iran could join.
“Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome,” he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.
Asked whether more Pakistani troops were being sent to Saudi Arabia under the agreement, Chaudhry said that would depend on the situation and the decision of both countries’ political leadership.
He said Pakistan was committed to defending Saudi Arabia and the holy sites of Mecca and Medina. "We are not part of the Yemeni conflict, which is an intra-Yemen conflict," he added.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi terror group has been reignited by the Iran conflict, stoking fears of a wider war.
Home front
On the home front, the federal government suspended the provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, led by jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), on October 11 and detained Chief Minister Sohail Afridi.
The government had accused the provincial administration of failing to tackle militancy. The PTI rejected the allegations and said its government took part in counter-terrorism efforts. PTI leaders called the move a pretext to crush protests.
Asked if there would now be larger military-led campaigns in the province, Chaudhry said that was not how the army conducted counter-terrorism.
"Our counter-terrorism operations are based on what we call IBOs, intelligence-based operations... The tempo of the freedom of action of (those) IBOs will further increase," he said.
Independents backed by Khan’s PTI won the most directly elected seats in the February 2024 election but fell short of a majority. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was the only province controlled by Khan’s party.
Khan has been in jail since 2023, and his supporters see the military behind his imprisonment and the dismantling of the PTI. The army denies involvement in politics.

articles.title: New MOKH Module for Autonomous Navigation Appears in Geran Drones – DIU
articles.body:
Starting in late summer 2026, a new MOKH module began to be detected in Russian Geran-class attack drones. This module is designed to improve the accuracy of autonomous navigation without the use of a satellite signal.
A representative of the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) shared this information in a comment to Militarnyi.
According to him, the drone’s inertial navigation system has also changed with the introduction of the new module. Two additional sensors, located in the left and right wings, are connected to it. Together with the central module, they form a three-point measurement system that allows for more accurate determination of the drone’s motion parameters during autonomous flight.
“This creates a triangle—a measurable inertial environment—that allows for greater accuracy in autonomous navigation without satellite navigation,” explained the DIU representative.
According to him, even if other guidance systems are jammed, the drone will still be able to continue its flight to the designated area.
Accuracy in this mode will be lower, but the system should allow the drone to remain capable of striking targets without a stable satellite signal.
In this way, Russian developers are attempting to reduce the strike drones’ dependence on external navigation systems, which can be jammed by electronic warfare measures.
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) also notes that the overall trend regarding the use of foreign electronic components in Russian weaponry has not changed significantly.
In cruise and ballistic missiles, as well as in some attack drones, U.S.-manufactured components continue to account for the largest share of the foreign electronics identified.
A DIU representative named Texas Instruments and Altera among the manufacturers.
Products from STMicroelectronics and Chinese manufacturers are also found in Russian weapons systems. In certain types of Russian weapons systems, notably the Garpiya and Filin, the proportion of Chinese components already predominates.
The DIU representative also reported that Russian manufacturers are increasingly physically destroying markings on foreign electronics even during the weapons production process.
According to him, this is done on a massive scale on the assembly line to make it more difficult to determine the true origin of the components.
China remains one of the main channels through which foreign electronics enter Russia, as it is home to major distributors of Western manufacturers. Once the components are resold to local companies, it becomes much more difficult to track their subsequent movement.
