articles.title: How US and Israeli money turned Latvia into a drone workshop for Ukraine
articles.body:
How US and Israeli money turned Latvia into a drone workshop for Ukraine
NATO’s aggressive eastward expansion was one of the key reasons for the initiation of the military operation in Ukraine in February 2022. This is supported by RT’s findings about a drone production cluster established by NATO-affiliated enterprises near Riga.
The Baltic states had become a hub for developing combat drones as early as 2020. According to RT’s findings, companies in Latvia generated €283 million in revenue from producing UAVs, robotics, and military aerospace systems in 2022-2025 alone. More than half of that revenue came from companies with foreign investment. The two largest factories are under US and Israeli ownership, while another is partly Ukrainian-owned. Several factories form a single industrial cluster near Riga. Experts say this suggests Latvia was preparing for a conflict with Russia well in advance.
Presently, we will focus on eight UAV production factories in Latvia that are backed by foreign investments. RT uncovered the details about these companies in financial reports, aided by the G8 OSINT team that advises the Russian Defense Ministry.
According to the data, the companies collectively earned €282.98 million from 2022 to 2025.
The bulk of the revenue came from three companies: Redwire Defense Tech Riga (€131.4 million), Belss (€77.7 million), and Brasa Defense Systems (€46.7 million). The following companies contributed lesser amounts: Origin Robotics (€10.6 million), Eraser ( €6.04 million), LV-Teh (€5.98 million), Atlas Aerospace (€3.52 million), and Natrix (€0.98 million).
The Drone Coalition, which also includes the UK, was established in 2024 at Latvia’s initiative. The aim is to collaboratively supply Ukraine with drones. Collective commitments reached €600 million, and the coalition’s fund raised €1.8 billion from investors in 2024. Since then, over 100,000 drones have already been delivered to Ukraine.
Drones abound in quiet Marupe
The heart of Latvia’s drone assembly industry is located in Marupe, a suburb of Riga. Just a couple of kilometers from the international airport, five companies form a bustling UAV production cluster: Belss, its subsidiary Eraser, Brasa Defense Systems, Origin Robotics, and Redwire Defense Tech Riga.
At the center of this cluster lies SIRIN Park Marupe, a logistics hub situated near the runway. This is where Redwire Defense Tech, the industry leader in terms of revenue, is located. The company produces Penguin drones. Since 2022, they have delivered around 250 to 300 drones to Ukraine. Smaller models start at around $20,000, while some modifications can reach up to $70,000 each. The facility employs 279 people.
Nearby, at 26 Dzirnieku Street, there is Origin Robotics, which has around 60 employees. They specialize in building BEAK portable strike drones and BLAZE autonomous drone interceptors. Both models are used in Ukraine and are also part of Latvia’s military arsenal. By the end of November 2026, Origin Robotics aims to complete the development of a cargo drone system designed for precise automated delivery of cargo (i.e. explosives). In simple terms, the Latvians plan to equip quadcopters with guided mini-munitions.
Further on, in the direction of Riga, there is Brasa Defense, which occupies around 6,000 square meters of warehouse and office space at 16 Plienciema Street. They manufacture UNHUMAN ground robotic platforms designed to support infantry on the battlefield.
Located furthest from the airport, Belss operates in Ezisi Industrial Park. It is the largest defense communications integrator in Latvia (operating since 1994). The company formerly focused on secure military communications but pivoted in 2023 to develop its own line of UAVs. By 2024, they were supplying thousands of modular military drones to Ukraine. In June 2024, Belss spun off its drone division into a separate subsidiary named Eraser.
There are no doubts as to who is the primary consumer of Belss products: Latvian and Ukrainian flags are proudly displayed at the entrance. A satellite view reveals a private runway just 100 meters from the fence, used for testing equipment.
The other production facilities are located in Riga, but the difference isn’t critical since Marupe is very close to Riga. The area is home to the NATRIX, LV-Teh, and AeroVictory Baltic factories. The latter is a Baltic subsidiary of a Ukrainian company that has relocated UAV production to Latvia and has yet to submit financial reports.
Also registered in Riga is Atlas Aerospace – a company with Ukrainian roots and Israeli ownership – producing reconnaissance drones like the AtlasPRO, Atlas UAVs, and AtlasTETHER tethered systems. These devices are supplied to Ukraine and NATO countries. The company has 43 official employees.
The choice of location is strategic, according to specialists from the G8 group. In addition to proximity to the airport, a railway runs through Marupe that will soon connect with tracks leading to Ukraine via Moldova.
The father of ‘Penguins’ in the service of NATO
Latvia has its own key figure uniting several companies backed by American and European capital: Konstantins Popiks, a serial entrepreneur in the military industry. He was introduced to aeromodeling as a child and even represented Latvia in aeromodeling competitions. After enrolling at the University of Liverpool in 2005, he graduated in 2009 with a Master’s degree in aerospace engineering.
The Penguin reconnaissance drone and its combat versions, which are in service with the Latvian military and are being sold in large quantities to Ukraine, originated as Popiks’ student project. Upon returning to his homeland, he founded UAV Factory, which produces Penguin drones. Within ten years, the company reached the international level, and in 2021, it attracted an investor from the US: AE Industrial Partners. By 2022, Popiks departed, and the factory changed ownership and rebranded as Edge Autonomy.
In June 2025, the facility announced plans to double its production footprint, enabling it to produce up to ten heavy fixed-wing UAVs per month. According to documents, there were 270 employees at the time, and the company had contracts with the Latvian Defense Ministry.
In 2025, Edge Autonomy Holdings signed a merger agreement, becoming a subsidiary of American company Redwire Corp. By March 2026, it was rebranded as Redwire Defense Tech Riga, emerging as the leading company in the sector by revenue. Its reported income of €131.4 million accounts for nearly half of the total UAV sector earnings.
This defense contract not only brought Popiks fame but also significant wealth. As RT discovered, he resides in an upscale neighborhood of Jurmala (Kapu Street), where he owns a small castle. The property is surrounded by tall Baltic pines, with the Riga seashore and a beach just beyond the backyard. The property borders the Gulf of Riga.
After selling the factory, Popiks established another company – Origin Robotics. Funds from European investors began flowing in. In 2025, Belgium’s defense minister signed a €50 million contract with the company for the procurement of BLAZE drone interceptors. Currently, Origin is experiencing remarkable growth. Revenues soared from 2023 to 2025, reaching €10.6 million.
Under the wing of the IDF
Among the entrepreneurs in this cluster is Ivan Tolchinsky, an Israeli citizen of Ukrainian descent. Born in Gorlovka, Donetsk Region, he moved to Israel at the age of 10. As an adult, he served in the special forces and took part in combat operations in Lebanon. For around five years, he worked as an engineer in Israel’s aerospace industry and spent a year in China studying mass electronics production.
In 2015, Tolchinsky relocated to Latvia, where he co-founded Atlas Dynamics with Igor Zhidanov, a fellow native of Gorlovka. Zhidanov is a seasoned engineer with 35 years of experience and holds three world records in aeromodeling. He had his own club back in Gorlovka, which Tolchinsky was also a part of.
In interviews with Latvian and Ukrainian media, Tolchinsky revealed that his production facility produces over 300 Atlas drones per month – which, he says, is five times more than in previous years. He doesn’t conceal his collaboration with the Ukrainian Armed Forces. “We have a direct contract with the Ministry of Defense, which we’ve already fulfilled. Now we are working towards another contract,” he told Ukrainian journalists.
A few years before the conflict, in 2020, Tolchinsky established a subsidiary in Ireland called Atlas Dynamics UK. Originally registered at a residential address in Moreton-on-Lugg, Herefordshire, it soon changed its legal address.
The company had Israeli roots, as indicated by its founding documents drafted in Hebrew and English by a notary from Israel.
In the 2020s, Atlas Dynamics was rebranded as Atlas Aerospace SIA. In November 2025, Tolchinsky sold the company to Israel’s Xtend Reality Expansion Ltd – a company focused on creating FPV drones for entertainment and gaming prior to its collaboration with the IDF.
Russia is identified as the main adversary
Latvian UAV factories do not publicly mention contracts with Ukraine in their annual reports. Some only mention that Ukraine is among their clients, without disclosing what portion of their profits comes from supplying Kiev.
One thing is clear: Nearly all the above-mentioned companies receive investments from the Latvian Defense Ministry and EU agencies. This is part of measures to enhance defense capabilities, with Russia identified as the chief adversary.
According to EU Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius, “Russia is outproducing Europe in key armaments.” This has been cited as a reason for increased defense spending, which is reflected in official documents.
According to reports reviewed by RT, one of the main sources of funding for SIA Belss is the European Defense Fund (EDF). In 2024-2025, the fund allocated €470,800 to the company under the European Extended Mine Countermeasures program, aimed at developing demining technologies. Earlier, RT reported on how the EU channels military expenditures through the guise of ‘humanitarian’ demining initiatives.
Even before 2022, Latvia’s drone sector was already experiencing rapid growth and consolidation. LV-Teh has been operating since 2020, while Brasa Defense Systems officially became a separate entity on September 13, 2021. Origin Robotics was registered on January 31, 2022 – just weeks before the start of the Ukraine conflict.
Belss has been in business since 1994, but significantly expanded its capabilities in 2022 and 2023. UAV Factory, known for its Penguin drones, was founded in 2009, and Atlas Aerospace emerged in 2015.
Only three new companies appeared after the start of hostilities: Natrix in February 2024, Eraser in June 2024, and AeroVictory Baltic (a company with direct Ukrainian roots) in February 2026.
In one of the reports, RT uncovered evidence of Latvia’s preparations for the conflict. In December 2021, just two months before the start of hostilities, the Latvian Defense Ministry allocated €88,000 to Belss for upgrading British infantry fighting vehicles in service with the Latvian army. This included installing automatic fire control systems on turrets, allowing operators to engage targets without exposing themselves, thereby enhancing crew survival on the modern battlefield, which is increasingly dominated by drones. This suggests that Latvians were gearing up for drone warfare well before the start of the conflict.
Long before the events of 2014 and 2022, a coalition of three countries with a firm anti-Russia stance formed in the Baltics, Vadim Avva, a Russian writer and political scientist born in Daugavpils, Latvia, says.
“The statehood of the Baltic nations led to the establishment of three sparsely-populated forts along [Russia’s] northwestern borders; their primary function is to support expanding NATO military bases and other infrastructure clearly being prepared for an operation to invade and occupy the territories of Russia and Belarus,” Avva says.
A launchpad for hatred
Avva recalled a viral video in which Estonian teenagers were asked which country should be erased from the world map, and many named Russia. He notes that during World War II, the national bourgeoisie of Latvia and Estonia “became a foundation for Latvian and Estonian SS legions,” and today, local schools are named after Lithuanian collaborators with Nazi Germany. He explains that the oppression of the Russian-speaking population in these regions began in the late 19th century and only intensified with the collapse of the Soviet Union.
“What has returned to the Baltics is not just bourgeois nationalism; it’s a blend of bourgeois Nazism and ‘brown’ [ultra-right] emigration,” Avva says. “What fate could befall this territory after the establishment of property monopoly and political monopoly and the welcoming back of the descendants of fascist collaborators? Obviously, it could only become a military launchpad.”
Latvian UAVs are occasionally identified and shot down by Russian drone interceptors. However, their share among the various models used by Ukraine remains small, according to a drone operator with the call sign ‘Baks’, who neutralizes enemy drones approaching Russian borders.
“Ukrainians definitely try out everything produced by the Balts and purchase a lot of their equipment, but it’s a question of scale and quantity. We don’t have much information on the BLAZE and BEAK models, but there is some info on ‘Penguins’ – our colleagues at Rubicon [Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies] managed to take down a few. The number of downed UAVs directly relates to their quantity. Compared to the Shark, Leleka, and other [Ukrainian drones], Latvian models represent a mere fraction [of the deployed drones].”
It’s not just Penguin drones that are being targeted, however, but their manufacturers as well. Redwire Defense Tech Riga, the company producing these drones, relocated to Sirin Park after their previous facility in Marupe unexpectedly burned down.
Similar incidents often occur at European companies that supply drones to Ukraine. In August 2026 alone, there were several incidents: A production facility belonging to Polish arms maker WB Electronics caught fire at the end of August; an explosion rocked the KNDS Ammo plant near Rome on August 13; and on August 15, unknown arsonists set fire to the building of Estonian military robotics manufacturer Milrem Robotics, which RT wrote about in the first part of its investigation.

articles.title: EU, Canada Vow More Pressure on Russia as Ottawa Moves to Join €90 Billion Ukraine Defense Loan
articles.body:
The European Union and Canada pledged to intensify pressure on Russia and maintain long-term military, financial and diplomatic support for Ukraine, as Ottawa announced plans to join a €90 billion ($105 billion approximately) European loan program that would allow Kyiv to purchase Canadian-made military equipment using EU funds.
The commitments emerged from the 21st EU–Canada summit in Montreal on Friday, Oct. 30, attended by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In a joint statement, the leaders reaffirmed their commitment to Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders, while promising to increase pressure on Moscow and pursue accountability for crimes committed during Russia’s invasion.
The summit also produced a potentially significant development for Ukraine’s military procurement: Canada’s intention to participate in the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan for 2026–2027.
According to the Canadian government’s official summit backgrounder, the arrangement would enable Ukraine to buy military equipment from Canadian defense companies using European financing, helping Kyiv address urgent battlefield needs while expanding transatlantic defense-industrial cooperation.
EU advances €45 billion in additional funding for 2027
The announcement coincided with a separate European Commission decision on Friday to advance the remaining €45 billion under the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, providing another source of predictable financing for Kyiv in 2027.
Canada and EU Launch New Alliance Covering Ukraine, Critical Minerals and AI
Of that amount, €31.7 billion is earmarked for Ukraine’s defense industrial capacity, while up to €13.3 billion would support the state budget through the Ukraine Facility and macro-financial assistance.
The Commission’s proposal, which still requires approval from the Council of the EU, would make the remaining funding available by Dec. 31, 2027.
Von der Leyen described the measure as essential to ensuring Ukraine can continue maintaining public services and defending itself against Russia’s invasion.
“Together with our allies, we must also do everything in our power to mount pressure on Russia to stop its barbaric war of aggression,” she said.
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius emphasized Ukraine’s immediate military requirements, including drone interceptors, ammunition, missiles and air defense radars.
The Commission said it would continue working to accelerate European defense production and timely deliveries to Ukraine.
Canada’s proposed participation would complement that effort by potentially making Canadian defense manufacturers an additional source of equipment under the EU-financed procurement framework. Ottawa has not announced a finalized participation agreement or a specific Canadian financial contribution.
EU and Canada pledge stronger pressure on Russia
In their joint declaration, the EU and Canada promised to continue providing Ukraine with comprehensive political, financial, economic, energy, humanitarian, military and diplomatic assistance.
“We will further increase pressure on Russia and seek its accountability for the crimes committed in and against Ukraine,” the leaders said.
The statement did not announce a specific new sanctions package but reaffirmed a shared commitment to holding Moscow responsible for its actions.
The leaders also endorsed a comprehensive, just and lasting peace based on international law and the UN Charter, explicitly supporting Ukraine’s territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.
They pledged to continue efforts to secure the immediate and safe return of Ukrainian prisoners of war, detained civilians and children unlawfully deported or forcibly transferred by Russia.
The declaration specifically highlighted the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children, an initiative in which Canada has played a leading diplomatic role.
Ahead of the summit, von der Leyen also addressed the human consequences of Russia’s invasion during a speech in Montreal, noting Canada’s longstanding support for Ukraine and its efforts to help return children taken by Russia.
She emphasized that the partnership was rooted in the principle that nations must be free to determine their own future.
Beyond immediate military needs, the summit statement reaffirmed support for Ukraine’s long-term reconstruction, institutional reforms and Euro-Atlantic integration.
The EU and Canada said they would continue supporting reforms intended to strengthen Ukraine’s institutions and prepare the country for closer integration with European and transatlantic structures.

articles.title: Pentagon facing up to $15 bn in Iran war base damages – WSJ
articles.body:
Pentagon facing up to $15 bn in Iran war base damages – WSJ
Iranian missile and drone strikes have inflicted up to $15 billion in damage on military installations hosting American forces across the Middle East, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday, citing sources and its own satellite imagery analysis. The massive destruction adds to the Pentagon’s mounting war bill, which has already reached nearly $50 billion.
The newspaper’s analysis identified a total of 274 damaged structures across 24 installations with an American military presence. At least 119 buildings at 13 installations were damaged in the opening two weeks alone; the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain was among the hardest hit. Tehran launched a retaliatory wave of strikes following the unprovoked US-Israeli attack which started the conflict on February 28.
An unnamed US official familiar with the matter told the WSJ that the Pentagon estimated damage to bases from Iranian strikes – which became increasingly precise as the conflict escalated – at a minimum of $5 billion. Another WSJ source suggested that the number could potentially be as high as $15 billion.
Many installations are shared with Washington’s regional allies, meaning they could potentially pay for some of the damage, the report says, adding that the Pentagon may elect not to restore some infrastructure at all.
In particular, Washington is reportedly considering pulling back from its installations in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia so that its personnel would be out of reach. Tehran has previously demanded a full-scale US military withdrawal from the region as a prerequisite for sustainable peace.
Iran, meanwhile, has been rapidly restoring missile facilities and recovering buried weapons stockpiles, the report adds, noting that the military build-up comes as US President Donald Trump is considering further strikes despite shortages in American interceptor inventories.
However, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has been dismissive about Tehran’s military potential, saying in August that “They still have some capabilities, but it’s nowhere near what it was at all.”
Meanwhile, Democratic Senator Chris Murphy, a member of the Foreign Relations Committee and the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, accused the administration of seeking to “mask the true cost of the war” after being denied access to Qatar’s Al Udeid Air Base, where the WSJ identified at least a dozen damaged buildings. The Pentagon said that the ban was due to regional travel restrictions.
According to the Pentagon’s latest estimate provided to Congress, the Iran war has cost $47.1 billion through October 16, excluding base damage. The figure includes roughly $29 billion to replace expended munitions, $11.9 billion in operational expenses, and $6.1 billion in equipment losses.
As for the casualties, the US military now acknowledges 23 deaths linked to Iran war operations, including 11 from enemy fire, and 865 wounded.

articles.title: Russian victories, Spanish tragedy, elections without answers: RT stories that shaped the week
articles.body:
Russian victories, Spanish tragedy, elections without answers: RT stories that shaped the week
Russia’s diplomatic victories
Four years of unprecedented sanctions and an active conflict didn’t deter four dozen African nations from sending delegations to Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit this week. Forty-eight out of Africa’s 54 countries were represented at the summit, 21 of them by their heads of state.
More than 140 bilateral and multilateral agreements were signed, including a Russia-Africa Action Plan for 2027-2029, and a joint declaration opposing unilateral sanctions and the unlawful seizure of civilian shipping, pledging deeper counter-terrorism cooperation, and supporting increased African representation on the UN Security Council. RT covered the summit minute-by minute, and broke down Putin’s plan to help bring about the “second awakening” of Africa.
Before he welcomed the African delegations to Moscow, Putin held a rare phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb – a figure repeatedly floated as a potential EU envoy to Russia – and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store. Putin later said that Russia welcomes “any steps aimed at restoring full-fledged and comprehensive relations,” and while the call brought the Russia/Ukraine conflict no closer to an end, Russian analyst Sergey Strokan noted that it should serve as a warning to Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky that “metal fatigue is setting in across Europe’s political machinery – and that time is running out for the regime in Kiev.”
With the EU nowhere to be seen, and Stubb and Store incurring the wrath of their fellow European leaders for even daring to speak to Putin, the tone in the US could not be more different. There, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov touched down in Atlanta for a meeting of G20 foreign ministers on Friday. Sanctions on Russian diesel exports have been lifted, trilateral talks between Moscow, Kiev, and Washington are slated for next month, and Putin has been invited to the G20 leaders’ meeting in Florida in December. However, the most tangible result of Russian-American diplomacy came 5,000 miles away from Washington, in the besieged town of Alyoshki.
The Alyoshki breakthrough
Moscow and Kiev agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the frontline town of Alyoshki in Russia’s Kherson Region last Friday, with both sides agreeing to suspend all military operations to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and prepare for civilian evacuations.
The Kremlin confirmed this week that the ceasefire was coordinated by US First Lady Melania Trump, who said she was moved by the plight of Alyoshki’s “elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water.”
Ukraine had accused Russia of preventing civilians from leaving the embattled town, but residents who escaped earlier this month told RT that Alyoshki was besieged by Ukrainian forces, who carried out drone attacks on vehicles carrying food, fuel, and medicine.
As Russian forces got to work clearing mines from the roads surrounding Alyoshki, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that the humanitarian truce, if successful, “could set a precedent” for other areas. The interactions between Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmitry Lubinets, who worked together on the ceasefire, certainly seem to confirm that cooperation is possible.
Three elections, fewer answers
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva narrowly defeated right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday, in the first of three major elections this week. After a first-round loss to Bolsonaro, whose father was jailed last year Brazil’s Lula-aligned Supreme Federal Court, Lula won the runoff election by a margin of 51.79% to 48.21%, securing a fourth term in office.
The drama did not end when the votes were counted. Bolsonaro was ordered by the court to surrender his passports the following day, but he instead fled Brazil to the US, with the help of Argentina’s right-wing government. After landing in Florida, Bolsonaro accused Lula of fraud, declared himself “the leader of Brazil,” and pledged to “lead the opposition” from abroad.
US President Donald Trump is a close ally of Bolsonaro, and it remains unclear whether Washington will turn up the diplomatic pressure on Lula in the wake of the election.
Hours after Lula claimed victory in Brazil, former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic lost his bid to extend his party’s decade in power. Serbia’s Student List defeated Vucic’s SNS party by 53.03% to 38.97%, and despite accusing the students of doing the “dirty work” of “various European countries and the American deep state,” Vucic conceded and congratulated his opponents.
Although the Student List entered politics as an outgrowth of youth-led protests, its base is broader than similar pro-Western movements in the region. Student List representative Jovo Bakic told RT that his party will not sever relations with Russia or impose sanctions on Moscow, while representative Radomir Saicic has promised to negotiate long-term gas contracts with Russia.
However, the Student List has not yet chosen a candidate for prime minister, and Vucic has claimed that the party will walk back these promises in the coming months.
In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faced voters on Tuesday for the first time since Hamas’ October 7, 2023 attack plunged Israel into a multi-front war. Netnayhu’s opponents – most of whom differ little with the prime minister on matters of war and national security – accused him of corruption, incompetence, and failure to heed forewarnings of October 7. These arguments succeeded in destroying Netanyahu’s right-wing majority, but left neither him nor the opposition bloc in a position to form a government.
Enter the Arabs. Israel’s Arab parties almost doubled their representation in parliament, and are now in a position to play kingmakers – if only Netanyahu’s opponents would work with them. This outcome is highly unlikely, and as RT Middle East correspondent Elizabeth Blade reported, the only certainty is that somebody will be left feeling betrayed.
Spain’s train tragedy
The collision of two high-speed trains near the Spanish city of Toledo on Wednesday was the country’s deadliest railway disaster in more than a decade. At least 69 people were killed and 179 injured when a high-speed Renfe AVE train struck a stationary Iryo train on the Madrid–Seville line.
The crash happened at a time of political crisis in Spain, after weeks of anti-government protests over housing and inflation. While the circumstances are still being investigated, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is already bearing the brunt of public anger, with the right-wing Vox party blaming Sanchez and the left-wing Frente Amplio coalition demanding political accountability.
Fires were set outside the Spanish Transport Ministry in Madrid on Wednesday night, at a protest organized by the far-right Falange and Revuelta groups. “How many more people have to die before we throw these murderers and traitors out of our institutions?” Falange spokesman Federico Campanero said in a speech.
La manifestación frente al ministerio de transportes exigiendo la dimisión de Óscar Puente se calienta. La gente está hasta los cojones. https://t.co/KGcoYNeIjU
— Capitán General de los Tercios (@capTercio) October 28, 2026
Ursula von der Leyen’s Canadian debacle
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen arrived in Montreal on Thursday on what should have been a straightforward mission: secure Canadian energy and resources, expand trade links, and extract money for Ukraine and backing for the EU’s latest push into the Arctic.
Instead, she picked a fight with the EU’s largest member states – France, Germany, and Italy – by insisting that Canada will become an “associate member” of the European Union. Although the term “associate member” is a legal fiction, the French, Germans, and Italians had insisted that she swap it out for “ever closer association.”
Von der Leyen, as her subordinates have repeatedly complained to the press, is not the type to listen.
Star Wars becomes reality
In space, not even Elon Musk’s Starlink network is safe from Israel’s sprawling spy-tech sector. RT has covered the activities of private spies in depth in our ‘Wired for War’ series, and this week it emerged that an Israeli advertising company targeted Starlink users in more than 200 countries with pop-up ads that allowed multiple Israeli spyware companies to plant surveillance software on their devices without their knowledge. The company was the largest purchaser of advertising space targeting Starlink users in more than 100 countries, with the leaderboard – Palestine, Syria, Libya, Yemen, and South Sudan – suggesting that its clients were more interested in picking targets than customers.
Finally, the following video is not taken from an upcoming Star Wars movie, but from Antarctica, where footage of Russia’s revamped Vostok Station went viral this week. Built in 1954, the “sci-fi fortress” received a futuristic makeover in 2024, and now sits on stilts above the snow, 1,500km inland on Antarctica and operating in temperatures as low as -89C.
RT has more fascinating details on the Metal Gear Solid-style complex here, and for more on the coming week’s top stories as they happen – including the pivotal midterm elections in the US – keep an eye on our home page.

articles.title: Roshel has sent nearly 3,000 Senator vehicles to Ukraine
articles.body:
- Canadian manufacturer Roshel says nearly 3,000 Senator armored vehicles have gone to Ukraine, as one of its Senator MRAPs went on display at the Canadian War Museum.
- Canada committed 383 more Senators in February 2026, and Mexico, Moldova and a U.S. federal agency are also buying the vehicle.
Nearly 3,000 Senator armored vehicles built by Canadian manufacturer Roshel have now gone to Ukraine, the company said on social media as it placed one of its first-generation Senator MRAPs on permanent display at the Canadian War Museum in Ottawa.
The figure makes the Senator one of the most numerous Western-supplied armored vehicles in Ukrainian service. Roshel did not give an exact count or say how many of the vehicles were paid for by Canada, by Ukraine itself or by other donor countries.
“Nearly 3,000 Senators have gone to Ukraine, a symbol of Canadian support for those defending their country,” Roshel said.
The company’s tally has climbed steadily since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Roshel said it had delivered 1,400 Senators by the fall of 2024 and more than 2,000 by December 2025, and the Canadian Defence Review put the number at more than 2,700 this week. The Senator is used by Ukraine’s armed forces and its Border Guard Service to carry troops, evacuate wounded and run patrols and reconnaissance.
Canada’s own donations make up only part of the total. Ottawa announced its first package of 200 Senators in January 2023, worth CAD 90 million, and in February 2026 it committed another 383 Senators along with 66 LAV 6 armored vehicles from General Dynamics Land Systems Canada. Other countries have bought Senators for Ukraine through aid packages, and Ukraine has purchased some directly.
The Senator is built on a Ford F-550 heavy commercial truck chassis, a choice that lets Roshel produce it faster and more cheaply than purpose-built armored vehicles. The MRAP version, short for mine-resistant ambush-protected, meets NATO STANAG 4569 protection Levels 2 and 3 and is designed to survive the detonation of up to 8 kg (17.6 pounds) of explosives. Founded in 2016 in Brampton, Ontario, Roshel began building the Senator in 2018, mainly for police and security agencies in North America, before wartime orders from Ukraine expanded its production. Canada’s defense minister said in March that the program supports close to 500 jobs in Brampton and nearby Mississauga.
Roshel also sells the Senator well beyond Ukraine, including to U.S. federal agencies. NASA used a Senator to escort astronauts Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley to the launch pad at Kennedy Space Center for SpaceX’s Crew Dragon Demo-2 mission in May 2020, the first crewed launch from U.S. soil in nearly a decade. In November 2025, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement awarded Roshel a sole-source contract worth about $7.3 million for 20 Senator emergency response vehicles, CBC News reported, citing procurement records that said only Roshel could deliver within 30 days. ICE said the vehicles qualify under Buy American rules because they are produced in the United States; Roshel opened a plant in Michigan in 2024. The deal drew criticism from some Canadian politicians and advocacy groups over ICE’s immigration enforcement. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives is also buying a Senator for its special response team.
Elsewhere, Mexico selected the Senator MRAP earlier this year after trials with its armed forces and national guard, and Moldova’s military is due to receive more than 100 Senators funded by the European Union by May 2027. The company has also supplied vehicles to Haiti, Brazil, South Korea, Costa Rica and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

articles.title: Japan’s FM urges Russia to release journalist detained on Sakhalin
articles.body:
Japan’s FM urges Russia to release journalist detained on Sakhalin
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by Kyodo News, citing a statement from Japan’s Foreign Ministry.
Motegi and Lavrov met on the sidelines of a G20 foreign ministers’ meeting that began the same day in the U.S. state of Georgia.
Tensions between the two countries escalated further in early October when a Japanese journalist was detained on Sakhalin on suspicion of espionage.
Japan’s Foreign Ministry said Motegi and Lavrov had agreed to maintain communication despite strained relations.
In addition, Japan’s foreign minister urged Russia to take steps toward achieving a just and lasting peace in connection with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Motegi also clearly outlined Japan’s position on unresolved bilateral issues, including those concerning islands off the coast of Hokkaido that are under Russian control.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Lavrov had stressed during the meeting that Japan must abandon its “unfriendly policy” toward Russia if it wanted to restore full-fledged dialogue. The ministry added that Friday’s meeting had taken place at Japan’s request.
The first official meeting between the Japanese and Russian foreign ministers in about five years took place amid deteriorating bilateral relations following the sanctions imposed on Russia by Japan and other G7 members over Moscow’s war against Ukraine. The last official meeting between the two countries’ foreign ministers was held in September 2021.
As Ukrinform reported, Yuki Imai, a journalist with Japan’s Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was detained in Russia’s Sakhalin region shortly before his scheduled departure from Russia. Moscow’s Lefortovo District Court ordered his detention for two months, until December 12.
Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) claimed that the journalist had allegedly collected information about Russia’s defense capabilities “in the interests of one of Japan’s intelligence services.”
Japan’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador and lodged a protest over the detention of a Japanese citizen without prior explanation to the Japanese government.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi rejected Russia’s espionage allegations against the Japanese journalist detained by Moscow.

articles.title: European countries fear being sidelined in Russia–Ukraine peace talks but can’t agree on how to secure a seat at the table, FT reports
articles.body:
European countries fear being sidelined in Russia–Ukraine peace talks but can’t agree on how to secure a seat at the table, FT reports
European countries fear they could be shut out of talks to end Russia’s war with Ukraine, but they cannot agree among themselves on how to secure a seat at the negotiating table, or who should represent their interests and how, the Financial Times reported.
That anxiety has grown since Washington eased sanctions on Moscow and accused Kyiv of being unwilling to end the conflict. European countries worry that, ahead of talks among the United States, Russia, and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, Washington and Moscow could reach a deal without them on issues that affect European interests, including security guarantees for Russia and restrictions on NATO.
Driven by these concerns, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke by phone with Vladimir Putin on October 27. The call drew criticism from other European countries because the Finnish and Norwegian leaders had not secured their allies’ support beforehand.
According to the newspaper’s sources — European diplomats and officials — these uncoordinated attempts at contact, and the backlash they triggered, highlight the dilemma facing Europe: how best to convey its interests to Putin and Trump.
“Before we can talk about choosing a representative [for Europe at the talks] we need a chair at the table. Putin doesn’t want to include us, he wants to talk to Trump and so to put [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelensky in a corner,” one senior European diplomat said.
The United States is still involving Europeans in the negotiating process to some extent, the Financial Times reported. Washington and Kyiv have been considering the so-called European troika — the United Kingdom, France, and Germany — as the most likely representatives of Europe at the upcoming talks, but diplomats say that option risks provoking objections from other European countries.
Pentagon officials recently asked several NATO countries to tone down their statements about the Russian threat. The countries that received these requests include the Baltic states — Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia — among others, Reuters reported.
Moscow says there is no need for European involvement. Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov, for example, commented on the possible participation of European representatives in the new round of talks:
If they buy plane tickets, fly to Abu Dhabi, and hang around there somewhere, then from time to time the same Ukrainians, or even the same Americans, might report something to them, consult with them, maybe take some points of view into account — in other words, the process there could become more complicated.
What’s happening in Oleshky, where the war has caused a humanitarian catastrophe
- Minesweeping of routes for the humanitarian mission has been completed.
- A humanitarian mission, led by the human rights ombudsmen of Russia and Ukraine, has departed for the city.
- The evacuation of residents and distribution of humanitarian aid have begun.
The war in photographs. The aftermath of Russian attacks in Ukraine’s regions.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: US approves $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US approves $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
The US State Department said on Friday it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion.
Ukraine will pay for the defensive interceptor missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through the US JUMPSTART programme, along with national funds financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan, the State Department said in a statement.
Delayed missile deliveries added to Ukraine's tensions with the US after President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Zelensky for Ukraine's unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies, as Russia stepped up attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure.
The Ukrainian leader has repeatedly called on the US, which supplies missiles purchased by NATO allies under a programme known as PURL, to speed up deliveries ahead of winter.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defence and precision-guided weapons.
In July, the US Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to $58.6 billion to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.
Lockheed has said that deal would allow it to follow through on a promise to triple PAC-3 MSE production capacity by the end of 2030 and increase jobs at its Camden, Arkansas, plant by 50%, to about 1,850 from 1,200. Lockheed previously announced Patriot PAC-3 missile interceptor production would go to 2,000 units annually.
Pentagon negotiators are pressing contractors to move much faster, with tentative production agreements struck earlier this year at the centre of efforts to increase missile output.

articles.title: Star Wars: Has Russia's war with Ukraine gone intergalactic?
articles.body:
Star Wars: Has Russia's war with Ukraine gone intergalactic?
Russian made an unprecedented combative move this month as one of its military satellites, the Cosmos-2612, encroached upon the orbit of Ukrainian commercial satellite, Iceye-X36, in behaviour deemed "threatening" by the US State Department. Norbert Pouzin, an orbital analyst at French space tech firm, Aldoria, described the mercenary manoeuvre as the first of its kind.
Has space become a new frontier in Russia's war with Ukraine?
Russian military satellite Cosmos-2612 carried out a manoeuvre between October 15 and 18 that brought it “dangerously close” to Ukrainian commercial satellite, Iceye-X36. The move was described by US Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security as "threatening".
Operated by Finnish company Iceye, Iceye-X36 is a Finnish-American civilian satellite equipped with Synthetic-aperture radar (SAR) to provide satellite images to the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
The US State Department said Russia's tactic was consistent with “in-orbit military operations”.
Analysts specialising in space surveillance have been following Cosmos-2612 since its launch in April.
"Cosmos-2612 was one of six satellites launched in total. It was immediately apparent that this wasn't a classic deployment. As soon as they took off, the satellites started changing orbit to pursue Iceye satellites,” said Norbert Pouzin, an orbital analyst at Aldoria, a French space surveillance firm.
Cosmos-2612 took off on April 6, 2026 alongside Cosmos-2609, Cosmos-2610, Cosmos-2611, Cosmos-2613 and Cosmos-2614. KeepTrack, a site specialising in satellite navigation, enables viewers to track their paths.
Orbit re-routing – as has been the case of the Cosmos satellites – is a move that consumes a lot of fuel. It’s also the first step in approaching another satellite, Pouzin explains:
 "If two satellites are travelling in the same orbit, then they don’t need as much fuel to approach one another. Changing directions in space uses a lot of fuel. But once in the same orbit as another satellite, you’ve already executed the most costly move fuel-wise, if you then want to carry out an approach.”
From a kilometre to within just a few hundred metres
As the imaging data via site, Satellite Tracker, corroborates, Cosmos-2612 diverted from its original position – around 400-500 km from Iceye-X36 – to get closer to the Finnish-American satellite.
"On October 15, Cosmos-2612 was within 5 kilometres of Iceye-X36. Its position continued to narrow in on the satellite on October 16 and 17, before finally getting to within a few hundred metres and a kilometre of Iceye-X36 ,” Pouzin said.
Satellite imaging company Vantor published a photo of the two satellites on October 22, depicting their orbits withing just 1.02 kilometres of one another.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Data from KeepTrack also revealed that Cosmos-2612 and Iceye-X36 later embarked on the same orbit, meaning the Russian satellite was “following” the Finnish-American satellite.
A bold move
So why did Cosmos-2612 carry out this “threatening” manoeuvre?
Given the lack of debris, it doesn’t appear that Iceye-X36 was the target of a “kinetic” attack – that is, a physical strike involving a collision or the launch of a projectile. But according to Pouzin, the manoeuvre by Cosmos-2612 could be interpreted as a form of exerting pressure on Ukraine, as it is the direct recipient of the data gathered by the Iceye satellite:
 "SAR satellites have unique observation plans [Editor’s note: a schedule that coordinates how radar satellites can scan specific parts of the planet.] If an operator knows about these, then he could – for a short time – disrupt the satellite’s mission, potentially causing repercussions for ground-based or maritime operations, for example."
Cosmos-2612’s move seemed to shock Western commentators, he added:
 "While Russia regularly launches military satellites in the same orbital planes as classified American military satellites; carrying out this particular kind of approach on a commercial satellite while in a low orbit is something new. Furthermore it seemed to be non-cooperative in nature: we are dealing with two actors who are not on the same side and these are satellites not operated by the same entity."
The initiative also revealed something about Russia’s capabilities, Pouzin concluded:
 "The move demonstrated a certain agility by the Russian operator, a skilled knowledge of the space domain, and a very high level of mastery in this type of navigation.”

articles.title: Putin’s African ties: Military cooperation, “history” wars, and sanctions
articles.body:
Russia and a range of African countries have adopted declarations on political and economic cooperation following the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow. In the outcome documents, the parties agreed to counter the “rewriting of history,” the blocking of sovereign assets, and the politicization of international justice while working to foster cooperation in security, space, mineral extraction, and AI. Vladimir Putin said that Russia already has agreements on military and military-technical cooperation with 45 African nations. The Insider has compiled the main statements and agreements of the two-day summit.
The third Russia–Africa summit took place in Moscow on Oct. 28–29, with delegations from 48 of the continent’s 54 countries in attendance. Two dozen states were represented by high-level officials, with sessions co-chaired by Putin and Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, who currently heads the African Union.
As a result of the gathering, the parties adopted three main documents: the final declaration of the summit, a declaration on cooperation in the civilian use of AI, and the action plan of the Russia–Africa partnership forum for 2027–2029. In addition, more than 60 official agreements were signed at the summit and at the parallel economic and humanitarian forum, Russian presidential adviser Anton Kobyakov announced via Telegram.
Countering sanctions, “rewriting of history,” and colonial legacies
A significant part of the final declaration is devoted to international politics. Russia and the African states in attendance agreed to oppose the blocking and seizure of sovereign assets, as well as to resist outside political and economic pressure. The parties intend to coordinate their positions when it comes to sanctions against African countries.
The summit participants also agreed to counter attempts at “rewriting and falsifying history.” These and other provisions are included in the final declaration, which consists of 101 points.
Another area will be assessing the damage “inflicted on African states during the colonial period.” Russian scientists are already developing a methodology for such assessment jointly with African colleagues. Preliminary results should be presented in 2027, and a special research laboratory is expected to open in Uganda in November 2026.
In his speech on Oct. 28, Vladimir Putin accused Western countries of trying to preserve Africa’s economic dependence and impose new debt obligations on it. The Russian president claimed that Moscow is ready to transfer technology and foster production on the continent.
African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf stressed in his speech that African states are interested in developing local industry and gaining access to international capital. He also called for reforming the U.N. Security Council by expanding African representation.
Military cooperation and fight against terrorism
Putin stated that Russia has intergovernmental agreements on military and military-technical cooperation in effect with 45 African states, noting that Moscow trains African servicemen and law enforcement officers at Russian educational institutions.
In the final statements, the parties reaffirmed their intention to expand cooperation in the fight against terrorism and extremism, counter the use of new technologies by terrorist organizations, and develop joint security mechanisms.
Special attention was paid to the Sahel states: Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger. Commenting on the statement of Assimi Goïta, the head of Mali’s military government, Putin stressed the global importance of resolving the situation in the Sahel.
Russia’s military presence in the region has expanded in recent years. After the Wagner Group wound down its activities following the death of founder Yevgeny Prigozhin in August 2023, Russia's state-run Africa Corps stepped in to take over the role in several African states. Russian military units currently operate in Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso, and the Central African Republic.
Two days ahead of the summit, African branches of Amnesty International appealed to its participants with a call to demand that Moscow stop the deceptive and coercive recruitment of citizens of African states to take part in the war against Ukraine. Human rights activists claim that Russia recruits foreigners under the guise of employment and then sends them to the front.
AI, space, and control over technology
The summit participants devoted a separate declaration to cooperation in AI — to promote equal and fair access to safe AI technologies, the development of joint educational programs, and capacity-building efforts. Satellite communications and the use of space were discussed separately.
According to Putin, approximately 40,000 students from African countries are studying in Russia, and Moscow is expanding training programs for foreign civil servants, including in the digitalization of public administration. Putin also characterized Russia as being one of three countries with full digital sovereignty — a claim The Insider has examined in its Antifake section.
Precious metals, nuclear power plants, and trade
The economic part of the summit focused on energy, transportation, agriculture, and the mining and processing of minerals.
Russia’s Rusal and the state-owned Ghana Integrated Aluminium Development Corporation agreed to create two joint ventures in Ghana. The companies plan to develop the Nyinahini deposit with annual output of up to 5 million metric tons of bauxite and build an alumina refinery with a capacity of 1.2 million metric tons per year, with Rusal receiving controlling stakes in both ventures. Reuters notes that the company is seeking to reduce its dependence on external suppliers of raw materials after losing part of its supplies from Ukraine and Australia in 2022.
Ghana’s President John Dramani Mahama also announced the start of negotiations with Rosatom on building the country’s first nuclear power plant.
According to Putin, Russia’s trade with African countries reached $27 billion in 2025, and since 2023 Moscow has opened eight new embassies on the continent. In the near future, Botswana, Seychelles, and Togo intend to open diplomatic missions of their own in the Russian capital.
Putin also said that in the first nine months of 2026, Russia had supplied African countries with 13 million tons of agricultural products. Deliveries of mineral fertilizers, he said, exceeded 2.2 million tons this year, compared with 1.5 million tons for all of last year.
Trade with Africa remains significantly below the level promised by Putin
Despite claims of successful cooperation, Russia’s trade with Africa has not yet reached the level that Putin promised at the first summit in 2019. As Chatham House notes, the Russian leader set a goal of bringing trade turnover to $40 billion; however, in 2025, it totaled only $27 billion. For comparison, also according to data cited by Chatham House, China’s trade with African countries reached $348 billion in 2025, and the European Union’s was about $395 billion.
At the same time, Russia continues to expand its political and military presence on the continent. Earlier, The Insider described how Moscow uses cooperation with African governments to gain access to natural resources and strengthen its influence in international organizations.
Six days before the current summit, The Insider identified a GRU officer who in April 2025 infiltrated the diplomatic residence of the African Union in Ethiopia. He turned out to be Alexander Dubikov, who worked undercover as an assistant to the Russian military attaché and is linked to hackers from the Sandworm group. The incident occurred at a compound used by the current chairperson of the African Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, who also took part in the Moscow summit.
Dialogue with Europe, possible war, and situation in the Baltic Sea
At the press conference following the summit, Putin took questions about relations with Europe. Commenting on his Oct. 27 phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Putin said the European leaders themselves initiated the call, stressing that they were acting in their national capacity, not on behalf of the European Union. Despite being critical of his counterparts, Putin called the conversation the right step and supported attempts to restore dialogue with European countries.
Nevertheless, Putin said that Russia is ready for war with Europe, even if it does not seek one. He criticized statements by European politicians about the need to prepare for a possible military conflict by 2030 and expressed confidence that Russia cannot be dealt a strategic defeat. “If it goes too far, there will be no winner at all,” he commented, adding that Russia remembers the lessons of the First and Second World Wars and is doing everything it can to prevent reliving them.
Finally, Putin touched on the situation in the Baltic Sea, which he had discussed with the leaders of Finland and Norway. According to Putin, his Nordic interlocutors had invoked the need to comply with international maritime law. Putin supported their position but warned that a situation similar to what is happening in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz could develop in the Baltic. Russia, according to him, does not want such a development but is ready to respond to any challenge.

articles.title: Azov says it struck more than 100 Russian trains in occupied Donbas in four months, in part thanks to donations
articles.body:
Fighters of the 1st Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine "Azov" struck more than 100 Russian trains carrying fuel and other supplies for occupying forces, the corps reported on social media on 28 October. The strikes disabled locomotives, fuel tank cars, and other equipment, the statement said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed on 16 October that seizing all of Donetsk Oblast remains one of Russia's main tasks. Azov notes that these strikes help "destroy" Russia's offensive capabilities.
Small Ukrainian drones strike Russia's 100-ton locomotives
Azov emphasizes that neither mobile fire groups nor electronic warfare systems can protect Russian logistics routes.
"The enemy is doing its utmost to create an image of successfully capturing settlements, but is unable to protect key railway stations through which the fuel supply chain runs toward the front," Azov said.
The rail hubs hit had carried Russian military trains to the fighting in Donbas and southern Ukraine, Defense Express reported on 29 October. The count of more than 100 trains covers Azov's operations over the past four months, the outlet said.
The mass of any diesel locomotive exceeds 100 tons, yet the Ukrainian military struck these large Russian targets using small UAVs, the outlet also notes.
Donations helped make the strikes possible
Donations and the work of the Come Back Alive foundation contributed to the operation's results, Azov said. In particular, the foundation provided the military with 440 Starlink Mini terminals, the corps added.
Azov announced Operation Hell back in the summer
On 2 July, the Azov Corps announced Operation Hell and released the first footage of strikes on Russian railway equipment. The video shows a strike on a diesel locomotive that was likely used by Russian forces for military logistics.
The corps said the strike was part of a carefully planned operation and promised details soon.
