articles.title: As Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s best-known independent newspapers, is forced to close after 33 years, three former staffers look back on its legacy
articles.body:
As Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s best-known independent newspapers, is forced to close after 33 years, three former staffers look back on its legacy
Novaya Gazeta has announced that it is closing. For more than 30 years, it covered Russia’s biggest events and told stories about Russians that readers couldn’t find anywhere else. Many outstanding journalists worked at Novaya. Some were killed for telling the truth. Meduza asked former Novaya Gazeta journalists Ekaterina Glikman, Elena Kostyuchenko, and Nadya Yurova to reflect on three decades of work by one of the country’s most important independent publications, which they were all part of.
Warning: This article contains profanity.
Ekaterina Glikman
Special correspondent and deputy editorial director at Novaya Gazeta from 2002 to 2022. Now deputy editor in chief of Novaya Gazeta Europe
My last years of high school coincided with Novaya Gazeta’s best years. I couldn’t get enough of it. Maybe that’s just my impression, but 1997 and 1998 were brilliant years. Above all, because of its star lineup of journalists. Novaya Gazeta was always a paper built around individual writers: Everyone had a very distinctive style, and the articles were fairly opinionated.
That’s not how people write now — everything has to be uniform, polished, and objective. There’s probably something to that; times have changed. But I miss that journalism, where the writer’s voice came through. You could start reading an article halfway through, without looking at the byline, and know who wrote it. Every writer was recognizable. I loved them all.
For my very first university internship, in 1998, I ran straight to Novaya — without arranging anything beforehand. I wanted to be like all those journalists, starting with [investigations editor Yuri] Shchekochikhin. I’m not sure Novaya deliberately recruited young people, but there were lots of kids like me.
Ekaterina Glikman on Yuri Shchekochikhin
I remember Novaya’s old website — it was terribly dated. There were two buttons in the menu linking to memorial pages: “Politkovskaya” and “Shchekochikhin.” For years afterward, I’d click on them to read their articles, until the old website was replaced. Shchekochikhin’s memorial site had an archive of his articles, people’s memories of him, and his prose.
For the first anniversary of his death, we put together a book of memories — a white cover with his signature on it. It was later reissued and expanded. We asked everyone who knew and loved him to write a short chapter. Those chapters were then posted on the memorial site.
Unfortunately, I don’t have any of it with me: I couldn’t take anything with me when the war began, and I can’t travel to Russia anymore. I’d like to reread it now — but I have neither the book nor the website. My whole library is still in Russia.
I joined Novaya in 2002, working in Yuri Shchekochikhin’s investigations department. Before that, I’d worked at the newspaper Segodnya, which was shut down [in 2001]. Salaries at Novaya were terribly low. You couldn’t survive on them. I really wanted to work there, but once you were no longer a student and had to pay rent, it was impossible. I’d stand at the newsstand at the journalism school, looking at the national newspapers — and I didn’t want to work for any of them. There was nowhere to go except Novaya. I had to resign myself to living in poverty but doing what I loved.
I think Shchekochikhin initially screened out most of my story ideas [for my safety]. Of course, that made me absolutely furious. But given how young I was then [Glikman was under 30 at the time], it’s understandable. My favorite kind of work was investigative reporting in the field: from Kuzbass, for example, about miners who’d died, or from Kamchatka, about a man wrongly sentenced to life in prison.
From 2004 to 2006, the last two years of Politkovskaya’s life, I was deputy to editorial director Sergei Sokolov. He handed some of his work over to me. That meant Politkovskaya’s articles, Chechnya — all the hardest stuff.
Novaya had like-minded colleagues at other outlets who reported on realities that made ordinary people uncomfortable. But some outlets were shut down, like Segodnya, and many others willingly turned to sensationalism to rake in cash. Novaya had to pick up the slack for everyone. There were so many stories that nobody but us would write that we could barely cram them into our poor little newspaper.
Everyone disliked us for that — except our loyal readers, who refused to give up access to information. Mainstream readers saw us as a fringe newspaper obsessed with misery. They preferred the sensationalist press, where they could find entertainment and gossip and hide from unpleasant information.
Of course, there are people now who read using a VPN. There aren’t that many of them, but it’s still worth it: This group will play an important role when change comes. But we’ve lost the mass audience. And that audience has lost more than objective information — it’s lost an understanding of the world.
To me, the scariest thing about propaganda isn’t the lies; it’s what gets left out. They don’t actually lie that much. Mostly, they leave things out. And we may even underestimate the effect. When refugees from the Belgorod region fled the shelling for neighboring regions, people there mistook them for Ukrainian refugees — they simply didn’t know the Belgorod region was being shelled.
Novaya was a very influential newspaper. Ministers were removed after our stories came out — remember what happened to [Yevgeny] Adamov. All the top officials read our investigations.
If you look through the print editions, you can barely find an issue without a piece by Politkovskaya. Because if someone had been abducted in Chechnya, the story had to be published as quickly as possible: If the person hadn’t been killed yet, there was a pretty good chance that publishing it in Novaya Gazeta could save them.
Here’s another example. It was 2003, the year Shchekochikhin was murdered. One of the investigations he did let me pursue was about the fishing mafia in the Far East (in fact, it wasn’t a mafia at all — it was the state). We planned a major series of investigations and published only a brief preview, not even the first installment. And after that tiny introduction, I was immediately invited to see the fisheries minister at the State Fisheries Committee, as it was called then. If we had no influence, why would the minister bother inviting a journalist in for a conversation?
On the other hand, many journalists felt disappointed, frustrated, and depressed. You write story after story about outrageous injustices, and nothing changes. Years go by, and suddenly you catch yourself describing the same situation you wrote about two years ago: a different region, a different official’s name, the same schemes. Sometimes even the region is the same — there was one governor, and now there’s another. A lot of people hit a wall with their work; some quit.
Journalism is an alarm that starts flashing and screeching when there’s smoke. Without it, one disaster follows another, until there’s no way out.
It’s very natural not to want to worry about other people’s problems. Why spoil a lovely moment by reading that a missile hit an apartment building in Ukraine today? Looking away isn’t a Russian trait — it’s a perfectly healthy reaction people have all over the world.
Real journalism gets in the way of that comfortable life. A thorn in your side. An irritant. But without it, we won’t have the very comfort we love so much.
Now I find myself wondering: Could we really do all that? When everything has been wiped out, censorship is total, and journalism and free speech have been destroyed, you keep thinking: Wow, back then we could actually write things, go places, talk to people.
Federal troops are killing people in one of the country’s regions [Chechnya]. Abducting civilians, carrying out “mop-up operations.” And Novaya Gazeta journalist Anna Politkovskaya goes to those villages to talk to the residents, and we publish it: who was abducted, who was killed, who was tortured, how they were tortured, where the body was found, and what condition it was in. In 2026, it’s hard to imagine that was ever possible.
Yes, journalists in Russia are threatened, beaten — even killed. But until 2022, we were publishing stories from inside the country about war crimes committed by our own country’s army.
Around the world, journalism is increasingly done at a desk rather than out in the field. But I hope reporting in the field survives. It’s the heart of real journalism — nothing can replace it. But the skills are disappearing, and there’s no one to learn from.
Because of the war and emigration, I suddenly found myself one of the few people in the [Novaya Gazeta Europe] newsroom who’d known Politkovskaya personally. All your life in Moscow, you were one of the younger ones, surrounded by so many people whose memories went back further — and suddenly people like me were the oldest.
I remember Shchekochikhin; I remember Politkovskaya. When she was killed, I was on the team putting that issue together. I was in the thick of so many events — I just never thought that was valuable. And then you suddenly realize you’re carrying all these memories, and you need to tell people how it happened.
Elena Kostyuchenko
Correspondent at Novaya Gazeta from 2005 to 2022
I remember exactly how I first found out about Novaya Gazeta.
I was 14, waiting to see the dentist, and I was really scared. It was going to be a long wait. There were some fashion magazines lying around, but I couldn’t look at them — I actually felt sick. I went outside. There was a newsstand nearby, and I decided to buy something. I noticed a newspaper I’d never seen before, because, as I later learned, Novaya Gazeta sold out very quickly.
I bought it, sat down on a bench in a little park, and opened it to an article. It was Anna Politkovskaya’s piece about a “mop-up operation” in the village of Mesker-Yurt, where Russian soldiers had killed 36 people, if I’m remembering correctly. And one of the local residents had been crucified. I was deeply shaken — I don’t even really remember the dentist’s appointment, because in my head I was still back there.
Afterward, I went to the library and asked for back issues of Novaya Gazeta. I sat there and read them all, one after another. And the more I read, the worse I felt, because I realized I knew absolutely nothing about my country, even though I’d thought I was a pretty well-informed girl, that I’d read a lot and seen a lot. And here were people writing things that didn’t fit my picture of the world at all — a picture that included, for example, “our boys,” “our valiant troops” in Chechnya protecting local people from terrorists.
After Politkovskaya’s articles, I didn’t believe that anymore. At first I was angry at Novaya Gazeta and at Politkovskaya personally. The way she writes, you can’t ignore it anymore, can’t push it out of your head — it stays with you.
Then I realized that this was what journalism was actually about. It has to bring people back to reality, even when they really don’t want to come back. That was when I decided I wanted to work at Novaya Gazeta and started thinking about how to get there.
I lived in Yaroslavl, and my family was dirt-poor. I needed to move to Moscow. The best idea I could come up with was to get into a university with a dorm. The only university I knew in Moscow was Moscow State University, so I applied there, and they accepted me. I’m still very grateful to Moscow State — it’s a wonderful place to grow up.
And here’s how I got into Novaya Gazeta. Russian media outlets usually hired people who’d made a name for themselves, who had experience and qualifications. Novaya Gazeta took us in when we were practically babies and helped us grow into journalists. My plan was to stand outside the newsroom door — like, “Take me on for anything, I’ll mop floors, make coffee, whatever you want.”
But I got lucky. I was writing poetry then, and I was shortlisted for a poetry competition whose judges included Oleg Khlebnikov, who worked on the paper’s culture desk. Oleg noticed me, this girl staring at him, found out from his colleagues that I was studying journalism, and came over: “Your writing’s quite good! You probably have an internship coming up. Would you like to do it at Novaya Gazeta?”
The first person I saw when I came to the newsroom was Politkovskaya. I didn’t recognize her, because Novaya Gazeta was in black and white then. So Oleg and I are walking along, and this incredibly beautiful woman comes flying down the hallway toward us. I ask Oleg, “Who’s that?” And he says, “Oh, that’s Politkovskaya.”
Oleg worked out pretty quickly that I wasn’t especially interested in writing about culture and sent me to the reporting team. That decision shaped my whole life. Nugzar Mikeladze — one of Novaya’s founders — taught an incredible number of reporters everything we know. Not just about journalism, but about being human.
When I joined Novaya Gazeta, I didn’t even know how to turn on a computer! And Nugzar sent me straight out into the field — to Khodorkovsky’s trial. Naturally, I had no idea who Khodorkovsky was or where the trial would be.
To me, one of the most important stories Novaya Gazeta covered was the shelling of parliament in 1993. That was a turning point: I think that was when Russia chose an undemocratic path. Putin won the election in part because people didn’t believe in democracy. Unlike many other supposedly “democratic” publications, Novaya Gazeta — which had only just been founded — didn’t support the shelling.
I also think everything Politkovskaya did was extremely important. Take her reporting on the Nord-Ost hostage crisis. That piece is special to me because it never lost sight of the human beings involved. Despite what was happening, Politkovskaya saw the terrorists as people.
That’s probably the most important thing she taught me and a whole generation of journalists — there’s no virtue in dehumanizing people. Even with an assault rifle pointed at them, journalists have a duty to see the person behind the gun. Such a simple rule. And such a difficult one.
Another hugely important story Novaya Gazeta covered, and a turning point for Russia, was Beslan. Lena Milashina flew there in place of Politkovskaya, who had been poisoned on the plane. Milashina was the first journalist to report that there weren’t 354 hostages, as the authorities were saying, but more than a thousand.
Novaya Gazeta investigated Beslan like no other newsroom. It found grenade launchers on the roof of a building near the school. It carried out a huge investigation whose findings were confirmed by the European Court of Human Rights. I’m talking about the fact that the assault wasn’t intended to save the hostages. I think that was when Putin stopped playing at democracy. Because why bother? You can literally blast a school full of hostages, children, with flamethrowers, tanks, and small arms on live television, and nothing will happen to you.
Novaya Gazeta published many other important stories — about the extermination of gay men in Chechnya, about events in the Donbas.
Why is it important to preserve this whole archive? On the wall of the journalism school in New York where I studied [after Moscow State], it said that journalism is the “rough draft of history.” Journalism is a way to understand what happened, what people thought, what the journalists themselves thought, what perspective they brought to it all.
The shorter the pieces and the smaller the events that prompted them, the more important it is to preserve them. Major events and investigations that make a lot of waves will be archived. But the small details of everyday life probably won’t be.
Novaya Gazeta’s archive is a chronicle of our fuckups as well as Putin’s. At Novaya Gazeta, we also wrote about how lots of small, individual choices lead to catastrophic consequences. I wouldn’t want my pieces “Internat” (“The Institution”), “Trassa” (“The Highway”), or any part of “Nam zdes zhit” (“We Have to Live Here”), about Kushchevka, to disappear.
Novaya Gazeta was founded by a group of journalists — and that same group owned it. We had no owner other than the staff. That meant we could elect the editor in chief, the editorial committee, and the editorial board. You listened to your bosses because you’d voted for them. And if you’d made the wrong choice, you could change it two years later. That made for much healthier relationships among the staff and a healthier approach to work in general. There was no authority you obeyed just because it was authority.
It was my home, my family, and the most important thing in my life.
Nadya Yurova
Podcast producer at Novaya Gazeta from 2020 to 2022. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, she moved to Latvia and continued working at Novaya Gazeta Europe as a YouTube and podcast host
I never particularly dreamed of becoming a journalist. After high school, I applied to drama school, but I hadn’t really dreamed of an acting career either. I spent two years at the Shchepkin drama school in Moscow and left — it was awful, and I decided I’d had enough.
The only option left that wouldn’t mean retaking entrance exams was journalism. I enrolled at the Higher School of Economics.
In my second or third year, I hosted a student talk show [“V tochku!” (“Right on Target!”)]. It was cool, a pretty big production. But in 2018, [Putin’s press secretary Dmitry] Peskov came on the show, and there was a scandal. They started censoring us and telling us who to invite and who not to invite. I really, really didn’t like that, and I started getting disillusioned.
I needed to earn money, so I started working at a coffee shop while I studied. Around the same time, I met Kirill Martynov — he taught us a course called “Media in the Post-Truth Era.”
Martynov noticed me because I worked really hard and always spoke up in his classes. At that point, I had pretty much no idea what my career was going to look like.
When COVID started, before the strictest restrictions came in, I was working at a small cafe that was part of a chain. Everyone wanted to support small businesses then, and Martynov came to my coffee shop. I remember taking off my apron, stepping outside for a smoke, and he goes, “Nadezhda, would you like to work at Novaya Gazeta?”
I had that feeling again that none of this was real, but I didn’t let it show and said with a straight face, “Well, maybe. Doing what?” He said, “What are you interested in?” I said I loved podcasts. He said, “We’re looking for someone for podcasts, actually. Come meet everyone.”
I’d been ready to give up and stay a barista for the rest of my life. Novaya Gazeta came out of nowhere. I’d grown up reading Politkovskaya; this was everything I could have dreamed of, but I had this feeling that it wasn’t real — like, “Is this possible?”
I suggested starting with the most straightforward thing — a news podcast. A Novaya Gazeta writer would write a piece, we’d invite them into the studio, and we’d talk about the article. I did the interviews.
During COVID, we recorded from home. I didn’t have a microphone, so I spoke into my iPhone’s voice recorder under a blanket. Interviewing someone for 30 minutes under a blanket is a bit tricky, but it was worth it.
It felt like fate handed me those first podcast episodes. The very first was with Elena Milashina, the second with Lena Kostyuchenko. It was freaking amazing: Here I was, a young employee who didn’t understand a thing, suddenly getting to know people across the whole newspaper.
A lot of young people joined the paper around the same time I did. We started doing YouTube, podcasts, TikTok — it was madness, and the best time of my career. This was the great Novaya Gazeta, with all these towering figures looking so serious. And we were just a bunch of goofballs and screwups. We sat on the floor during editorial meetings and rode skateboards down the newsroom hallways. They let us do all of it.
[Dmitry] Muratov told me that, in a way, we’d breathed new life into the newspaper.
Then February 24 came. During the first weeks of the war, we were in the newsroom around the clock, putting on daily livestreams with a team of four. We were shouting as loud as we could.
At the end of March 2022, Novaya Gazeta suspended publication. That was a huge blow. It felt like that was it — I no longer had the work that had kept me afloat.
Before I joined the paper, of course, I knew nobody could have written about Chechnya the way Novaya did. Nobody else had that enormous legacy handed down by Politkovskaya and Milashina. The newspaper had always been built around its writers’ individual voices. But only gradually did I come to understand just how great a newspaper I worked for.
Lena Kostyuchenko looks like a beautiful, delicate little flower, but then she goes and spends two weeks living in a residential institution for people with psychiatric and neurological disabilities. Right after Lena returned from the institution, she came onto my podcast [to talk about her piece “The Institution”]. It was as if you could still smell the horror on her — it chilled you to the bone. She was one of the first to say publicly that these institutions are a Gulag — and, in a way, to articulate that idea for the public. I remember not being able to believe I was part of all this.
There’s one project I’m very proud of. I’d dreamed of making a narrative podcast, and Kostyuchenko went to Taimyr to investigate the fuel spill in Norilsk. Around the same time, she also went on assignment to visit the Nganasans, an indigenous people of northern Russia.
When the oil spill happened, it polluted the river where they fished, and the fish disappeared. Lena went to talk to them, partly just to understand how they lived. I gave her a recorder to take along and asked her to record everything that happened to her. Lena brought me dozens of hours of material. That [the podcast “Poka ne vypal sneg” (“Before the Snow Falls”)] was the most interesting work I’ve ever done in my life.
That was also when I realized just how expendable people are to the authorities. This [what’s happening to the Nganasans] mirrors what’s happening across the country, including in the war.
I think that as long as I keep telling people what’s happening in Russia, as long as I keep the idea [of Novaya Gazeta] alive, it won’t be so easy to erase us and shut us up. In the newsroom, people are always talking about [Novaya Gazeta’s] legacy, remembering the journalists who were murdered.
From beginning to end, Novaya Gazeta was a thorn in the authorities’ side. In a country where nothing is allowed, there was one newspaper that caused them trouble — so much trouble that people were killed over it.
Novaya Gazeta is a memory, a record, and a chronicle of the Russian authorities’ fuckups.
On November 5, RIMA and Kronika will open the Novaya Gazeta archive. All 3,373 issues of the Moscow edition from 1993 to 2022, special editions, and much more will be freely available. Some of this material was previously inaccessible. It includes, for example, articles the newspaper was forced to remove on orders from the Prosecutor General’s Office and the media regulator Roskomnadzor. Among them are Elena Kostyuchenko’s reporting from occupied Kherson and the full versions of four issues from February to March 2022 whose contents are hidden on the newspaper’s website. For the first time, Novaya’s entire print archive will be available in one place. Researchers will also be able to request datasets containing the archive’s metadata from RIMA.

articles.title: Russia-Ukraine humanitarian truce: What is happening in Alyoshki?
articles.body:
Russia-Ukraine humanitarian truce: What is happening in Alyoshki?
Russian and Ukrainian humanitarian teams have begun delivering aid and evacuating civilians from the frontline town of Alyoshki under a temporary ceasefire brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump.
Residents of the town in Russia’s Kherson Region have faced months of severe shortages, with Ukrainian drone attacks and mines disrupting supply routes, according to Russian officials and evacuees interviewed by RT.
An RT correspondent is on the ground covering the mission, which has brought representatives from both sides together to assist civilians. Here is how the agreement came about, what is happening on the ground and what residents have said about conditions in the town.
Where is Alyoshki?
Alyoshki lies on the left bank of the Dnieper River, opposite the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson. It has been under Russian control since 2022 and is part of Russia’s Kherson Region, which Ukraine continues to claim.
The nearby Antonovsky Bridge, once a key crossing between the two cities, was put out of action in 2022. The river has since formed part of the front line separating Russian and Ukrainian forces.
The humanitarian mission is using land routes into Alyoshki, which Russian military engineers have been clearing of mines and unexploded ordnance.
Why was a humanitarian ceasefire needed?
Russian authorities estimated that between 1,500 and 2,000 civilians remained in Alyoshki before the operation, including elderly residents and children. Food, medicine, drinking water and fuel have been scarce, while damaged utilities have deprived residents of basic services.
Kherson Governor Vladimir Saldo has accused Ukrainian forces of attacking supply vehicles and remotely mining access roads. Russian Foreign Ministry envoy Rodion Miroshnik described the situation as a “medieval blockade using modern methods.”
Ukraine, meanwhile, has accused Russia of preventing civilians from leaving. However, evacuees interviewed by RT blamed Ukrainian attacks for making both aid deliveries and evacuation attempts dangerous.
What have residents told RT?
“There’s nothing to eat. No medicine. Drones are constantly hovering above you,” one evacuee said. He described residents being unable to step outside without encountering drones and recalled three supply vehicles being destroyed in succession in the spring, leaving people to survive on vegetables grown in their gardens.
Others recounted receiving food, water and fuel from Russian soldiers and volunteers.
One woman said her husband was killed by a mine while collecting potatoes. She described how Russian troops guided her to safety using drones and a radio during a five-hour journey to a hospital.
Another resident, whose husband was killed in a Ukrainian attack, described houses being “blown away” during bombardments. Another evacuee noted that the people of Alyoshki were treated by Ukraine as “scum” and “traitors.”
Who negotiated the agreement?
The humanitarian crisis was raised during an October 9 telephone conversation between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump. The two leaders agreed to establish direct contact between Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova and Melania Trump’s office.
Subsequent negotiations secured a temporary pause in fighting around Alyoshki, with the US first lady and Pope Leo XIV helping advance the initiative.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has credited Melania Trump with coordinating the effort, linking her involvement to earlier work reuniting children separated from their families during the conflict.
Is the EU involved?
The EU has played no role in negotiating or carrying out the mission. The operation has instead relied on direct Russian-Ukrainian coordination, US mediation and logistical support from Belarus.
Who is leading the humanitarian teams?
Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmitry Lubinets, have coordinated the practical arrangements and are taking part in the mission.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev has also participated in contacts and public announcements related to the operation.
Belarus has provided logistical assistance, with delegations from both countries traveling through the Belarusian city of Gomel before proceeding toward Alyoshki.
How long does the ceasefire last?
The truce took effect at 4am Moscow time on October 27 and is due to expire at 10:59pm on November 1. It covers the humanitarian mission and the routes used to bring in supplies and evacuate residents.
On Friday, Melania Trump said the ceasefire had held for 80 hours, allowing Russian and Ukrainian teams to deliver aid and prepare civilian evacuations.
Lantratova confirmed that both sides were honoring their commitments, reporting no violations.
What is happening on the ground?
Aid distribution and the boarding of evacuation buses were underway on Friday, according to Lantratova.
The humanitarian convoy includes 25 buses and vehicles carrying food, medicine, drinking water, hygiene supplies and fuel for generators.
Residents are free to stay or leave, with evacuation options available for those wishing to travel deeper into Russia or to Ukrainian-held territory.
Those remaining in Alyoshki are receiving essential supplies, Lantratova said. Some have chosen not to leave because they want to remain in their homes or care for relatives.
More than 50 journalists from several countries have arrived to cover the mission, according to Lantratova. They include an RT correspondent and four Newsmax reporters whom Melania Trump identified as observers documenting the operation.
What did securing the routes involve?
Military engineers had to clear mines and unexploded ordnance before humanitarian vehicles could enter Alyoshki.
The Russian Defense Ministry released footage of remotely operated mine-clearing equipment and said many of the explosives discovered along the routes had been dropped by Ukrainian drones.
The operation has already claimed a life. The ministry confirmed that Sergeant Andrey Vedernikov of the 98th Guards Airborne Division was killed on October 28 while clearing a road leading into the town.
According to the ministry, he was fatally wounded by a drone-laid explosive device equipped with a proximity sensor.
Could the operation be repeated?
Although the agreement applies only to Alyoshki, Peskov has suggested it could serve as a model for future humanitarian missions.
He said a successful truce “could set a precedent,” opening the way for similar ceasefires in other areas of the conflict zone.

articles.title: Iran targeted USS Abraham Lincoln with cruise missile, Navy Cmdr. says
articles.body:
Iran targeted USS Abraham Lincoln with cruise missile, Navy Cmdr. says
TEHRAN - Iran's Navy targeted the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier with a strategic cruise missile during the 40-day Ramadan War, the Iranian Navy's deputy coordinator has said, noting that the force carried out more than 20 operations against U.S. warships and around 300 operations against American interests in various locations.
Rear Admiral Jalil Moghadam said Iranian forces identified the carrier during the first two days of the conflict, using visual observation and available surveillance systems to track its position.
Speaking to the IRNA news agency, Moghadam said the Navy launched the missile after locating the carrier. He added that the vessel halted flight operations for three days following the strike before moving farther away from Iran's coastline.
According to the official, Iranian naval forces concluded that the carrier had been hit after examining a series of developments following the operation.
Moghadam said aircraft operating from the carrier attacked Iran's second and third naval regions on the third day of the war. He noted that the carrier conducted no launches or flights for three days after Iran's operation.
He added that, on the day of the attack or that night, the carrier requested assistance from a coastal country and reported having injured personnel.
"Later, it was announced that the carrier had caught fire," Moghadam said, adding that images released from the site of the damage did not, in his assessment, correspond to an ordinary fire.
He said the images showed ruptures in the hull and deformation of the structure, which he interpreted as evidence of a missile strike.
 
Iran Navy rejects claims of destruction
Moghadam also rejected U.S. claims that Iran's naval forces had been destroyed, arguing that developments during and after the war demonstrated that the force remained operational.
He said U.S. and Israeli forces had refrained from approaching Iran's coastline, particularly the Strait of Hormuz, and questioned why they had remained hundreds of kilometers away if Iran's naval capabilities had been eliminated.
The official mentioned that Iranian naval forces had continued to inflict damage on U.S. and Israeli interests during the 40-day conflict and after the ceasefire.
He added that the Navy had reviewed its military doctrine following the conflict, incorporating lessons from the war and reassessing its equipment and operational priorities.
Moghadam said that, in the event of another war, Iran's naval operations would extend beyond the scope of the previous conflict, citing improvements in the force's equipment and capabilities.
He also described the Strait of Hormuz as a strategic advantage for Iran, arguing that regional maritime security would not return to its desired state while U.S. forces remained in the region.
The Iranian Navy official's remarks come amid continued tensions between Tehran and Washington over regional security and the strategic waterway, through which a significant share of global oil shipments passes.

articles.title: Iran’s nuclear doctrine debate reflects national demand for stronger deterrence
articles.body:
Iran’s nuclear doctrine debate reflects national demand for stronger deterrence
TEHRAN — Tehran’s interim Friday prayer leader, Mohammad Javad Haj Ali Akbari, has described calls to review Iran’s nuclear doctrine as a growing national demand rooted in the Iranian people’s experience of Western conduct, heightened security concerns and the need to strengthen the country’s deterrence capabilities.
Addressing worshippers during Friday prayers in the Iranian capital on October 30, Haj Ali Akbari said the debate over a possible revision of the country’s nuclear doctrine should not be dismissed as an emotional reaction or attributed to a particular political faction. Rather, he argued, it reflects a broader public reassessment of the security requirements facing Iran following years of confrontation, unfulfilled commitments and hostile actions by its adversaries.
His remarks come amid renewed public discussion in Iran about the country’s nuclear policy and the relationship between its established positions, national security requirements and the evolving regional and international environment.
A debate shaped by security concerns
Haj Ali Akbari said Iran’s adversaries had crossed the nation’s red lines, pointing to the assassination of the martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, and 'repeated failures' to honor commitments and agreements.
He argued that the Iranian people’s accumulated experience had prompted a more considered debate about the country’s deterrence requirements, including whether its nuclear doctrine should be reviewed in light of the security challenges it faces.
According to the cleric, the proposal is rooted in the Iranian nation’s right to live in dignity and security. He stressed that the discussion should be understood as a matter of national concern rather than an initiative belonging to any single political group or current.
Haj Ali Akbari also said that some people had reacted angrily to the proposal but maintained that the public discussion surrounding it reflected a broader demand that policymakers should examine seriously.
Citing previous surveys, he said more than 70 percent of respondents in some polls had supported reviewing Iran’s nuclear doctrine.
He added that calls for reconsideration had subsequently emerged from a range of social and professional groups, including university students, school students, academics, intellectuals and professional associations.
The cleric urged universities, researchers, security specialists and other experts to contribute to the debate by conducting substantive studies and developing policy proposals. He also called on the relevant authorities to undertake further assessments, with the aim of submitting the resulting recommendations to the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei.
He emphasized that the final decision rested with the Leader and said that any decision he made would be followed.
Negotiations and the question of vigilance
Alongside the nuclear doctrine debate, Haj Ali Akbari cautioned against interpreting US calls for negotiations, diplomatic correspondence, or the involvement of intermediaries as grounds for relaxing Iran’s vigilance.
Drawing on Iran’s experience of dealings with Washington, he argued that diplomatic overtures should be assessed in the context of the other side’s conduct and actions, rather than its statements alone.
He warned that, in some circumstances, US messages and proposals for negotiations could coincide with more serious threats than those conveyed through explicit declarations of hostility. His remarks underscored the importance of maintaining vigilance while assessing diplomatic initiatives.
The comments reflect a central concern in Iranian political and security discourse: that diplomatic engagement must be evaluated alongside practical guarantees, respect for commitments, and the broader security environment.
For Tehran, the question is not simply whether negotiations are proposed, but whether the process can produce credible and lasting commitments while safeguarding Iran’s national interests.
From public debate to policy assessment
Haj Ali Akbari’s remarks place the nuclear doctrine debate within a wider discussion about deterrence, national sovereignty and the country's response to changing security conditions.
 
By calling for contributions from universities, professional bodies and relevant specialists, he presented the issue as one requiring sustained examination rather than a decision driven by immediate political pressures.
The distinction is significant: a public demand for a review does not, in itself, constitute a formal change in national policy. Any revision would require consideration by the competent authorities and a decision through the country's established institutional framework.
Iran's nuclear policy has long been a subject of international debate, particularly in relation to its stated position against nuclear weapons, its nuclear program and the country's security concerns. A discussion about revising the doctrine therefore raises questions that extend beyond technical nuclear policy to include deterrence, strategic calculations and the country's assessment of the international environment.
Haj Ali Akbari called for the debate to be informed by expert analysis and national considerations, while reaffirming that the Leader would make the final decision.
His remarks signal that calls for a reassessment of Iran's nuclear doctrine have become an issue of public and political discussion, with supporters framing the debate around national security, deterrence and the lessons drawn from past confrontations. Whether that discussion results in any change in policy remains a matter for the country's competent decision-making authorities.

articles.title: US oil companies tripled profits during Iran war – NYT
articles.body:
US oil companies tripled profits during Iran war – NYT
The US’ largest oil companies almost tripled their profits during the US-Israeli war on Iran, the New York Times has reported, at a time when soaring energy costs threaten to wipe out US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the upcoming midterm elections.
The American oil giants – including Chevron, Exxon Mobil, and Valero – earned $130 billion in profits between April and September, according to six months worth of financial results covering more than 50 companies, combined by the New York Times. In the same period last year, these companies made less than $47 billion.
This windfall is an almost direct mirror of the extra $147 billion Americans spent on gasoline and diesel since American and Israeli warplanes began striking Iran on February 28.
With the Strait of Hormuz closed to shipping for almost all of the last six months, and Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi extraction sites and shipping in the Red Sea, American producers have reaped the benefit of high oil prices, with Chevron and Exxon Mobil recording higher profits than at any point since the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022.
Exxon’s third-quarter profit more than doubled this year, while Chevron’s almost tripled.
American refiners have taken advantage of the widespread destruction of refining sites in the Gulf region, and the threat of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries, leveraging their safe location inside the US. Valero and Phillips 66 both posted all-time record third-quarter profits this year.
Europe’s oil giants have posted similar results, with Shell, TotalEnergies, and Repsol all more than doubling their earnings last quarter over the same timeframe in 2025, as Europeans grapple with record energy bills. Some European finance ministers have demanded that the EU impose windfall taxes on these companies in response.
At $4.29 per gallon as of Monday, US gasoline prices are now higher than they were at any point during former President Joe Biden’s four years in office, with the exception of the first three months after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict. Trump has described the elevated prices as a “small price to pay for” preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, but voters aren’t convinced.
This week, 72% of respondents told a Gallup poll that gasoline prices are “extremely” important in how they plan to vote in next week’s midterm elections. Most polling organizations show the Republican Party on track to lose one or both houses of Congress next week, with the GOP trailing the Democrats by between eight and nine points nationwide.
Trump has tried to alleviate some of this damage by lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, and at least three diesel tankers have left Russian ports en route to the US. Trump has also pressed Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky to cease attacks on Russian refineries, but Zelensky has apparently ignored these requests.

articles.title: Ukrspecsystems Developed a Lower-Cost RAM-2X — Black Betty. Prytula Foundation Already Delivered 45 of Them
articles.body:
Serhiy Prytula’s Foundation has, for the first time, delivered 45 Black Betty loitering munitions — a new, cost-effective variant of the RAM-2X — to the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
The foundation told Militarnyi that the drone is designed for high-precision strikes against enemy logistics.
They were part of a batch of reconnaissance and strike assets with a total value of UAH 69.8 million, which was distributed to seven units as part of the “Shchelypy” fundraising campaign.
In total, the military received 45 Black Betty systems, 14 Shark-M systems, and nine systems equipped with RAM-2X loitering munitions.
The equipment was received by the 429th Separate Achilles Unmanned Systems Brigade, the 74th Separate Reconnaissance Battalion, the 65th Separate Mechanized Brigade, the Intelligence Command Center, the 1st Separate Center of Unmanned Systems Forces, the 98th Special Operations Reconnaissance Center, as well as units of the Security Service of Ukraine.
Black Betty is a new, cost-reduced variant of the RAM-2X developed by Ukrspecsystems.
It is designed for mass production and intended for high-precision strikes against enemy logistics, particularly moving targets.
The Shark-M and loitering munitions operate in tandem. The Shark-M can remain airborne for up to seven hours, cover a distance of up to 180 km, and relay signals to operational-tactical-level kamikaze drones. The first drone detects the target, and the second strikes it.
In September, it was reported that RAM-2X strike drones had already hit over 450 targets.
The RAM-2X loitering munition operates at the operational-tactical level and has a range of up to 180 km. The drone is designed to strike enemy targets and can remain airborne for over two hours.
The drone is equipped with a warhead containing a 2.7- or 3.5-kg strike core and supports the integration of artificial intelligence systems. The system is characterized by a high degree of automation and a variety of communication channels.
The drone can operate via multiple radio frequency bands as well as through a Starlink terminal.

articles.title: Two ‘Non-Hostile’ Deaths Raise Iran War Toll to 23
articles.body:
Two Airmen supporting the U.S. conflict against Iran died this month in “non-hostile” incidents, according to the official count recently updated by the Pentagon.
The Pentagon has not publicly identified the two Airmen nor said where their deaths occurred, but both were assigned to U.S. Central Command, U.S. officials said. Listing a death as “non-hostile” means the cause was something other than direct military action.
One of the deaths was described as the result of “illness/injury.” That Airman died in the United States after being medically evacuated due to an illness, U.S. officials said. The other death’s cause is listed as “pending,” according to the Defense Casualty Analysis System, or DCAS. The Airman died in the Middle East and the cause is under investigation, the officials said.
The deceased service members, both men, were mid-to-senior enlisted personnel, between the E-5 and E-9 paygrades. Statistics indicate one was 31-35 years old and the other was older than that, according to the database, which is current as of Oct. 29.
At least 23 U.S. service members have died during the conflict with Iran. Fifteen of those occurred during Operation Epic Fury, the initial strike campaign against Iran that the Trump administration says lasted until early May. Eight more have died during operations that followed. The Pentagon has used “Overseas Operations” to refer to its ongoing military pressure campaign and blockade of Iran.
Iranian missile and drone attacks attacks have killed U.S. personnel at Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia, and Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, Jordan. Some deaths have also been caused by accidents. Six Airmen were killed in a mid-air collision between two KC-135 Stratotankers over Western Iraq on March 12, when one of the tankers crashed, killing its crew.
At least 865 service members have been wounded in action since hostilities kicked off on Feb. 28. The vast majority are attributed to “hostile” acts, including 64 Airmen.
A shaky ceasefire is now in place between the U.S. and Iran, and the U.S. has maintained a blockade of the country since early April.
The Trump administration is weighing its next move and the Wall Street Journal reported Oct. 28 that President Donald Trump met with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, and U.S. Central Command’s Adm. Brad Cooper U.S. Central Command boss Adm. Brad Cooper on military options beyond the blockade. Trump later hinted at future action, saying during a mid-term campaign event, “We may do another little Epic Fury.”

articles.title: Saudi Arabia Urges Trump administration to prioritise diplomacy amid fears of renewed conflict with Iran
articles.body:
Saudi officials have urged US President Donald Trump’s administration to “give diplomacy a chance” before pursuing renewed military confrontation with Iran, amid concerns that another conflict could expose Saudi oil and energy facilities to Iranian missile attacks, according to Israeli news network i24News.
The report said Riyadh’s message to Washington followed a visit to Tehran by Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, accompanied by Pakistan’s army chief and Turkey’s intelligence chief.
The visit was reportedly part of a diplomatic initiative aimed at facilitating mediation between Washington and Tehran and reaching an agreement that could prevent another round of hostilities.
According to the report, Saudi Arabia is concerned that renewed US-Iranian military confrontation could trigger retaliatory strikes against critical energy infrastructure in the kingdom.
Meanwhile, Iran confirmed receiving a message from US Vice President J.D. Vance concerning the possibility of resuming negotiations.
Tehran said it had not yet responded to the American message, reiterating that Washington must first commit to seven conditions previously established by the Iranian side.
The developments come amid continuing regional diplomatic efforts to reduce tensions and prevent a renewed military escalation between the United States and Iran.
The reported Saudi appeal reflects Riyadh’s preference for a diplomatic resolution as regional governments seek to avoid the security and economic consequences of another confrontation.

HIMARS Just Learned to Hit Moving Targets—Bad News for Russian Guns and Air Defenses
Lockheed Martin and the US Army have demonstrated a new way for HIMARS-launched GMLRS rockets to strike moving targets by updating their coordinates while the missile is already in flight—a capability that could make it much harder for mobile artillery and air-defense systems to escape after being detected.
The test was conducted at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico, according to Defense Express on October 30.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
During the demonstration, a GMLRS rocket launched from an M142 HIMARS was redirected in flight using updated target coordinates transmitted through Lockheed Martin’s Strigo datalink and a Remote Interceptor Guidance-360, or RIG-360, targeting device.
The rocket successfully struck a moving target. What makes the test particularly notable is how the capability was achieved.
Weapons designed to hit moving targets usually require a dedicated seeker capable of finding and tracking the target during the final phase of flight. In this case, however, Lockheed Martin used radio-transmitted targeting updates rather than making major modifications to the GMLRS itself.
That could offer a comparatively inexpensive way to expand the missile’s capabilities without installing a specialized seeker on every rocket.
Lockheed Martin said the equipment was integrated using company funding and could potentially be paired with other precision weapons as well, including Extended Range GMLRS and the Precision Strike Missile, or PrSM.
PrSM Increment 2 is already being developed with a multimode seeker intended to provide a moving-target capability, particularly against ships. The GMLRS demonstration takes a different approach by continuously updating the target’s location through the RIG-360 system rather than relying on an onboard seeker.
For battlefield targets, that distinction could be significant.
Mobile artillery, air-defense systems, command vehicles, and other high-value equipment often depend on “shoot-and-scoot” tactics—firing or operating briefly before rapidly relocating to avoid counterstrikes.
A GMLRS rocket capable of receiving fresh coordinates after launch could reduce the effectiveness of that tactic, provided friendly sensors can continue tracking the target and transmit updated position data to the missile.
Defense Express notes that Lockheed Martin and the Army have not disclosed exactly what type of moving target was used during the test. The location offers one clue: White Sands is dominated by desert terrain and lacks large permanent bodies of water, making a ground vehicle or another mobile land target more likely than a ship.
For Ukraine, the development is particularly relevant because HIMARS is already routinely used to hunt Russian artillery, ammunition sites, command posts, and other high-value targets.
Ukrainian forces have previously combined US-made HIMARS with systems such as French CAESAR self-propelled howitzers to destroy Russian artillery and field ammunition depots in sectors including Pokrovsk.
Earlier, the 45th Artillery Brigade of the 11th Army Corps destroyed a Russian 9A316 transporter erector launcher and radar element from the Buk air defense system using an M142 HIMARS rocket system.

articles.title: Slovakia reopens criminal case over fighter jet, air defense systems donation to Ukraine
articles.body:
Slovakia reopens criminal case over donation of fighter jets, air defense systems to Ukraine
Slovakia's Prosecutor General Maros Zilinka said on Oct. 30 that he had reopened a criminal case against former Prime Minister Eduard Heger and former Defense Minister Jaroslav Nad over their decision to donate Slovakia's fleet of MiG-29 fighter jets and Soviet-era KUB air defense systems to Ukraine in spring 2023.
Slovakia's caretaker government, headed by Heger, approved the donation of 13 MiG-29 fighter jets and part of the country's KUB air defense systems to Ukraine in March 2023. All 13 jets had been delivered by April that year, making Slovakia the first country to send fighter aircraft to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Prime Minister Robert Fico — widely seen as sympathetic to Moscow — has long criticized Western military aid to Ukraine and the defense assistance provided by the previous Slovak government. In June 2024, his administration filed a criminal complaint against Heger and Nad over the jet transfer.

and it may appear in our Letters section.
The defense ministry accused the two of sabotage, abuse of power, and mismanagement of public property — allegations both Heger and Nad have denied. Current Defense Minister Robert Kalinak also accused his predecessor of "treason."
The investigation had been closed by Bratislava regional prosecutor Rastislav Remeta in February. On Nov. 10, 2025, the Bratislava prosecutor's office said Slovakia's transfer of military aid to Ukraine did not constitute a criminal offense.
Zilinka said on Oct. 30 that the previous investigation had been "closed prematurely," prompting him to reopen the case.
"During the preparatory proceedings, the facts were not established to the extent necessary to make a decision," Zilinka said.
Zilinka reassigned prosecutorial supervision of the case from Bratislava to a regional prosecutor in Trencin to ensure that sufficient evidence is gathered.
The MiG-29 is a fourth-generation fighter jet designed in the Soviet Union, meant to establish air superiority and provide front-line air defense. Both Ukrainian and Russian forces use the fighter jet in their air forces.
The KUB, also known as the 2K12 Kub or SA-6 Gainful, is a Soviet-era, medium-range surface-to-air missile system designed to intercept aircraft and other aerial targets. It uses radar-guided missiles and was developed to protect ground forces and military facilities from air attacks.
The system is mobile and typically consists of radar-equipped vehicles and missile launchers, allowing it to provide air defense cover for troops and strategic sites.

articles.title: Ukraine hits Russian Mi-8 during raid on supply lines in Luhansk
articles.body:
- Ukraine’s Third Assault Brigade said it destroyed a Russian Mi-8 helicopter in the Luhansk region with two Hornet attack drones after it landed.
- The helicopter outran the first drone in flight, so the crew struck it near its fuel tanks once it touched down, the brigade said.
Ukraine’s Third Assault Brigade destroyed a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter in the Luhansk region with two Hornet one-way attack drones after waiting for it to land, the brigade said on social media on Oct. 30.
A drone crew from the SKYFOM strike-wing platoon of the brigade’s unmanned systems battalion spotted the helicopter during a raid on Russian supply lines and launched a Hornet to intercept it in the air. The Russian crew changed course after noticing the drone, but the helicopter was faster than the Hornet and pulled away, the brigade said. The brigade did not say where in the Luhansk region the strike took place or when.
“The helicopter’s cruising speed exceeded the speed of the strike drones, but as soon as the Russian aircraft landed, the fighters struck it in the area of the fuel tanks. The second Hornet successfully finished off the target,” the Third Assault Brigade said.
The brigade said the helicopter burned out completely. Russia uses the twin-engine Mi-8 as the workhorse of its military helicopter fleet, flying troops and cargo, evacuating wounded and providing fire support. Russia has not commented on the loss.
The Hornet is a fixed-wing one-way attack drone built by Perennial Autonomy, a U.S.-based company that multiple published reports have linked to a network of firms connected to former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Ukrainian units use it to hit Russian supply routes deep behind the front, and Ukraine’s 1st Azov Corps has flown it more than 50 km (31 miles) from the front line over occupied Donetsk. In May, Ukraine tested launching a Hornet from an aerostat at about 8 km altitude.
Ukrainian drone units have increasingly gone after Russian helicopters, usually catching them on the ground or while hovering, since most strike drones cannot match a helicopter’s speed in level flight. In February, Ukrainian strike drones destroyed a Ka-52 attack helicopter and a Mi-8 at a forward airfield in Russia’s Oryol region. In September, a single drone destroyed a Mi-8AMTSh at a helipad near Anapa, Russian sources reported. In July, the Unmanned Systems Forces’ Rarog unit said it brought down a Mi-28 attack helicopter, and in April a joint team struck a Mi-28 and a Mi-8 together at a Russian airstrip in the Voronezh region more than 150 km (93 miles) from the front line.

articles.title: Affordability, AI and Iran: Americans on the key issues guiding their midterm votes
articles.body:
Millions of Americans will head to the polls on 3 November in elections that will determine control of the Republican-held House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships of 36 states.
The midterms come amid mounting public frustration over issues ranging from the rising cost of living and immigration to the climate crisis, artificial intelligence, big tech and the US’s overseas wars. Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 36%, according to a New York Times/Siena poll conducted this month.
Voters across the US described to the Guardian their concerns and disillusionment with the current political climate, with one characterizing the country under the Trump administration as a “rogue nation, ungoverned by the rule of law”. (Some respondents only shared their first name or declined to share their name for privacy reasons.)
For many, the cost of living is a central concern ahead of the midterms, particularly as inflation reaches 3.7%.
Kathryn Warren, a retired staff member from Dare county schools who lives on Hatteras Island, North Carolina, said she and her husband had already voted early.
“We are dying on the vine in this economy. We live in a remote area and the cost of gas is taking a big chunk of our social security. Groceries and medicine are outrageous. The medicine that keeps me alive costs $7,000 a month before insurance. In what world is that reasonable?” Warren said.
A 36-year-old counsellor in Tennessee described financial pressures compounded by health issues and expressed concern about the US “sliding into an authoritarian state”.
“I have a migraine medication that costs nearly $2,000 out-of-pocket for a month’s supply. My health insurance has agreed to pay for five months. That’s it. After 24 years of chronic migraines, I have tried everything under the sun and this is the first medication that has ever reduced the pain levels, so it isn’t like I can try some cheaper, knock-off brand. But I find it absurd and financially prohibitive to spend that much on medication every month,” she said.
Vicki Stein, a 66-year-old retired marketing communications professional from Alpine Township, Michigan, said she had already voted for Democrats across the ticket.
“Working Americans can’t afford healthcare, let alone gas nor groceries due to tariffs, and children are losing Snap benefits while we blow our gold on [Israeli prime minister Benjamin] Netanyahu’s war. We can’t even trust our lettuce under this administration’s [Department of Health and Human Services],” she said, referring to a cyclospora outbreak across 27 states this summer that was traced to contaminated lettuce.
George, a 23-year-old business school graduate in Houston, Texas, also linked the affordability crisis to the administration’s policies, criticizing “Trump’s idiotic tariff scheme”.
“The priorities of both parties are clearly more in line with billionaires than regular people … It has been heartening to see politicians like [James] Talarico abandon that side of politics to focus on affordability and quality of life for average Americans. Who cares about 1% of the population when everyone is struggling?”
George also criticized the US’s war in Iran and called for the US to divest from Israel, saying: “Billions upon billions of American taxpayer dollars spent on killing children. No matter how you cut it, all we get from our investment in Israel is a mountain of dead bodies. Any politician who refuses Aipac money or promises to stop funding Israel’s perma-war has my vote and many other Americans’ as well.”
Opposition to the US war in Iran and military aid to Israel remains a driving concern among voters.
Joel Young, a 66-year-old retired civil litigator in Albuquerque, New Mexico, said: “The single most important issue in any election for federal office is whether the candidate or incumbent will approve another dollar, weapon, or material to support Israel, or support the US’s historical pattern of cover for Israel’s apartheid regime and program of ethnic cleansing in place since 1948, which has now clearly become genocidal.”
A 30-year-old machine operator and father in Bogalusa, Louisiana, who voted for Trump in 2024, also criticized the “evil war against Iran which must end”.
“Every day it continues is another day that the president scandalizes our service members, taxpayers and nation. It’s also another day of stealing present day purchasing power from embattled American workers, stealing future prosperity from our children through a climbing national debt and stealing tranquility from people in the Middle East,” he added.
Beyond economic pressures and foreign policy, voters also raised concerns about the growing influence of AI and big tech.
Dave Neps, a 74-year-old retired teacher in Georgia, said: “I’m … concerned about the AI financial bubble. This market reminds me of the dotcom crash in the late 90s and the financial crash in 2008. My wife and I lost money both times in those markets. Now I’m looking at a pension and a country that’s heavily invested in AI that so many of us don’t want. Give these guys time and they’ll just turn it into another commodity that we’ll have to pay for like cable TV.”
Joy, a 47-year-old insurance executive in north Georgia, similarly raised concerns about the expansion of datacenters and the influence of technology companies on local government.
“I live in rural Georgia where they are buying off local officials to build datacenters and the county and city reps are ignoring their constituents and offering massive tax incentives,” she said, calling for datacenter moratoriums.
The climate crisis and environmental protection were also prominent concerns, particularly among older voters who described witnessing the degradation of natural spaces over their lifetimes.
David Tucker, a 57-year-old registered nurse in Washington, said: “The climate crisis and public lands protection are my main concerns, along with protecting democracy and healthcare funding cuts. I grew up in Utah and spent a lot of time camping and fishing with my parents and siblings on public forests and deserts. Natural spaces and our ecosystem are essential for our survival.”
Similarly, Kaye, a 71-year-old resident of Bothell, Washington, said: “While Donald Trump is evil and incompetent in so many ways, the degradation of the planet is my greatest concern as it is larger than all of us and we’re so close to a tipping point that will be catastrophic. I’m old enough to have known a world with more birds and animal species; where the forests, coasts and plains were so much more alive. Our vile destruction of the land that feeds us is tragic.”
Another 78-year-old Washington resident similarly described the climate crisis as the “biggest threat to the planet and causes suffering, disease, fear, inequality”.
“A candidate with a clear track record of ethical standards, who is direct about the threat, and who can muster a coalition to face it will have my vote. This issue is bigger than political affiliation,” she added.
Immigration enforcement and fears of voter intimidation were other major concerns, with some readers expressing alarm about potential federal interference in the midterm elections.
Katie, a 34-year-old arts professional in Denver, Colorado, pointed to the killings of two Americans, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, by federal immigration agents in Minnesota earlier this year.
“Maga lost America when they murdered Renee Good and Alex Pretti. First and foremost I’m concerned about Trump’s immigration secret police, and I am voting for candidates who will defund and prosecute ICE,” Katie said.
Julie Stielstra, a retired librarian living in rural Kansas, said she was worried about the potential presence of immigration agents and armed individuals at polling stations. Stielstra said she would be working as a poll worker the following week.
“I am apprehensive about the possible presence of ICE, which has been active in my state recently … [and] armed government agents or self-appointed ‘poll watchers’ who may be intimidating at best. I trust my county clerk’s vigilance and honor, but worry about federal minions and officials who could disrupt or try to negate or overturn our ballots,” she said.
Those concerns extended beyond intimidation at polling stations to the possibility that the Trump administration could challenge the election results.
Richard Corcoran, a 63-year-old licensed clinical social worker in Lumberton, North Carolina, said: “I do not have faith that the federal government under Trump and Republican control of Congress and the supreme court will respect the outcome of this election. I expect problems in the aftermath,” he said.
Michael Pitts-Campbell, a 78-year-old law enforcement retiree living in Brookings, Oregon, similarly worried that Trump would reject a Democratic victory.
“My biggest concern is that if the results of the election are overwhelmingly Democratic, Trump will claim that the election results are false. Whether the appropriate member of the government attempts to not certify the vote or not seat the new representatives and senators, the proclamation from Trump will only widen the current political chasm,” he said.
But even among voters hoping for a Democratic victory, there was little consensus that the party would be prepared to deliver the changes they want.
Several readers expressed concern that Democrats could fail to use a potential congressional majority to enact effective change.
For a 52-year-old insurance professional in New Lenox, Illinois, their “biggest fear is that despite a likely massive Democrat wins, they will not have the guts to do what is necessary to prosecute this administration and pass laws that are sorely needed limiting the powers of the president, abolishing [the Department of Homeland Security] and establishing Medicare for all”.
D Turner, a California resident, similarly said: “I’m concerned that the reflexive centrist impulses of current Democratic leadership and advisers will assume that if they just get a majority, everything will be back to normal. There is so much hard work that needs to be done to preserve the rights of all.”
Brad Southard, a 54-year-old teacher in Irvine, California, criticized Democratic leaders for focusing “too much on courting the illusive ‘undecided middle’ to the detriment of the needs of working-class people”.
“I worry that the party will again choose to seize defeat from the jaws of victory by supporting pro-corporate neoliberal candidates and policies and refuse to pay attention to the real material pain felt by so many Americans,” Southard added.
For other voters, disillusionment extended beyond either party’s leadership, reflecting a broader lack of faith in the US political system.
Mark, a 68-year-old retiree in Parma, Ohio, said both parties had become too beholden to wealthy interests to represent ordinary Americans.
“Both political parties share the blame. The GOP has morphed into something even worse than the [Democrats]. Neither party offers policies that meet the needs of the people. Rather, both parties are captured by moneyed interests. It just turns out the GOP has openly embraced the dark side while the [Democrats] are more coy about their corruption.”

articles.title: Russian Energy Strikes Cut Power to 280,000 Across Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure over the course of Oct. 30 have triggered acute electricity disruptions across several regions, leaving approximately 280,000 families without power, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday, Oct. 31.
Writing on Telegram, the head of state outlined the geographical spread of overnight and morning strikes, which targeted thermal power and heating plants (CHPs), electrical substations, gas distribution hubs, and railway logistics across northern, central, and eastern Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Yesterday evening, Russian Shaheds struck a combined heat and power plant in Kyiv,” Zelensky stated. “In the Dnipro region, strikes hit four electrical substations during this night alone. Toward morning in Shostka, a Russian drone hit a combined heat and power plant... Following these Russian strikes, the electricity supply situation in our regions is difficult.”
According to official figures provided by the president, roughly 200,000 households remain without power in the city of Dnipro and the wider Dnipropetrovsk region.
In Kyiv region, more than 80,000 households were severed from the electricity grid as emergency dispatchers and engineering repair crews deployed to stabilize voltage levels and clear debris.
Targeting of rail networks and gas distribution systems
Beyond electricity generation and transmission infrastructure, Russian forces expanded strikes over the past 24 hours to target strategic transport corridors and natural gas transit facilities.
4 Planes With Oleshky Evacuees Land in Belarus En Route to Kyiv
Zelensky confirmed that Russian munitions struck railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, complicating passenger travel and freight logistics along central and eastern rail trunks. In the Dnipropetrovsk region, adversary fire also struck a natural gas distribution facility, raising concerns over fuel deliveries for municipal heating networks.
“Emergency repair teams are working on liquidating the consequences of the strikes and doing everything to restore the supply of electricity,” Zelensky noted.
The Ukrainian president emphasized that the systematic destruction of civil life-support networks demands decisive countermeasures from international partners.
“The world sees how Russia makes civilian infrastructure a daily target,” Zelensky said.
“And everyone who does not want to see how this Russian escalation could expand further in Europe must help Ukraine. Strong steps are needed genuinely in the direction of peace. This means sanctions against the aggressor and new packages of support for Ukraine.”
UN report warns strikes may amount to crimes against humanity
The latest barrage unfolds against mounting international legal scrutiny of Moscow’s campaign to disable Ukraine’s municipal utilities ahead of winter.
A United Nations report published on Oct. 19 concluded that Russia’s coordinated assaults against Ukraine’s energy grid may constitute crimes against humanity.
Prepared by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine and transmitted by the UN Secretary-General, the findings established that Russian military operations demonstrate a deliberate intent to deprive civilian populations of the basic means of survival.
“The Commission assesses that the Russian commanders ordering the attacks had the knowledge that the heating facilities they targeted in large civilian agglomerations were indispensable to the civilian population, in particular during the winter,” the UN report stated.
Investigators documented that Russian political and military authorities have issued formal declarations articulating the intent to destroy Ukraine’s power grid, finding that the operations were “carried out with intent and pursuant to a state policy to deprive the civilian population from essential energy supplies and cause suffering.”
The report noted that while systematic infrastructure strikes began in late 2022 – including during the winter of 2025-2026, when targeted bombardments disabled urban district heating during sub-zero temperatures – the offensive has intensified in late 2026 as Moscow seeks to coerce Kyiv into political capitulation.
Intensified pre-winter grid offensive
The strikes on Kyiv, Shostka, and Dnipro reflect an escalating pre-winter campaign to exhaust Ukraine’s power repair reserves.
Ukrainian Minister of Energy Denys Shmyhal recently disclosed that intelligence agencies had obtained operational blueprints outlining Russian plans to deploy approximately 1,000 precision weapons to disable electrical generation and transmission networks across the country.
On Oct. 19 alone, Russian forces damaged 28 electrical substations overnight, triggering widespread emergency shutdowns.

articles.title: Delivery of 500 PAC-3 Missiles to Ukraine May Take Several Years — Zelensky
articles.body:
The delivery of 500 PAC-3 interceptor missiles for the Patriot air defense systems—the sale of which to Ukraine was approved by the U.S. just yesterday—will not begin for several years.
This was announced by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
“Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is significant, and if delivered soon—this winter—it could be a very effective defense package. However, it has been determined that deliveries can begin only in a few years,” he emphasized.
Kyiv had asked Washington to put together a winter military aid package consisting of 100 interceptors per month.
Such a quantity would allow for strengthening air defense during the period of greatest threat of Russian strikes on critical infrastructure.
As an alternative, the Ukrainian side proposes using existing PAC-3 stockpiles in the U.S. and among other partners.
The transferred missiles could be replenished over the coming years through production funded by Ukraine and its allies.
The need to accelerate deliveries stems from Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. In the last two weeks of October alone, the occupiers carried out more than 30 strikes on critical power grid facilities.
Kyiv also recently discussed the issue of obtaining interceptors with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
According to American journalist Alex Raufoglu, these are new missiles, and deliveries to Ukraine are not expected before 2030. He reported this, citing his own sources.
As previously reported, the U.S. State Department approved the sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles and related equipment to Ukraine for $2.1 billion.
Funding for the purchase is to come from international partners, including Canada, Germany, Norway, and the European Union.
