articles.title: Sudan civilians face drone strikes and arbitrary arrests: UN
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Sudan: El Obeid's civilians face RSF drone strikes and arbitrary arrests by army, UN warns
Civilians in the Sudanese city of El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, are facing the threat of drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and an increase in arbitrary arrests by Sudanese army-affiliated forces amid escalating violence in the war-torn country, UN-appointed investigators have warned this week.
In its latest report, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan said that, more than three years after the conflict broke out in April 2023, the war was becoming increasingly widespread and dangerous for civilians.
The latest warnings also highlight deteriorating humanitarian conditions in El Obeid, which had already been identified as being at risk of famine, alongside other parts of Sudan.
"Thousands have been arrested by SAF security cells, detained and tortured in unofficial locations and in El Obeid Central Prison, kept under appalling conditions,” said Mona Rishmawi, an expert member of the UN's Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan.
“These practices must stop immediately.”
Roughly 30% of hospitals in El Obeid are currently functioning following RSF drone attacks, according to the UN report.
It added that the strikes had continued to kill and injure civilians in the city, while also targeting homes, schools, displacement sites, and electricity and water systems.
The report cited a drone attack on a market in Abyei earlier this month, reportedly carried out by forces aligned with the military government, which killed at least 80 people.
The UN also said it would investigate reports of Egyptian airstrikes on goldmining sites near the Sudan-Egypt border, which reportedly killed at least 72 miners.
The UN further highlighted an increase in detentions, with approximately 2,000 people reportedly being held at El Obeid Central Prison.
The report cited a former detainee who said people were being confined in a cell measuring roughly 2.5 metres by 2 metres.
UN investigators have warned that security actors affiliated with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have increased surveillance and are "targeted people engaged in humanitarian, human rights and peace work".
The latest findings come a year after the brutal RSF takeover of El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, where more than 10,000 people were reportedly massacred by the paramilitary group over two days after it seized the city in October 2025, following an 18-month siege.
A reported surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas since June has prompted the UN to warn that the city could face a repeat of the atrocities in El Fasher.
Joy Ngozi Ezeilo, another expert member of the UN's Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan, has renewed calls to extend the UN arms embargo to cover the whole of Sudan, as it is currently limited to Darfur.
"Sovereignty should not shield mass atrocity crimes, period," Ezeilo said.
"One year after the devastation of El Fasher, civilians in other parts of Sudan continue to pay the price of a conflict that is becoming increasingly destructive and difficult to escape."
She added: "In El Obeid, attacks on electricity networks, water facilities, hospitals, schools and displacement sites demonstrate how damage to critical civilian infrastructure can reverberate through entire communities long after an attack has occurred."
“The passage of time should not diminish attention to what has happened in El Fasher. On the contrary, it should remind us of the cost of impunity.”
Now in its fourth year, Sudan's war began in April 2023, when fighting broke out in Khartoum between the RSF and the Sudanese military before spreading across the country.
The conflict has killed at least 59,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED, although other aid groups argue that the true death toll is likely to be higher.

articles.title: Ukraine working to speed up delivery, maintenance of F-16s – MFA
articles.body:
Ukraine is working to expedite the delivery and maintenance of F-16 fighter jets, which have proven highly effective in combating Russian jet drones, Spokesperson for the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) Heorhiy Tykhy said.
"Yes, work is underway to secure additional platforms – that is, additional aircraft – to expedite the delivery of those already promised, to secure additional parts, and expediting aircraft maintenance," he said at a briefing in Kyiv on Friday, responding to a question from an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
Tykhy separately expressed gratitude to partners working with Ukraine on fighter jet maintenance and refuted "rumors that they are failing to fulfill their obligations or are somehow behind schedule."
"We are grateful to our partners for their support, which we consider very important. But during the war, you see, we have a different sense of time. We need everything yesterday. We need more of everything," the spokesperson added.
In early October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that about half of Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets are undergoing repairs in European countries. The president shared this information with the Financial Times.
Zelenskyy said the U.S.-made F-16 fighter jets have proven effective against new Russian jet-powered drones, but too many of the aircraft – about half – have been in Europe for an extended period for repairs and maintenance.
Zelenskyy said he aims to move the maintenance of the F-16s to Ukraine to save time.

articles.title: Zelenskyy urges US to speed up Patriot deliveries
articles.body:
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked the U.S. for approving the sale of Patriot interceptors but urged Washington to fast-track the delivery of the defensive missiles.
Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision” by the U.S. to approve the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptors to counter Russian ballistic missiles — but said the years-long wait to deliver them was too long for Ukraine's urgent needs.
“It has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelenskyy wrote in a Facebook post on Friday night.

“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” he added.
Patriot interceptors are crucial for Ukraine to defend itself against Russia’s ballistic missiles, amid fears that Moscow will ramp up its attacks on energy facilities to bring winter blackouts in Ukraine.
In the Facebook post, Zelenskyy said an immediate delivery of Patriot interceptors would allow Ukraine to defend its energy infrastructure during the winter season.

articles.title: Two civilians killed in Ukrainian strike on Russia – governor
articles.body:
Two civilians killed in Ukrainian strike on Russia – governor
Two people have been killed and five others wounded in Ukrainian drone attacks on Bryansk Region, western Russia, local governor Egor Kovalchuk has said.
A 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man lost their lives after a kamikaze-drone struck a private home in the settlement of Klimovo, not far from Russia’s border with Ukraine, Kovalchuk wrote in a post on Max on Saturday.
“A tragedy in the border area – civilians killed,” he said, expressing condolences to the relatives of the victims.
Four females and one male were injured by Kiev’s UAVs elsewhere in the region, including a 73-year-old woman in the village of Pogar and a 19-year-old boy in Voronok, he added.
Earlier in the day, Belgorod Region Governor Aleksandr Shuvayev said that he had received information from emergency services about a civilian being killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in Schebekino District. The exact time it happened is not yet known, he added.
Four people were also wounded in Ukrainian UAV and artillery strikes across the region over the past 24 hours, Shuvayev said. Three of them are still hospitalized, according to the governor.
Kursk Region has also been extensively targeted by Ukrainian forces, with one man wounded in the village of Chernitsyno and another one in Lgov, Kursk Governor Aleksandr Khinshtein has said.
Bryansk, Belgorod, and Kursk regions, which all border Ukraine, have come under regular attacks since the escalation between Moscow and Kiev in February 2022.
The Russian Defense Ministry said on Saturday morning that a total of 433 fixed-wing Ukrainian drones were destroyed by air defenses in 19 Russian regions overnight.
Moscow has accused Ukraine of deliberately targeting residential areas and civilian infrastructure to compensate for setbacks on the battlefield where Russian forces continue to advance.
In response to Ukrainian terrorist attacks, Russia has intensified its long-range missile and drone campaign against Ukraine’s military facilities and infrastructure supporting Kiev’s war effort. The Defense Ministry in Moscow maintains that it never targets civilians.

articles.title: Iran's supreme leader warns US, Israel against new attacks
articles.body:

Iran's supreme leader warns US, Israel against new attacks
Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday warned the United States and Israel against returning to war, according to a written statement, following threats from the Islamic republic's foes of a possible resumption of strikes.
"If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine the time and conditions for ending them," said a statement attributed to Khamenei posted on his website.
The remarks came during a reported meeting between Khamenei and senior military commanders, including armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi. It was the first reported meeting between them.
Khamenei has not been publicly seen since he became supreme leader, following his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei's killing in US-Israeli strikes at the start of the Middle East war in February.
According to the statement, Khamenei ordered the commanders to ensure that "any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response".
It also said that Khamenei ordered the commanders to update Iran's target list to include "all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy".
The war began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which swiftly responded with attacks on countries around the region.
The supreme leader's statement came as fresh diplomatic efforts were under way to avert a resumption of fighting.
A Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran on Friday for talks with Iranian officials, after Iran reportedly received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance.
According to Iranian media, Tehran had yet to respond to the letter.

articles.title: Britain’s most powerful nuclear sub enters final build phase
articles.body:
The Dreadnought programme has entered a phase that will take the first boat through the completion of her build, sea trials and certification before she enters service in the early 2030s, while the second submarine progresses to sea trials of her own, according to an answer given in Parliament.
James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat member for Lewes, asked what progress has been made on the Dreadnought programme in the context of the delivery confidence assessments for Government Major Project Portfolio defence projects.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence, said: “Good progress is being made on the Dreadnought programme. In July, we announced Delivery Phase 4 (DP4), the latest phase of the programme, which will enable the first-in-class submarine, Dreadnought, to complete her build, sea trials and certification, ahead of entering service in the early 2030s. During this phase, the second boat will progress to sea trials, while the third and fourth boats will achieve key construction milestones.”
Delivery Phase 4 is the funding and contracting step that carries the programme from construction into the trials and certification work needed before a ballistic missile submarine can take on operational patrols. Dreadnought, Valiant, Warspite and King George VI will replace the four Vanguard boats that have maintained continuous at sea deterrence since 1969, and the oldest of those, HMS Vanguard, commissioned in 1993 against a design life of twenty-five years.
Stretching the Vanguard class beyond that design life has produced the longest deterrent patrols in Royal Navy history, including a 204-day patrol completed by HMS Vanguard, and the Defence Committee has examined the strain that places on crews and on the maintenance cycle. The programme’s schedule matters for that reason as much as for the capability itself.
Construction runs at Barrow-in-Furness, where BAE Systems is expanding the yard to build Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS alongside each other, and Rolls-Royce Submarines in Derby supplies the reactor cores. Major facility upgrades needed for Dreadnought core production have been delivered, with work now focused on commissioning and manufacture.
The Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise, taking in the submarines, a new sovereign warhead and the infrastructure at Barrow, Derby, Faslane, Coulport and Aldermaston.

articles.title: Queen Ursula comes to Canada with velvet handcuffs
articles.body:
Queen Ursula comes to Canada with velvet handcuffs
I’m trying to spend a few weeks back in Canada for some peace and quiet from the usual European drama. Just my luck that Queen Ursula would follow me here, circus and all.
She hadn’t even landed in Montreal for the EU-Canada Summit, and already everyone around me was saying that Canada’s “associate membership” had been canceled. They’d heard that countries like France and Germany objected to the idea, even as Von der Leyen was saddling up her broom for a trip across the Atlantic.
Someone even asked me if that meant that we’re now kicked out of Eurovision. I had to explain that the title never existed in the first place. EU treaties refer only to association agreements. It’s just the usual sort of branding that von der Leyen, the unelected EU chief executive, likes to roll out, much like her endless riffs about unity, as though dissent weren’t an actual virtue in a functioning democracy.
Or like the way she talks a good game about sticking it to Russia while simultaneously celebrating the €977 million spent this winter alone on gas purchases for Ukraine – much of which comes from Russia via Hungary and Slovakia. The EU writes cheques to Kiev. Kiev pays Hungary and Slovakia, who then pay Moscow.
Those middlemen exist mainly so that Queen Ursula can maintain a certain public image while engaging in more practical considerations behind the scenes, albeit at considerably greater expense to the European taxpayer.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney got a taste of the spectacle when Ursula’s marketing campaign became the focus of the event. He was forced to acknowledge that he honestly didn’t give a damn what they called this new cooperation, so long as it was good for Canadians. Meanwhile, other EU leaders, like German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, had started referring to it instead as an “alliance for the future.”
But von der Leyen had already landed in Canada and continued promoting the “associate membership” label, smiling as Carney, sitting beside her, subsequently echoed the term.
Of course, all that the mental midgets are going to take away from this whole event is the intrigue over whether or not Canada is joining the EU. Spoiler alert: it isn’t. And never will. It’s not even legally possible. But this idiotic intrigue is distracting from the details of what lurks underneath, which could amount to a whole lot of iron-fisting through velvet gloves.
Turns out someone had already leaked a draft statement on these future relations to Politico, dated September 22, 2026. Cut out the diplomatic fluff and here’s what you’re left with.
Both sides are clearly looking for new markets as they diversify trade away from the US. Great. But it seems rather stupid for the EU to be begging Canada for its natural resources – gas, metals and minerals – while simultaneously slapping on carbon tariffs that get downloaded onto European citizens and companies. What’s the point of trying to bring prices down by increasing supply if you’re just going to top up the cost anyway.
You jokers also killed off your own nuclear industries, only to realize (a bit late) that perhaps it was preferable to having to resort to coal, before subsequently reviving it as the future of clean energy. So maybe you’re not exactly the best people to be doing commie-style central planning.
Technology is already advancing in favor of the environment, with those improvements increasingly built into the conditions for funding and financing. Just let it breathe already. Not every industry needs a Brussels bureaucrat hovering over it.
It also sounds like they’ve roped Canada into their scheme to skim Russian cash from its Western-held assets to pimp themselves out under the pretext of Ukraine’s defence and their own, then just hope that Russia’s ultimately cool with that so they don’t have to stick their own taxpayers either the final bill.
Perhaps the most troubling part is the Orwellian digital cooperation section of the agreement, which aims to “advance cooperation on artificial intelligence security and sovereignty, trusted data flows and digital governance and to align emerging AI and digital regulatory frameworks through associated country status for Canada.”
Does this mean Canadians get to have Queen Ursula block their bank accounts now, too, since we’ll all be connected and harmonized inside one giant digital panopticon? Or worse, some AI bot? It’s hardly reassuring that Carney’s government has just appealed the federal court decision condemning his predecessor Justin Trudeau’s government for unconstitutionally invoking the Emergencies Act, which allowed it to block the bank accounts of Covid-era anti-mandate Freedom Convoy participants without a court order – all for the crime of honking too loudly. Nor is it reassuring that Canada and the EU have already signed an agreement on digital “trust services” involving things like government-controlled digital identity wallets.
One honk too many, one wrong opinion on some social media platform linked to the online ID system that they’re all ushering in – ostensibly under the pretext of adults needing to prove that they aren’t children requiring protection from online pedos – and there goes your whole life with the flip of a switch. It’s not like Queen Ursula’s European Commission isn’t already doing that with sanctions and asset freezes, in the absence of due process, for those whose views it qualifies as “propaganda.”
And if this is what they mean by an alliance for the future, then Canadians – the average citizens of this country – need full and open debate over the fine print before anyone signs us up.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Zelensky: 500 Patriot interceptors could provide Ukraine with strong defense this winter

Zelensky: 500 Patriot interceptors could provide Ukraine with strong defense this winter
The President of Ukraine made the statement in a post on Telegram, Ukrinform reports.
“Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defense package. However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS. We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” he wrote.
Zelensky noted that Russia is striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure every day. In the last two weeks of October alone, there have been more than 30 Russian strikes on critical parts of Ukraine’s energy grid. Now, on the eve of winter, Putin has begun carrying out his strike campaign against the essential services that sustain Ukrainian cities and communities. The targets are electricity, heating, water supply, bridges and life in the cities in general.
“We did ask our American partners to provide Ukraine with a winter support package – at a rate of 100 Patriot interceptors per month. Five hundred missiles would be enough to protect our skies over the coming months – precisely when it is so important for Ukraine to be in a strong position in negotiations and for Russia NOT to succeed in breaking life in Ukrainian cities and communities,” the head of state said.
He recalled that the United States, European countries and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors: “Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach. And it is entirely feasible.”
Zelensky expressed gratitude to President Trump, the State Department and the U.S. administration as a whole for the authorization.
“But we are asking for decisions that can guarantee the protection of lives not the day after tomorrow or sometime later, but at the very moment the threat is there – when Russia is killing and destroying. I thank everyone who stands with Ukraine!” the President concluded.

articles.title: Trump may order major Iran strike if Republicans suffer losses in midterm election: Report
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump may be more inclined to approve a large-scale military operation against Iran if Republicans fare badly in the midterm elections next week, according to a report on Friday.
“If he feels embarrassed or disenfranchised, he will do something bold,” a US official told Axios, adding that it is the message being passed to Iranian officials, who are being told their best chance for a deal is now.
A White House official rejected the idea, telling the outlet that election results will not factor into Trump’s decisions on Iran.
The report said Qatari mediators spent more than 12 hours on Friday in Tehran, staying in regular contact with the White House, to restart direct talks between Washington and Tehran. A diplomatic source described “positive progress,” and discussions are due to continue Saturday in Doha.

Pointing to divisions within Trump’s circle, the report said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are skeptical of any deal and favor further weakening of Iran’s leadership. Vice President JD Vance and envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner back resuming talks.
The report comes amid heightened tensions between Iran and the US over the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway for global energy shipments.

Despite subsequent diplomatic efforts and a memorandum signed by Washington and Tehran in June, tensions have persisted over security arrangements and navigation through the strait.

articles.title: FLEX L12 “forest monster” makes autonomous debut with 5-ton load
articles.body:
- UGV Defence’s FLEX L12 drove a 1.7 km off-road course fully autonomously with 5 tons of cargo at Norway’s Camp Rødsmoen on Oct. 29.
- About 100 participants, mainly from the Norwegian and Swedish armed forces, saw the demo alongside partners including Kongsberg and BAE Systems.
Norwegian company UGV Defence has run its FLEX L12 heavy unmanned ground vehicle fully autonomously through a 1.7 km (1.1-mile) off-road course while carrying 5 metric tons (11,000 pounds) of cargo, in a demonstration for Nordic military officers at Camp Rødsmoen in Norway, Chief Executive Carl Ivarsson said on social media.
The tracked vehicle climbed steep inclines and drove through mud, water, large rocks, narrow passages and sharp turns without a driver, Ivarsson said. About 100 people attended the event on Oct. 29, mainly from the Norwegian and Swedish armed forces along with defense industry representatives.
UGV Defence used the day to present what it calls the Nordic Autonomous Mission Platform, a group of companies building equipment around the FLEX L12. The partners include Kongsberg, BAE Systems, Swedish sideloader maker Hammar, Safe-Tec, SKJOLDR and Nordic Shelter. Each company explained how the vehicle could support its products, and several showed their own systems at the event, though Ivarsson did not say which payloads were demonstrated on the vehicle.
“The feedback from defence and industry representatives was very encouraging. More importantly, the day demonstrated what can be achieved when leading Nordic defence companies bring together their expertise around a common autonomous platform,” said Ivarsson.
The FLEX L12 is far larger than most unmanned ground vehicles in service. Its L12-L cargo version is rated for up to 12 tons of payload, and a power-generation variant, the L12-P, carries up to 9 tons with a much larger battery. The vehicle uses a diesel-electric drive, has a top speed of 25 km/h (16 mph) and a stated range of up to 800 km (500 miles), the company said when it showed a civilian version at the DALO Industry Days exhibition in Denmark in August. By comparison, Ukraine’s Protector, one of the largest ground drones in Ukrainian service, weighs about 4 tons in total.
UGV Defence built the FLEX L12 on a civilian tracked carrier and has been reworking it for military use, with a military configuration being prepared for series production. The company has said on its website that deliveries of the FLEX L12-L cargo version are planned from the first quarter of 2027, and it has described possible uses including cargo transport, weapons integration and mobile power generation.
Rødsmoen, near Rena in eastern Norway, is a Norwegian Army camp, and the surrounding training area has hosted earlier unmanned vehicle trials, including a 10-day European Defence Agency test of armed ground robots in February.

articles.title: SSU detains suspect accused of guiding Russian strikes on defense plants and military units in Khmelnytskyi region

SSU detains suspect accused of guiding Russian strikes on defense plants and military units in Khmelnytskyi region
As reported by Ukrinform, the SSU said this in a statement.

According to investigators, in preparation for the attacks, he “walked around the regional center and its outskirts, where, under the guise of making phone calls, he filmed the locations of potential ‘targets.’”
SSU officers detained the suspect while he was conducting additional reconnaissance near one of the strategically important facilities.
“It has been established that the agent carried out assignments from the FSB after being recruited as a local unemployed man who had previously been convicted of drug possession. He came to the attention of the Russian intelligence service while looking for work through Telegram channels. After being recruited, he tracked the locations of defense industry enterprises and the permanent deployment sites of Ukrainian troops. He then ‘switched’ to identifying the coordinates of logistics hubs and sorting terminals operated by postal companies. He stored the data he collected on his smartphone in the form of marked locations on electronic maps,” the SSU said.
According to the SSU, a mobile phone containing evidence of his work for Russia was found during searches of the suspect's premises.
SSU investigators served the man with a notice of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law).
The suspect is being held in custody. He faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.

Pentagon’s Top Military Planner Reportedly Fired After Admitting Ukraine and Iran Leaks
The Pentagon’s top military planner admitted to leaking classified information about Ukraine and Iran to two reporters from separate outlets over roughly a year, Axios reported on October 30.
Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was fired this week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the alleged disclosures, which a US official told Axios Sylvia acknowledged on video after failing four polygraph tests.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
An internal Pentagon report accused Sylvia of making “unauthorized disclosures to the media” and noted that he cooperated with investigators, including by providing his personal phone for forensic examination. The investigation was conducted by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations.
The report stated that Sylvia’s contacts with reporters began as early as June 2025 and continued through Signal and in-person meetings. In one case, he met a reporter at a Silver Diner in Arlington, Virginia, after the journalist’s Pentagon access had been revoked.
During that meeting, Sylvia allegedly relied on notes taken while reviewing a classified secret report and verbally disclosed information on US assistance to Ukraine, according to Axios. The reporter was writing a book and met Sylvia twice.
The report noted that Sylvia did not coordinate the meetings with the Pentagon’s Public Affairs Office or seek review of the information before providing it to the reporter.
Investigators also examined Sylvia’s Signal communications with another reporter. The report stated that Sylvia received messages believed to concern Iran and later deleted the entire message thread, removing records of Signal messages and calls from his personal phone.
US officials told Axios they suspected the deletion was intentional, while Sylvia maintained that he believed he had erased the thread accidentally.
The report further stated that Sylvia admitted being one of 20 officials cited in another story criticizing Pentagon leadership.
Another US official told Axios that Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle’s office had pushed the Joint Staff to release a statement supporting Sylvia before the reason for his dismissal became known internally. An Army official disputed that account, calling it “a coordinated campaign of lies” and stating that Telle’s office had not advocated for such a statement.
Sylvia’s dismissal comes amid a wider Pentagon crackdown on unauthorized disclosures. In July, the Defense Department announced a joint task force with the Justice Department aimed at identifying leakers and prioritizing prosecutions for unauthorized disclosures to the media, Axios reported.
Sylvia’s firing comes as Hegseth is separately withholding approval for a major transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine. The missiles have already been paid for by Ukraine’s allies, but their delivery remains pending authorization from the US Defense Department.

articles.title: Dockworkers launch global strike against Israeli and US military shipments (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Dockworkers launch global strike against Israeli and US military shipments (VIDEOS)
Dockworkers across five continents have launched a coordinated anti-war strike, targeting Israeli arms shipments, US military cargo, and the growing militarization of civilian ports.
Organizers say more than 25 unions are mobilizing across 113 ports in 22 countries and regions on Friday in an unprecedented international action. The campaign includes 24-hour strikes, shorter walkouts, blockades, and solidarity rallies.
Major European ports joining the action include Genoa, Marseille, Le Havre, Hamburg, Valencia, Barcelona, and Piraeus. Beyond Europe, protests are planned at Tangier Med in Morocco, Nhava Sheva and Chennai in India, and Oakland and San Francisco in the US, with further actions across Türkiye, Cyprus, Sweden, Denmark, Ireland, Portugal, Brazil, Mexico, and Australia.
France’s CGT Ports et Docks has called 24-hour strikes across 24 ports, while Italy’s USB has declared a nationwide general strike, with protests in more than 40 cities. Unions in Germany, Greece, Spain, India, and the US are also taking part.
Dockworkers at the port of Piraeus, Greece, walked off the job as part of a global day of action, with protesters in more than 100 ports worldwide striking against the arms trade with Israel.

— Press TV 🔻 (@PressTV) October 30, 2026
Dockworkers at Piraeus, Greece’s largest port, were among the first to join the action, with a three-hour stoppage scheduled from 08:00 to 11:00 GMT. Other Greek maritime unions announced 24-hour strikes affecting seven ports, threatening ferry services to the country’s islands.
Dockworkers across 21 major ports in Europe and the Mediterranean shut down operations in a coordinated day of action. Under the call “Port Workers Do Not Work for War,” 
They blocked arms shipments and demanded a full trade and arms embargo on Israel. pic.twitter.com/43Srp1pYE5
— The Resonance (@Partisan_12) February 7, 2026
Videos of demonstrations and gatherings at other ports have emerged online, although the full extent of the disruption to shipping operations remains unclear as actions are taking place at different times.
What do the dockworkers want?
The unions demand a halt to weapons, ammunition, military equipment, and troop shipments through commercial ports, targeting both Israeli and US military supply chains. They also oppose turning civilian ports into military hubs and diverting public funds into rearmament while workers face stagnant wages, job insecurity, and worsening conditions.
Protesters gather outside Tilbury Docks in the UK, urging dockworkers to join an international mobilisation involving over 100 ports in solidarity with Palestine and against arms shipments to Israel. pic.twitter.com/7fulNOmU82
— IP VOICES (@ipvoices1) October 30, 2026
“From planes to tanks, guns to bullets, explosives to ammunition, uniforms to boots, our ports have become replenishing and forwarding bases for war and genocide,” the organizers said at a press conference on October 15 in Rome.

The unions accused governments and shipping companies of keeping military supply routes open despite the Gaza ceasefire announced over a year ago, which they say has been rendered largely meaningless by continued Israeli strikes.
‘No Harbour for Genocide’, the campaign coordinating the action, claims that it tracked 315 shipments of components for Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems through 56 ports in 29 countries over 14 months. It says it identified 3,400 shipments of US military cargo through 67 ports in 42 countries over ten months. The group also says US military cargo volumes at some European ports rose as much as tenfold following the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran. The figures have not been independently verified.
Organizers estimate the action could delay 40,000 containers carrying cargo worth over $2 billion, potentially costing shipping companies up to $43 million.
Is it the first strike of this kind?
Dockworkers have challenged military shipments for years, though resistance was largely scattered and localized. Since 2019, workers in Italy, Greece, Morocco, and France have staged sporadic blockades and stoppages, targeting arms shipments to Israel, US bases, and other conflict zones.
The movement gained momentum in late 2025 after Israel intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla, a 40-plus-vessel convoy attempting to deliver aid to blockaded Gaza. Hundreds of activists were detained, sparking strikes and port blockades across Europe. The flotilla campaign also pledged to join the action on Friday with “coordinated, strategic actions on the water.”
100+ PORTS. WORLDWIDE. NO MORE WEAPONS.
On October 30th, dockworkers, seafarers, students and communities in more than 100 ports around the world are standing together to say one thing: NO MORE WEAPONS.

International coordination intensified in February, when dockworkers at more than 20 ports across seven countries staged their first joint day of action, reportedly stopping five suspect ships.

In May, dockworkers’ unions from France, Greece, Italy, Türkiye, Morocco, and Spain’s Basque Country adopted the Istanbul Declaration, in which they pledged to block military cargo and troop shipments to war zones, including those supporting Israel and US military operations. The agreement laid the groundwork for Friday’s global strike.

On Thursday, the coalition said its air defenses had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward the capital, Riyadh.
The Houthis have also claimed responsibility for a series of attacks targeting Saudi oil facilities, airports and military installations in recent days.
The Saudi-led coalition intervened in Yemen in March 2015 to support the internationally recognized government against the Houthis, who have controlled the capital, Sanaa, since September 2014.

articles.title: Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point claims to have overcome Starlink restrictions for long-range strikes – Reuters
articles.body:
Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point claims to have overcome Starlink restrictions for long-range strikes – Reuters
Iryna Terekh, CEO of Ukrainian missile and drone manufacturer Fire Point, says the company has found a way of delivering long-range strikes in Russia and Russian-occupied territories without relying on Starlink satellite communications.
Source: Terekh in an interview with Reuters
Details: Terekh said the company has found workarounds that allow it to conduct strikes without using satellite communications.
Quote: "We have built with this in mind. Fire Point systems are designed to finish a mission without a satellite link. Navigation that works without any external signal is a priority."
Details: Terekh declined to disclose details of the solutions.
Quote: "We found a way to technologically overcome this challenge, but this only covers probably 15 to 20% of what we could do if the Starlink was working (over Russia)."
Background:
- On 19 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Starlink and Starshield equipment had stopped working at speeds of 130-161 km/h in various sectors of the front line, disrupting logistics and limiting Ukraine's use of drones.
- On 21 October, after news of the slowdown became public, SpaceX owner Elon Musk tweeted: "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
- According to The Wall Street Journal, Musk ordered the slowdown for the military version of Starlink for Ukraine, which made some Ukrainian strike drones and interceptor drones practically unusable.
- On 22 October, the WSJ reported that US President Donald Trump had allegedly called Elon Musk and asked him to lift the restrictions on Starshield in Ukraine.
- On 24 October, Musk commented on the Starlink restrictions, claiming that the Ukrainian military had violated the terms of use for this type of communications system. He also said that if Starlink were switched off, "the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately".
- Zelenskyy said he believes that the publicity surrounding the connection restrictions helped to restore the Starlink system's operation to the required speed.
